speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS. APPOINTMENT OF TRANSLATORS.
speechtext: That the recommendation of His Honour the Speaker as to the appointment of Mr. J. A. D'Astous, as a reviser of translation, and Mr. Henri Trudel,' as translator, on the Debates staff of the House, presented to the House on the 6th inst., be concurred in.

maintopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS. APPOINTMENT OF TRANSLATORS.
speechtext:
Before this motion is
adopted I wish to reiterate the protest I made last night, ot early this morning, not against Mr. Trudel or Mr. D'Astous, but against the mode of procedure. I claim that the appointments ought to he on merit, and ought to be made by the 3321
Debates Committee. And while this motion may be adopted I wish to enter my protest against the mode of the -selection of the candidates.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS. APPOINTMENT OF TRANSLATORS.
speechtext: As I understand it, these appointments must lbe made according to the Civil -Service Act in the usual way, as we are doing now. ISince that A-ct came into force it is not under the control of any committee of the House to make such appointments.

maintopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS. APPOINTMENT OF TRANSLATORS.
speechtext:
The examination -and
selection of the candidate should have been made by the Debates Committee in this case, but that committee has been completely ignored; therefore we have poor translation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS. APPOINTMENT OF TRANSLATORS.
speechtext: I have no personal knowledge of the circumstances attending the appointments of these -gentlemen, but 1 understand they have been made in accordance with the provisions of the Civil -Service Act. If theTe is any objection based on the view that the provisions of that Act have not been complied with, that would be good ground for it. The Civil Service A-ct does not give power of appointment to the Debates Committee. The appointment, of employees of the Senate and th-e House of Commons has to be made under the Act. The Act was amended in that respect, I think, by the late Administration.	.

maintopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS. APPOINTMENT OF TRANSLATORS.
speechtext:
The report which has been placed before th-e House is in these -terms:
I have the honour to report that provision having been made for the appointment of a reviser of translation of the Debates translation staff of the House and of an additional translator on the same staff, and the Civil Service Commission having held an examination of persons applying for qualifying certificates for such positions. M. J. A. D'Astous and M. Henri Trudel have been presented with the required certificates from the commission. The work attached to these positions is of an exceptional character and the certificates are based upon that fact and the sum of two hundred dollars each is added to the initial salary of these officials, who are to be graded in subdivision A of the second division as provided by the organization of this - branch of the service of the House. [DOT]
I must take exception to this report. The work which is done by -the gentlemen who are to be appointed is not of a special character. It is the work of translating the debates of this House, a work which

has been going on for the last twenty-years. There is nothing special in that; it is work o,f an ordinary character. The initial salary, which, I understand- because I am not familiar with the Civil Service Act-is paid in subdivision A of ' the second division, is $1,600. These gentlemen are, upon entering, to get $1,800. This is a distinct discrimination against those longer in the service. One of the former appointees wias employed nnder exactly similar circumstances, and came on at $1,600 a year; and there can be no reason at all why this discrimination should be made. It it is intended that these gentlemen should receive $1,800 it is not fair to the others that they should not receive the same and the consequential annual increase of salaries as well. Neither is it fair that these gentlemen should be placed at once on the same basis. If they receive the benefit of a larger salary the same privilege should be allowed to those already in the service.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS. APPOINTMENT OF TRANSLATORS.
speechtext:
Occasionally there has
been in the House some criticism of the manner in which the translation is conducted, not so much perhaps as regards the debates as with regard to the official records of the House. It is desirable that this work should ;be well done, and it appears that it is difficult, if not impossible, to get men to undertake the work for a smaller remuneration. As a matter of fact, I think there is no one on the staff who enjoys a salary of less than $1,800, and I am informed that the salaries range from $1,800 to $2,650; and the two gentlemen now to be appointed, one a reviser of translation, and the other an additional translator, will be called upon to perform exactly the same work as is performed by the other members of the staff. We have the report of the proper officer of the House that the work attached to these positions is of an exceptional character, and under the circumstances it does not seem to me that there is any legitimate ground for objection.

maintopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS. APPOINTMENT OF TRANSLATORS.
speechtext:
My objection is not so much against the amount to be paid to the new translators as it is against the mode of their appointment. A gentleman who is quite new in translation work *is appointed chief, whereas there are many persons on the staff who deserve that appointment by right of seniority. Although translation work is not of an exceptional character, yet, in my judgment, it is quite complex; we have only to look at the French 'Han-

sard' to see how difficult it is to translate English into French. What I complain of is that an outside influence seems to be exerted and that appointments are made which, in the judgment of those who happen to know a little about French translation, should not be made.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS. APPOINTMENT OF TRANSLATORS.
speechtext: That the recommendation of His Honour the Speaker as to the appointment of Messrs. Frangois Armand Terrault and Joseph Wilfrid Barii, as translators on the blue-book staff of the House, be concurred in.

maintopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS. APPOINTMENT OF TRANSLATORS.
speechtext: There can be no objection to this motion and to accepting the report that has been made, but this shows the force of the objection which I made with regard to the other appointments. In one case two gentlemen who are to be translators are appointed at the salaries provided by the statute, and in the other case the terms of the law which provide that the minimum salary shall be $1,600 are directly set aside and an additional amount of $200 given. It seems to me that there can be no other opinion than that this must be done simply through outside influence. Why should a man who is a translator on one staff be better paid than a man who is a translator on the other staff? The work of translating ' Hansard' is precisely the same as the work of translating the blue-books and I do not think that two employees should he paid $200 a year more than the law allows them while the others are regularly appointed under the law.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS. APPOINTMENT OF TRANSLATORS.
speechtext:
To the assertion that
somehow outside influence is being exercised I give an emphatic denial; the matter has been arranged solely between the Civil Service Commission and myself. With regard to the two men who receive $200 more than the minimum, this was due to the fact that one of the men has had long experience in newspaper work and is regarded as an exceptionally good man to act as revisor of translation. The weak feature of the work appeared to be that the translations were being sent to the Bureau without revision, and a suitable man was required as revisor. This man was temporarily put on the staff, and in view of his long experience in that line and of the assurance that he is exceptionally clever, I advised that he be appointed

as revisor. With regard to the man who is appointed as acting chief, it was a question as between himself and Mr. Lasalle. Mr. Lasalle is well up in years; he has been on the sick-list for two or three years, and an assistant has been doing the work. It does not. appear to me that in reorganizing the staff it woulid be desirable to put a man of his years at the head of it, especially in view of the fact that the certificate of his doctor states that he may be permanently disabled at any time. As to Mr. Trudel, I consulted the commissioners and got the very best recommendation I could get, and T thought it was the proper thing to put him there for the time being. The two men for the blue-book staff have passed the examination in the ordinary way, and, of course, start at the minimum of their class.

I do not doubt the qualifications of these men, nor am I jealous of the salary which they are receiving, but the law provides that men who go into that class, whether better or less qualified, shall get a certain minimum salary. That is the law, and the law should be observed. It cannot be conceived that the other men in the service will accept this as fair; there is no reason why the law should be followed in the one case and not in the other.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is a provision in the Civil Service Act to the effect that where the man to be appointed is to do work of a special or technical character, the amount of the salary may be increased up to $500 above the minimum. As the man who previously occupied the position of chief received $2,100, it seemed to me that as this man had been doing the work for a long time and had been giving evidences of the highest qualifications, it was at least reasonable to recommend an increase of $200 instead of $500. No person on the staff receives a lower salary than $1,800; the salaries range from $1,800 to $2,600 or $2,750.
Mr. LEM1EUX:	I cannot let pass, the
*opinion expressed by Your Honour with regard to the qualifications of Mr. Lasalle as compared with the qualifications of Mr. Trudel. I say most emphatically that Mr. Lasalle is one of the ablest men on the translation staff. Beside,, by right of seniority, he ought to have been appointed chief officer. Your Honour says that Mr. Trudel is much younger, and that he is qualified; with that I fully concur. Your Honour adds that Mr. Lasalle is disabled. It is true that he has suffered from rheumatism owing to the strain of writing continuously for thirty years, but if we were to give promotions over senior officers for similar reasons in other cases, what consequences would follow? Take the editorial staff of a paper.
A young man of twenty may come in as a reporter. He is young and physically very healthy and so on, and according to the opinion of your honour he would immediately take the place of the old editor who had been writing the leader i and editorials because, forsooth, the editor might be disabled. The translation work on the ' Hansard ' as well as in a newpaper office is done not only with the hands but with the brain, and for that reason I claim that Mr. Lasalle and many others with their experience are better equipped .for this transcript work than any new young man who might be appointed to the staff.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Civil Service Act
makes express provision for the slight increase of salary alluded to. Section 33 of the Civil Service Act declares, in the first place, that every person appointed to a particular class must be appointed at the minimum of that class. Each class has a range of about $600. But it also provides that if the work is of an exceptional character, and if the Civil Service Commissioner certifies that the person to be appointed possesses the exceptional qualities alluded to, then he may be appointed at a higher salary than the minimum; but in no case at more than $500 in excess of the minimum. The procedure in this case is not in defiance of the Civil Service Act, but under the Civil .Service Act, and in accordance with its terms, the proper officers of this House and his honour the Speaker having concurred in the recommendation.	As far as any
extraneous influence respecting this or any other case is concerned, I never heard of it. I have not the pleasure of knowing either of these gentlemen or anything of their records. I know nothing of the record of any of the members of the translation staff. Mr. Lasalle has been referred to. The Speaker commends him as a very good officer, but he has spoken of his unfortunate disability and the frequent necessity of his absence from duty. Under those circumstances I think it will be agreed

that in the public interest such an appointment could not be made. There is not the slightest desire to discriminate against any one, but to promote the interests of the service in this particular branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I know the two gentlemen whose names have been mentioned in connection with the office of chief of the translators of the ' Hansard,' Mr. Trudel and Mr. Lasalle. I had an interview with you, Mr. Speaker, in your office about this matter. I gave to your honour the reason why I think that Mr. Lasalle should have been made chief of the translators. Mr. Trudel is a new member of the staff, while Mr. Lasalle is one of the oldest members. I ^annot see why Mr. Trudel should be appointed chief. I am sure that Mr. Trudel, although he is a good and excellent translator, is not as good as Mr. Lasalle, who has had a great deal of experience. He is not disabled at all.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I know. I have been in his room many times. Last year, and the year before I asked him to try to have the Government pay the services of a stenographer for him. Mr. Lasalle has paid for one out of his own pocket. He has employed this stenographer because, as the hon. member for Rouville has said, he has some slight rheumatism in his right arm and so can not write all day long, although he can write for a quarter of an hour at a time. That is a further reason why he should be appointed chief of the translators. He is one of the best among the best of the translators, and I feel that it is an injustice, although I do not mean to say that you realize it, not knowing the two men as I know them. I feel that an injustice which is being committed against Mr. Lasalle for no reason whatever.

'And towards the
Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It is difficult to-day for us to find competent translators who will consent to come on our staff for $1600 a year. There are two classes of translators, who although they are doing the same class of work they are paid on two different scales and I think this is unjust. One class is composed of men whose salary starts at $2100 and goes up to $2800. The other class is composed of only one man, Mr. Desaulniers, whose salary started at $1600

and by yearly increases has now advanced to $1750. There is no reason why there should be two classes. That is the reason why I believe it is almost impossible to find competent translators who will come on the staff at $1600 a year. It is possibly for that reason that an injustice is now being committed as it is sought to give an extra $200 by this means to the new man. If the new men could receive the salaries which the others have received from the start there would be no question of taking the chiefship from Mr. Lasalle or any of the older members.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There appears to be a
misunderstanding on the part of some of those who have spoken, because they are proceeding on the assumption that Mr. Trudel has been appointed chief. He has not been appointed chief but he is doing the work of the chief.
I do not see why a chief is not appointed.

I mentioned last night
the case of Mr. Desaulniers who is the only one in the inferior class and I am corroborated this morning by the statement of the Secretary of State. Mr. Desaulniers has been on the staff since 1909. He eame on at $1600 a year and is now receiving $1750 or $1800. I do not see any reason why he should not be put in the higher class and receive the initial salary of $2100.

I agree absolutely with the remarks that have just been made by the Hoij. the Secretary o.f State. I have known Mr. Lasalle for many years. He was long ago admitted t-o the bar; while he practised he was a distinguished advocate, and I have never' lost sight of him. He is a man of high intelligence, with the best education and .the greatest competence for his work, and he is temperate and hardworking, therefore he certainly merits promotion. Why is a branch .so important as this without a chief? It formerly had a chief; why ie not another appointed ? Everybody knows that in every department properly organised it is necessary to have a chief, a directing head, to supervise the work. Why not appoint Mr. Lasalle to this position? He is not a political 'friend of mine, for he is a Conservative, but he has eminent qualities to fit him for that position. I hope that Mr. Speaker will do justice to Mr. Lasalle by appointing him to it.

Some of the remarks that have heen made are certainly very appropriate, and, ae a member of the Commission on Internal Economy, I think it my duty to bring to the attention of the Speaker and the members of the commission representations which have been made and which certainly deserve consideration.
Motion agreed to.

maintopic: ADDRESS TO HIS ROYAL HIGHNESS THE GOVERNOR GENERAL.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ADDRESS TO HIS ROYAL HIGHNESS THE GOVERNOR GENERAL.
speechtext:
The approaching departure of His Royal Highness the Governor General in the month of October next makes it appropriate that reference should be made in this House to his services as representative of the Crown in this Dominion.
The Crown personifies the power and majesty of the Empire and thus the Crown also personifies its unity. With the growth and development of the overseas dominions the powers and responsibilities of their parliaments have continually increased, so that in a certain sense and within certain limitations the Empire is to-day a federation of sister nations united by the ties of a common and undivided allegiance. We have been fortunate from the first in the selection of men who have been called
upon to fill the office of Governor General. They also have been fortunate in their association with this country during a most interesting and important period of its history. While they have seen wonderful material progress, they have also witnessed important constitutional growth and development.
Nearly three years ago the Duke of Connaught came to our shores as Governor General of Canada. It was by no means his first visit to this country, for he had served with his regiment at Montreal when this Dominion was in its earliest infancy and before the progress and development of later years had set their indelible mark upon its history. His Royal Highness had visited Canada in the meantime, but coming here as Governor General he has	had	unequalled	opportunities ofstudying and understanding all that has been accomplished in the great march of events since the days of 1870. He brought with him the record of a distinguished and honourable career in the public service as	soldier and	as	diplomat. Thatcareer had enabled him to know and to realize	the	empire,	to	comprehend itswonderful power and its still more wonderful possibilities, and to understand the forces	that	serve	to	unite its vast
dominions in one allegiance.
I have spoken of the career and the record of the Duke of Connaught. I am convinced that his course as constitutional representative of His Majesty in this country will add additional lustre to that record. He undertook the great responsibilities of the office which he now holds at the personal request of His late Majesty King Edward VII, whose high example in devotion to duty and in the constitutional discharge of the responsibilities of the Crown has found its counterpart in the course which His Royal Highness has pursued as Governor General of this Dominion.
His Royal Highness has availed himself to the fullest extent of the opportunities which have been afforded him of noting and studying the conditions of our national life and of observing and understanding the ideals and aspirations by which it is animated. The great extent of our territory, the vastness of the distances to be traversed, and the varying conditions which prevail in different portions of the Dominion have made this a great task. To accomplish all that he desired His Royal Highness has not spared himself; and he may be assured that his visits will be held- in

happy remembrance by our people in every province from the Atlantic to the Pacific. He has associated himself with sympathy and, indeed, with enthusiasm in all that would advance the future of our country, and as to that future he has been an optimist amidst a nation of optimists.
It was with the deepest regret that more than a year ago the people of Canada learned of the serious illness of Her Royal Highness the Duchess of Connaught, who has taken the keenest interest in all that tends to the welfare and* advancement of the country, and whose most earnest desire to be in every way helpful to the Governor General in the discharge of his official duties has always made itself most clearly manifest. In offering our very sincere congratulations that Her Royal Highness has made such splendid progress to complete recovery of her health, we trust that she and the Princess Patricia, whose equal tact and graciousness have also endeared her to our people, may retain the kindest remembrance of their sojourn in this Dominion.
In saying farewell to His Royal Highness we hope that many years of active service to the empire lie before him, and that in the years to come his association with this country will recall to him, as it will to the Canadian people, the happiest memories.
Therefore, I have very great pleasure in moving, seconded by the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that the following address be presented to His Royal Highness:
To Field Marshal His Royal Highness Prince Arthur William Patrick Albert, Duke of Connaught and of Strathearn ; Earl of Sussex (in the Peerage of the United Kingdom) ; Prince of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland; Duke of Saxony ; Prince of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha; Knight of the Most Noble Order of the Garter; Knight of the Most Ancient and Most Noble Order of the Thistle; Knight of the Most Illustrious Order of Saint Patrick; one of His Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council; Great Master of the Most 'Honourable Order of the Bath ; Knight Grand Commander of the Most Exalted Order of the Star of India; Knight Grand Cross of the Most Distinguished Order of Saint Michael and Saint George; Knight Grand Commander of the Most Eminent Order of the Indian Empire; Knight Grand Cross of the Royal Victorian Order; His Majesty's Personal Aide-de-Camp; Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of the Dominion of Canada.
May it Please Your Royal Highness:
We, His Majesty's dutiful and loyal subjects, the Members of the Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled, desire to approach Your Royal Highness with an expression of the deep regret with which we have learned that your 
official connection with this country is about to cease.
We beg to assure Your Royal Highness of the deep appreciation with which we have witnessed your assiduous care over the affairs of the Dominion as His Majesty's representative in the high office of Governor General.
In visiting every portion of our Dominion, and in the earnest endeavour to acquire by personal contact with all classes of the community a full and accurate knowledge of the varied conditions prevailing in this country, and of the purpose and aspirations which animate our national life, Your Royal Highness has but given another evidence of that high devotion to duty which has always inspired your actions and has ever been associated with your career.
The Canadian people will not fail to cherish a happy remembrance of the deep and practical interest which Your Royal Highness has invariably manifested in literature, art and industrial pursuits in the Dominion, as well as in all philanthropic and charitable undertakings; and they recognize most fully that Your Royal Highness has always been ready to associate yourself with every movement designed to improve the conditions and add to the happiness of those to whom has been entrusted the great task and duty of possessing and developing this portion of the empire.
Any acknowledgment of Your Royal Highness's important services in this regard would be incomplete if it should omit to recognize the gracious and kindly co-operation of the Duchess of Connaught, whose prolonged illness brought to each member of the community a sense of deep and personal concern. We share with Your. Royal Highness and the members of your family the happiness of welcoming back to health one whose name will ever suggest to to our people all that is dignified in her exalted station, and all that is gracious in private life.
In the appointment of Your Royal Highness we have not failed to perceive our Sovereign's recognition of the growing importance of this Dominion and of his solicitude for all that concerns its welfare.
We venture to hope that when Your Royal Highness resigns your trust into the hands of the King, you will assure His Majesty of the unalterable loyalty and devotion of the Canadian people to His Majesty's Throne and person, of their abiding affection for the motherland and of their firm resolve to accomplish their part in the maintenance and upbuilding of our great empire.
We trust that Your Royal Highness may have many years of usefulness before you in which to continue your work on behalf of that empire and that you will preserve in the years to come a kindly recollection of Canada and its people.
In bidding farewell to Your Royal Highness and to the Duchess of Connaught and the Princess Patricia, we are privileged to tender on behalf of the Canadian people our warmest wishes for your future welfare and happiness.

maintopic: ADDRESS TO HIS ROYAL HIGHNESS THE GOVERNOR GENERAL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be ungrateful on the part of the Canadian people if they did not, in every possible way open to them, testify to the deep regret which must be caused by the early departure of His Royal Highness the Duke of Connaught. This regret arises

not so much from the fact that we are going to lose the services of one of the Royal family, a Prince of the blood, hut from an even higher cause; for we realize that in losing the services of the Duke of Connaught we lose the services of one who since he has been amongst us has proved himself a man in the truest sense of the word.
Our people are, above all things, a democratic people. There are evidences not a few which go to show that titles, decorations, pageants, ceremonies and the append-ances of royalty do little if anything towards increasing the respect for the Crown which is felt in this as well as in other parts of the British possessions; but the Canadian people were deeply touched to find in this scion of a long line of kings all those domestic virtues and those unobtrusive and solid qualities which, after all, are acknowledged to be the soundest in the human race. They were deeply touched to find that His Royal Highness on all occasions was easily approachable, simple, and considerate, ever willing to oblige and ever the first to forget the high rank to which he had been born. Certainly it can ibe said with perfect truth that they were more than moved by the cordial frankness and the invariable kindliness with which he performed the duties of his high office of whatever kind they may have been.
If there is one thing more than another which has impressed the mind of the Canadian people, it is the quality that has been touched upon by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden)-the unswerving devotion to duty that has characterized the career of his Royal Highness amongst us. It was his evident desire, from the day that he landed in Canada, to discharge the duties of the office to which he had been called in no perfunctory way, but with cheerfulness and alacrity, sparing no pains to obtain the ibest results both for Crown and people. Within the short space that was allotted to him he endeavoured to visit all parts of Canada, to bring himself into contact with all classes and to take a part in all the events which constitute our national life.
The same thing, and perhaps more, should be said of Her Royal Highness the Duchess of Connaught, for the reason mat, while she, in her sphere-the sphere properly allotted to her sex-seconded as best she could the efforts of her noble spouse, she did so under the burden of constantly impaired health. Though there was an impression among many among us that
perhaps this illness was due to the rigors of our climate, Her Royal Highness has! been kind enough on more than one occasion to say that she had nothing to complain of in that respect, but that she had enjoyed her sojourn amongst us, and that she would count the years of her stay in Canada as amongst the most memorable and delightful of her life.
What has been said of the Duke and Duchess can also be said, and even with greater emphasis, of the Princess Patricia.
In these days kings and dukes, princes and princesses, have to live in the fierce glare of modern publicity, and when that searching light reveals nothing in the lives of these august personages but what is noble and elevating, no one can be blind to the fact that such an example as that exhibited by the noble lives of the Duke and Duchess oif 'Connaught must be productive of good results among the mass of the people. When the Duke and Duchess sail from our shores, they will not altogether leave us, for they will leave behind them the elevating traditions which they brought with them and which they themselves learned from that great and good woman, Queen Victoria.
I have great pleasure in seconding the motion of my tight hon. friend the Prime Minister.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.

speechtext:
Rt. Hon. R. L. BORDEN moved that the House go into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that a humble address be presented to His Majesty praying; that he may graciously be pleased to give his consent to submitting a measure to the Parliament of the United Kingdom to amend certain provisions of the British North America Act, 1867, in the manner set forth in the draft Bill hereto attached.
An Act to amend the British North America Act, 1867.
Be it enacted by the King's Most Excellent Majesty by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal and Commons, in this present Parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows:
1. Notwithstanding anything in the British North America Act, 1867, or in any Act amending the same, or in any Order in Council or terms or conditions of union made or approved under the said Acts, or in any Act of the Parliament of Canada;
(1)	The number of senators provided for by section 21 of the British North America Act, 1867, is increased from seventy-two to ninety-six.
(2)	The divisions of Canada in relation to the constitution of the Senate provided for by section 22 of the said Act, are increased from three to four, the fourth division to comprise the

western provinces, Manitoba, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta, which four divisions shall (subject to the provisions of the said Act and of this Act) be equally represented in the Senate as follows:
Ontario, by twenty-four senators; Quebec, by twenty-four senators; the Maritime provinces and Prince Edward Island, by twenty-four senators, ten thereof representing Nova Scotia, ten thereof representing New Brunswick and four thereof representing Prince Edward Island; the western provinces by twenty-four senators, six thereof representing Manitoba, six thereof representing British Columbia, six thereof representing Saskatchewan and six thereof representing Alberta.
(3)	The number of persons whom, by section 26 of the said Act, the Governor General may, upon the direction of the King, add to the Senate, is increased from three or six to four or eight, representing equally the four divisions of Canada.
(4)	In case of such addition being at any time made the Governor General shall not summon any person to the Senate, except upon a further like direction by the King on the recommendation, to represent one of the four divisions until such division is represented by twenty-four senators and no more.
(5)	The number of senators shall not at any time exceed one hundred and four.
(6)	The representation in the Senate to which, by section 147 of the British North America Act, 1867, Newfoundland will be entitled, in case of its admission into the union, is increased from four to six members; and in case of the admission of Newfoundland into the union, notwithstanding anything in the said Act, or in this Act, the normal number of senators shall be one hundred and two and their maximum number one hundred and ten.
2. The British North America Act, 1867, is amended by adding thereto the following section immediately after seotion 51 of the said Act:
(51 A) Notwithstanding anything in this Act a province shall always be entitled to a number of members in the House of Commons not less than the number of senators representing such province.
He said :
It is proper that I should make certain explanations as to this proposed resolution. There are now upon the Order Paper four Bills: one providing for an-increase in the representation iim the Senate of the province of British Columbia; another containing a like provision with regard to Alberta; another with regard to Saskatchewan; and another with regard to Manitoba. These provinces are now represented in the Senate as follows: British Columbia by three members; Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, each by four members. The provisions of the British North America Act, under which these appointments have been made and under which they are proposed to be increased, have been brought to the attention of the House in the dis-

cussion upon these Bills. So far as the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan are concerned, we are agreed on both aides of the House that the Parliament of Canr ada has the constitutional power to increase the representation in the Senate of each of these provinces from four to six, as is proposed. So far as the province of Manitoba is concerned, we are of the opinion that the Parliament of Canada has likewise the power to increase its representation in the Senate from four to six. In respect to the province of British Columbia, which is represented in the Senate at the present time by only three members, there is an agreement on both sides of the House that, for the purpose of increasing the representation of that province in the Senate, an amendment of the British North America Act will be necessary.
Under the British North America Act of 1867 it was provided that there should be three divisions in Canada in respect of the Senate, and that each of those divisions should have a representation of twenty-four members. The three divisions in the first instance were: the province of Ontario, constituting one division; the province of Quebec, constituting one division and the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, constituting one division. At that time each of the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick was represented in the Senate by twelve members; but under the provisions of the British North America Act, that representation was reduced upon the admission of the province of Prince Edward Island into Confederation; and thereafter no appointments were made in the Senate for the province of Nova Scotia or the province of New Brunswick until the representation of each of those provinces had been reduced below ten. So that at the present time the representation of the Maritime provinces stands at ten for Nov.a Scotia, ten for New Brunswick, and four for Prince Edward Island.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, in the course of the de-
12 noon, bate upon these Bills, suggested-what had occurred I dare say to some of us before-that a fourth division should be constituted, which should comprise the four western provinces of the Dominion, namely, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. He suggested to me that the better course would be this: that we should not proceed with the Bill at this session;

but that, inasmuch as legislation was necessary for the purpose of increasing the representation of the province of British Columbia in the Senate, we should accomplish that result as to all the provinces in that way; and that, further than that, we should constitute a fourth division and ask for the necessary amendment to the British North America Act for that purpose. My right hon. friend also suggested to me that he thought that, in case of the future constitution of any additional province in Canada, it was desirable that that province should be represented by not less than six members in the Senate. We have the power to deal with that under our constitution at the present time. I concurred in the view which my right hon. friend presented to me in that regard; and I suggested to him that, if that were a proper consideration in respect to any province hereafter to be constituted in Canada out of what are now territories, it would also be desirable to make a similar provision with regard to the island of Newfoundland, which may some day enter this Confederation. So far as the admission of Newfoundland into Confederation is concerned, there seems to be no present prospect of any early con-sumation of the union; and, of course, we all realize that in any case it could be brought about only on the initiative and by the free will of the people of Newfoundland, as any proposals or advances that might be made by the Parliament in Canada in that connection might be misunderstood. It is needless to say that the people of Canada would receive in a very cordial manner proposals with that end in view; but it is desirable and proper that the initiative in that regard, if any action is taken in the future, should be taken by the Government and legislature 'of Newfoundland. But, as it is a possibility which was contemplated by the British North America Act as far back as1 1867 that Newfoundland might some day enter Confederation, it would seem proper-.as it is undesirable to have frequent amendments to the British North America Act-that that contingency should be provided for now, and consequently a clause has been introduced into the Bill for that purpose.
The first section of the proposed Bill provides that the number or senators fixed for by section 21 of the British North America Act is increased from '72 to 96. The normal number of senators at the present time is 87; that is, 24 for each of the three divisions originally constituted, four for
each of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and three for the province of British Columbia. If the representation of each of these provinces is increased to six, constituting a new division represented in the Senate by 24 members, then the normal number of Senators will be 96 instead of 87, as it is at present.
Subsection 2 of the Bill provides that the divisions in Canada in relation to the constitution of the Senate shall be increased from three to four. That means the constitution of a fourth division comprising the four western provinces, as I have already explained. Subsections 3 and 4 deal with section 26 of the British North America Act, which is as follows:
If at any time, on the recommendation of the Governor General, the Queen thinks fit to direct that three or six members he added to the Senate, the Governor General may, by summons to three or six qualified persons (as the case may be), representing equally the three divisions of Canada, add to the Senate accordingly.
The provisions of these sections amount to this:	inasmuch as there is a fourth
division now to be constituted, and as it is proper that that division should have equal consideration in case the member- . ship of the Senate should 'he increased under section 26 of the British North America Act, the necessary amendment is made by these two sections for that purpose.
'Subsection 5 provides that the number of senators shall not at any time-exceed 164; that is 96 the normal number, plus eight additional senators, who may be appointed under the authority of section 26 Of the British North America Act.
Subsection 6 'provides that in case Newfoundland should enter the union it shall be represented in the Senate by six instead of by four members.
Subsection 2 of the resolution is based upon the report of the Committee on Redistribution, which recommended unanimously that the British North America Act should be amended in that respect. It provides that, notwithstanding anything in the British North America Act, a province shall always be entitled to a nuthber of members in the House of Commons. not less than the number of Senators representing such province. In speaking upon the question of redistribution in this House during the present session, attention was called by other members and by me to the incongruity of having any province of Canada represented by a smaller number of members in the House of Commons than

its representation in the Senate. That is quite possible under the British North America Act, and, in fact, it occurs to-day, because the representation of Prince Edward Island has been reduced by the result of the census of 1911 to three, whereas that province is represented in the Senate by four members. I do not think a condition of that kind can be found anywhere else in the world. As a general rule, in all legislatures which possess two branches the members in the branch elected (by popular vote outnumber the members of the appointed branch by at least two to one, and in some cases three, four and five to one. It seemed undesirable, therefore, that this condition should be permitted to continue, inasmuch as it is a condition that plainly was not foreseen or contemplated by the framers of the British North America Act.
The provision will have application at this time only to the province of Prince Edward Island. That province, as iwe know, has made strong claims that its representation ought to continue at six, the number allotted to it at the time it entered Confederation. The terms of the Order in Council under which Prince Edward Island was admitted to the Union are plain and unambiguous. That province has rested its case upon certain written communications prior to the Union, and also upon the well kpown feeling in the island at that time that the province should not enter the Union with less than six members. The Committee on Redistribution, whose report will be under consideration at a later stage to-day, have not found themselves able to recommend that the representation of Prince Edward Island shall be continued at six; but they have made this unanimous recommendation, which commends itself to my judgment, for the reasons I have already mentioned. Therefore I have embodied it in the proposed resolution, and I trust it will receive the favourable consideration of the House.
At the moment I do not know that there is any further explanation which can be offered with regard to the terms of the resolution. I trust it will be received a~s a proper measure, and one which will preclude the necessity on the part of this House and of the Senate of considering the Bills which stand upon the Order Paper, and which, in the event of the passage of this resolution, will, of course, be dropped as entirely unnecessary.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as stated by my right hon. friend (Mr. Borden), four measures have been standing on the Order Paper since the early days of the session, providing that the representation in the Senate of the four western provinces should be increased. The discussion which occurred on one or two occasions, when these Bills were called, showed that, on both sides, we were agreed as far as the two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were concerned. There can be no doubt that this Parliament as constituted has the power to increase the representation of those two provinces. With regard to the province of British Columbia, it was, I believe, also agreed on both sides, after discussion, that this Parliament had no power to add to the representation of that province. With regard to the province of Manitoba, my right hon. friend entertains the idea yet that we have porwer, but, for my part, I am sure that this Parliament has no power to increase the representation of Manitoba.
These views, divergent though they were on some points, were of minor consequence when compared with the broader principle of having some uniform legislation in regard to these provinces based upon the principle of the British North America Act. My hight hon. friend has stated, and very accurately, that at Confederation the representation of the. provinces in the senate was divided into three groups, one for Ontario, the second for Quebec, and the third for the Maritime provinces, and the representation of these groups in the Senate was to be equal. Since Confederation we have assumed that we should carry the same principle to the western provinces and create a fourth group with similar representation in the Senate. The resolution of my right hon. friend has that object in view, and it is one to which we on this -side are ready to .assent; but this can only be done by an Imperial Act based upon a joint recommendation of the House of Commons and the Senate. The resolution, when passed, will go to the Senate to receive their concurrence. I have no observation to make at the present time with regard to what concerns the Senate except this. My right hon. friend is applying to the new order of things which will be created by this amendment the provisions of section 26 of the British North America Act, which is as follows:
If at any time, on the recommendation of the Governor General, the Queen thinks fit to direct

that three or six members be added to the Senate, the Governor General may, by summons to three or six qualified persons (as the ease may be), representing equally the three divisions of Canada, add to the Senate accordingly.
This provision, which was an exceptional one, has not been acted upon since Confederation. It did not contemplate an increase of representation, but simply provided that the representation in the Senate might be temporarily increased, and that no new appointments should be made in excess of the number of six. As I said a moment ago, this legislation has long since been obsolete, because it has not been applied once in the forty-seven years since Confederation. The Government of Mr. Mackenzie, as is well known, tried in 1874 to obtain from the imperial authorities power to anticipate the appointment of three senators-one for Ontario, one for Quebec and one for the Maritime provinces, but after some correspondence the imperial authorities did not think it advisable to interfere to that extent with our autonomous powers. I presume that in the year 1914 such power is even less likely to be exercised. My right hon. friend has thought it advisable to have this provision repeated in this amendment. To that I have no objection to offer; I have no doubt that it will remain in the future inoperative, as it has done in the past.
The most important consideration with which we have to deal at the present time is contained in the last paragraph of the resolution, as follows:
The British North America Act, 1867, is amended by Adding thereto the following section immediately after section 51 of the said Act.
(51 A) Notwithstanding anything in this Act a province shall always be entitled to a number of members in the House of Commons not less than the number of senators representing such province.
Section 51 of the British North America Act provides that the representation shall be readjusted every ten years, after the census, and that the representation in every province shall be regulated by its population as shown by the census. The representation of the Maritime provinces has been steadily decreasing. This year the representation of Prince Edward Island, which was six when it entered Confederation, is to be reduced to three. This matter was brought particularly to the attention of my -right hon. friend in connection with the Redistribution Bill, and of course the committee came to the conclusion that this Parliament has no power to change the representation of Prince Edward Island, which has to be reduced to three. But they have recommended an amendment to the constitution which will provide that in the future the representation of any province in the House of Commons shall not be reduced below the number of its representation in the Senate. My hon. friend has said that there are some incongruities in the representation in the Senate and the House of Commons. I do not share his view as to that. The representation of the provinces in the House of Commons is based upon population. In the Upper House it is not based upon population; there the smaller provinces have abnormal representation, the larger provinces have the smaller representation according to population and the smaller provinces have the larger representation according to population. I remember when any amendment of the kind now suggested could not be passed.
I may say that there are precedents for some of the present conditions in respect of representation in the Senate and in the House of Commons. In the United States the representation in the Senate is fixed at two for each state, whereas representation in the House of Representatives is according to population. I have not looked into the subject recently, but I have a distinct recollection that when Rhode Island entered the Union it was representated by two members in the Senate and only one in the House of Representatives. This is a precedent which might apply to conditions here at the present time. If we are to adhere strictly to principle, we should not pass the amendment which is now before us.
However, for my part I am not disposed to insist upon the principle; I believe that, although the principle of representation by population is violated by this new provision, on the whole no serious incon-convenience can arise to the different members of Condeferation. We are aware that unfortunately the population of the provinces of Nova Scotia,	New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island is not likely to keep page with the population in the other provinces. The other provinces have vast territories; we have added to the territory of Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec, and it is possible, indeed it is most certain, that there shall be a large increase of population in some parts of the territories which

we have added to those provinces. It is ^impossible to conceive, that there can be except by an abnormal industrial development, any increase of population in the eastern provinces. From the viewpoint of agriculture alone, it is not possible for them to have an increase; they have no new territories to settle; their territory is practically all occupied. Therefore, as it is not possible to conceive that there can be any increase in those provinces, no harm can be done, I believe, to the larger members of Confederation if it is provided that the representation of any province in the House of Commons shall not fall below its representation in the Upper House. I am not disposed, therefore, to offer any objections; on the contrary, I am disposed to agree to the provisions which are here adopted upon the recommendation of the Committee on Redistributions

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext:
We have heard from the right hon. gentlemen representing the great Conservative party and the great Liberal party in this country on the matter of the revision of the constitution in so far as the Senate of Canada is concerned. To my mind, however, they have not expressed the views of the plain people of this country, the democratic spirit of this country, in regard to the constitution of our Senate. I believe that it is the opinion of the people of this country that when this House proceeds to consider, as it does in this resolution, the constitution of the Senate, they should consider more than the question of the number and appointment of members; they should consider the actual constitution of the Senate and the manner in which members thereof are selected. Especially should they have regard to this section containing the resolution which says:
In case of such addition being at any time made the Governor General shall not summon any person to the Senate-
The people in this country, I believe, are of opinion that the Senate of Canada should not be summoned but like the House of Commons, should be a body responsible to the people of Canada in some way and that its members should not be summoned to it by the Governor General and His Council. In other words, the Senate of Canada should be responsible to the people, their term o* office should be limited, and the Chamber should be more democratic. It is neither; it is not democratic and it is not responsible. These
[Sir Wilfrid Laurier 1
men are appointed for life; they are irresponsible and that is absolutely out of harmony with the democratic institutions of this country and with the British constitution generally as it is to-day, and I am going to proceed to develop that idea.
The greatest progressive measure under British constitutional rule to-day is the Parliament Act which was recently passed in England. What was the object of the Parliament Act? It was to do away with the undue influence on progressive legislation of the irresponsible and hereditary body known as the House of Lords, and the Parliament Act took away the veto power from that irresponsible body and brought it within the zone of parliamentary responsibility; or rather it has so limited its powers that if the people, Voicing their views through, the House of Commons in three succeeding sessions, declare in favour of a measure, that measure becomes law irrespective of the veto of the Lords. What the mother country has done we in this democratic country ought to do, and we do not propose to continue in Canada a body which is irresponsible, which is not democratic and which is appointed for life and appointed by whoever happens to be the Governor in Council for the time being. The great question in England to-day-and all England is ringing with the struggle there- is not so much Home Rule, is not the coercion of Ulster but the greater principle whether the people shall rule or whether the voice of the people shall be stifled by an irresponsible hereditary body like the House of Lords. Therefore the people in England have this greater and wider issue even than Home Rule and while I do not want to see any coercion of Ulster, I do want to see the people of England win out on this principle of responsible parliamentary rule, and at the same time have it maintained. It is sometimes said that we are coercing Ulster. That is not the great issue in Great Britain, it is the maintenance of the Parliament Act, the maintenance of democratic rule, and the principle of having everybody who has any voice in the control of legislation responsible to somebody, or if they are not responsible, having their Acts capable of being overridden by those who are responsible to the people. They have accomplished that in England to-day and the hereditary House of Lords has been deprived of its veto on the public opinion of England, as expressed by the House of Commons. Here we in Canada, after forty-six years' experience of the British North America Act, are going to

further crystallize this condition of affairs, and not one word of protest is being made. I have proposed in this House on several occasions that the time has come and more than come when there should be constitutional revision in this country in the direction of improving the British North America Act and, above all, of giving us democratic, responsible government. But no protest is being heard in that respect although we have had experiences in this House on different occasions when we have thought the popular will has been overridden by the Senate.
I believe in a double Chamber system if we have both Chambers responsible; but if we cannot have a Senate responsible like we ourselves are, I am inclined to believe, and I do believe, the people of Canada are in favour of the abolition of the Senate.

speechtext:
Public opinion must rule in this country. In my opinion.

the peop-le of this country want to have an absolute say in the constitution of our Senate. The right hon. leader of the Opposition criticised this last clause because it deale with the representation of this House. For the first time in history, this House of Commons, responsible to the people of Canada, is, by this clause, to be measured by the irresponsible Senate. We have glorified here to-day the idea of an irree-ponsibile^ Senate, and it is now proposed that we should cut our cloth by them. I do not like it, and it is my determination, unices I hear further from the people of this country, to oppose every increase in Senate representation until that body becomes responsible to the people of this country, and I believe that is what the people of this country want to-day. I am in favouT of a second chamber, if it is responsible to the people. There is great work for a Senate to do in this country; there are a great number of questions they could deal with, but it is because they are not in touch with public opinion that they accomplish little. Almost every other upper chamber throughout the empire is susceptible to public opinion. Neither Australia nor South Africa has a system like ours, and all this Parliament has to do is to declare that it wants a constitutional revision or leave the matter to the Imperial Parliament. I am content to leave to the Imperial Parliament the question of making the Senate of this country a responsible chamber in harmony with public opinion, and, until that is done, I am opposed to any increase in the Senate representation whatever. If something is not done, some day this House will take charge of the whale constitution of Canada, and declare itself to be absolutely free in regard to its power, saving that it is under the British Crown. That, at least, should be the width of the powers of the Parliament of Canada. This Parliament ought to be supreme in this Dominion, even to the extent of having power to make a constitution of its own, and respecting the original contract rights, provided it Temains under the Crown. We are moving in that direction, but the one thing in the way is this irresponsible, appointeu-for-life Senate. I am making no party appeal, but I tell the members of this House that the question the people of Canada are concerned with is not the number of senators and their distribution throughout the Dominion, but the question of bringing the irresponsible Senate of this country into 
harmony with our democratic institutions and in harmony with responsible government. It. has taken ns a hundred years to achieve what we call responsible government in this country, but we have not responsible government to the fullest extent even yet, and never will have so long as there is an irresponsible, appointed-for-life Senate.
Mr. SAM. SHARPE: I desire to endorse in their entirety the remarks of the hon. member for South York. In my opinion, he has expressed the sentiments of a great majority of the people of this country. Senate reform has always been a live question with the party out of office, but not so live when the party gets into power. In 1893, Senate reform was part of the Liberal platform, and I think they prepared a resolution whereby a joint committee was to he appointed to consider the method by which the Senate should be reformed and made responsible to public opinion. Both parties are pledged up to the hilt to amend the Senate in some way or other. We had an example only a few days ago in connection with the Farmers Bank Bill showing that the Senate does not represent public opinion in this country. Four recent appointees to the Senate supposed to be responsible to public opinion voted against this Government that is fresh from the country. The Government, which is supposed to represent public opinion in this country, brought down a measure to provide relief for the depositors of the Farmers Bank. When the Bill got to the Senate these four new appointees discharged their functions in a manner not at all satisfactory to the people of this country or to the Government in power. In my opinion, this country" is looking for some method of Senate reform rather than to increasing the number of senators which only adds to the difficulties of reform. I desire to go on, record that the Senate should be abolished in its entirety or be so amended as to make it responsible to public opinion. It has demonstrated time and again that it is the bulwark of privilege and the big interests, and not a democratic institution. All democratic countries are getting away from the predominating influences of the privileged classes. The mother Parliament has amended the House of Lords so that it -cannot thwart the will of the people.
