speechtext:
I
am sorry that the committee to whom this representation Bill was referred did not see eye to eye with the representatives from Prince Edward Island who presented the ease of that province before the committee. It is an old story in this House and in the country the manner in which the province of Prince Edward Island refused to enter into Confederation in 1864. The refusal was based upon the question of representation. The conference composed of representatives from Upper and Lower Canada, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, offered to Prince Edward Island a representation of five in the House of Commons. This the delegates 333
from Prince Edward Island absolutely refused, and gave valid reasons for their refusal. The Hon. Edward Palmer, who was one of the members of the Government at that time, spoke at the Quebec conference as follows:
Representation by population is not applicable when a certain number of provinces are throwing up their self-government and individuality. When a colony surrenders that right she should have something commensurate in the Confederation. We give up such great certainties where we have only a feeble voice. I never understood that any proposition at Charlettetown was to be binding as to representation by population.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition to-day made the statement that the representation had to be based on population. It seems to me, from my reading of the history of Confederation that that was not the idea in the several conferences which took place previous to 1867. We have the speeches of the representatives of Prince Edward Island at the conferences denying that that principle should be adopted in setting their representation in the House of Commons. Prince Edward Island, principally on that ground, held out until 1873. Then we had Earl Granville asking the Dominion of Canada to round out the Confederation and bring in Prince Edward Island. A special request was made by the British Government that generous treatment should be held out to Prince Edward Island. What was Prince Edward Island asking for? There was only one thing that we were asking for and that is that the representation should be six instead of five and that is what was offered by us to the delegates from the different provinces previous to 1867. When the delegation came here from Prince Edward Island in 1873 the 'question which was put to the Government of Canada was: Will you concede us six representatives in the House of Commons? There is a record of what took place; it was put in writing, it is entered upon the journals of the House of Commons and upon the journals of the House of Assembly of Prince Edward Island. It has been stated to me several times by some of my colleagues that there was no evidence to go before the committee to which this Bill was referred of any arrangement or understanding whereby a representation of six was to be granted to Prince Edward Island in 1873. There is ample evidence; there is the evidence of the records of Parliament and of the House of Assembly. Here we



are sitting as a supreme court of justice and the committee to which the Bill was referred is a part of this House. The evidence was submitted to the members of that committee and when they report that they would not be justified in recommending to this House that Prince EdwardJ Island is entitled to a representation of six they are committing an error. There was ample evidence of the fact that Prince Edward Island is entitled to six. This report, in my opinion, was simply a matter of expediency. They were not, in any way, entering into the merits of the case. This report does not deal with the merits of the case except in regard to the recommendations which would apply to more than one province; that is, that no province should be represented in the House of Commons by a less number than the number of its representatives in the Senate. That will, of course, apply to Prince Edward Island, but as far as carrying out the contract made between the people of Prince Edward Island and the Dominion of Canada in 1873 is concerned, this committee did not consider the matter and when they reported upon it they were not justified in stating that there was no evidence. I repeat there was ample evidence.
This matter has been put before this Parliament before on former occasions. In 1903 it was before Parliament and- at that time it was agreed to submit to the Supreme Court of Canada the question of whether Prince Edward Island was entitled to a representation of six. The Supreme Court decided that, according to the letter of the law, Prince Edward Island was not entitled to any more than the Parliament of Canada was then conceding to if. But the Supreme Court did not enter upon the merits of the case. The chief justice stated:
It might be that it was the impression of Prince Edward Island at the time, in the minds of the public men when they consented to this, that they did not expect a decrease, hut that is not a consideration in the interpretation of a clear Act of Parliament.
That I concede. There was no evidence before the Supreme Court at the time and the judges were simply giving a decision upon the wording of the British North America Act and the resolutions which were passed by the Imperial Parliament admitting Prince Edward Island into the union in 1873. They were bound by the

words of that Act. The counsel, Mr. Williams, stated:
It is not entirely an impression. If we can give you the express wording of the Act to show what was the meaning of it in the minds of the conference.
The Chief Justice: The framers of the Aot may have intended a different meaning from the mind of the British Parliament.
There is no doubt that the men who were connected with the framing of this Act did intend that Prince Edward Island should have a representation which would not be decreased below six. That is conceded on all hands. But these hon. gentlemen say that it would not be expedient to give Prince Edward Island the number to which she is entitled and to leave Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and some other provinces without any increase. I do not think that is the way this Parliament should enter into the discussion of the Act or to undertake to decide the matter. The matter should be looked at fairly and squarely and justice and right should be done. You must view the matter in the proper light and you must treat it as the people concerned at the time intended it should be treated. When this question was before the House in 1907 the right hon. leader of the Opposition stated that if it were proven that a mistake had been made in the drafting of the resolutions admitting Prince Edward Island into the union it should be remedied. The right hon. gentlemen, addressing the House in 1907,	' Hansard,' volume 2, page 2199,
said:
For my part I say without hesitation that this is a matter in which we can afford to be generous. Even if the balance of representation by population be not absolutely and minutely kept, even if Prince Edward Island or Nova Scotia or New Brunswick should have one or two members on the floor of this House beyond the number provided by the original constitution, the granting of such excess of representation would perhaps be a gracious and generous act and one which would redound to the benefit of confederation. But this House ought to hesitate in passing judgment until it has before it the views of all the provinces affected.
That was showing a proper spirit. The matter came up upon a resolution asking the House to declare that the Maritime provinces should retain the representation which they had when they entered Confederation. The leader of the Opposition, who was then the leader of the Government, thought that more time should be taken by the House to consider this matter, and he said that, after consideration, he had no doubt that Parliament would

act in a generous manner in order to prevent these provinces from losing their representation
At that time the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) also made some noteworthy remarks. He was of opinion that the representation of Prince Edward Island should be restored to six. The question was discussed in all its phases; all the evidence was presented to the House, and the hon. member for Pictou had an opportunity of hearing the arguments pro and con and of reading the evidence adduced iby the members twlho argued in favour of Prince Edward Island. This is what the hon. member for Pictou said at that time:
Whether you are dealing with the ordinary affairs of life or whether you are dealing with constitutional problems and constitutional rights which perhaps should be given a higher regard than the other; it is only common sense and fair-play to say that the people of Prince Edward Island who were given six members in 1873, although they had no right to that number according to the unit of population, are entitled to preserve that number of six members right through so long as the Confederation of Canada lasts.
Here is a strong opinion. The hon. gentleman, who was almost as conversant with the politics of Prince Edward Island as the members for that province, declared in this House, after hearing the arguments, that, in his opinion, Prince Edward Island should preserve the number of six members right through as long as the Confederation of Canada lasts. I have no doubt that is the opinion of the hon. member for Pictou to-day, because he is a man who does not rapidly change his mind; and I would ask him to-day in this House to give a declaration to the same effect as he gave at that time.
There are other hon. gentlemen who have *taken part in the discussion of this matter at various times in this House, and who nave expressed similar views to those expressed by the hon. member for Pictou; and I have no doubt that, if the matter were cairly presented to the members of this House to-day, there would be only one opinion on both sides, namely, that a contract was made in 1873 between the people of Prince Edward Island and the Dominion of Canada whereby that province for all time to come was to have a representation in the House of Commons of six members. It is my intention, before this matter goes before the committee, to move a resolution. In doing so I think I would be derelict in my duty if I did not strongly urge that this resolution be approved by 333i
this Parliament. The resolution would provide that the original representation of Prince Edward Island in the Senate of six members be restored.
At one o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at three o'clock.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext:
Before recess I
mentioned that it was my intention to move this amendment in committee:
(b) Prince Edward Island shall be entitled to be represented in the House of Commons by six members. The representation to be increased under the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867. Prince county shall constitute one district to be designated [DOT] Prince county district ' and return two members; Queens county shall constitute one district and be designated 'Queens county district' and return two members; and Kings county shall constitute one district, to be designated ' Kings county district ' and return two members.
When the resolution asking for the admission of Prince Edward Island to the Union was passed by this Parliament and sent to the Imperial Parliament and there made law, it provided that each of the counties should return two members. This is what I now ask to be incorporated in this resolution.
There is no doubt that, if you take this Order in Council of the Imperial Government of the 26th June, 1873, the resolution .of this Parliament, and the resolutions of the Legislature of Prince Edward Island, you will find that the clear and distinct intention of the Legislature and of this Parliament was that Prince Edward Island should have minimum representation of six members; otherwise, why was it stated that each county should return two members ?
The provision in the resolution of this Parliament,
That the population of Prince Edward Island having been increased by 15,000 since the year 1861, the island should be represented in the House of Commons by six members; the representation to be readjusted from time to time under the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867.
was not intended to be in that form. The insertion of the word ' readjust' was an error. It was agreed between the Dominion Government and the Prince Edward Island Government that the island should have an irreducible representation of six, similar to British Columbia. It was not intended that the representation could be reduced under the provisions of the British North America Act. It was contended in this House some time ago

that we should have been reduced in representation in 1881, but that it was found that there was no record of a census of the island for 1871. That could never have been successfully contended, as the resolution passed by this Parliament on the 20th May, 1873, distinctly declares that the island's population. ' as shown by the census of 1871,' was 94,021. The resolution of this Parliament is incorporated into and forms part of the Imperial Order in Council admitting the province into the union. The population being only 94,021 in 1871 we could not possibly be entitled to a representation of six in this House if it were the intention of the agreeing parties that the terms of the 51st section with respect to re-adjustment should apply. There was no justification in giving us six members in the first instance with our then population if the contracting parties thought for a moment that the provisions of the 51st section with regard to readjustment applied. You must read all the documents, all the records together and thus judge the case. My opinion is that any fair-minded man will admit after .reading all the documents and correspondence that the intention was to give the island a minimum representation of six. The Order in Council provides that each county should return two members. In 1881 Sir John Macdonald was premier. He had a full knowledge of what passed in the Confederation conferences and subsequently. He negotiated the terms of union in 1873 and he evidently thought when the redistribution Bill was passed in 1882 that Prince Edward Island had a minimum representation of six, otherwise he would have reduced it to five. All the facts have been before Parliament many times. In 1865, immediately after the conference took place in Quebec, and when the matter was fresh in the minds of the men who were present at that conference, we find the matter was discussed in the legislature of Prince Edward Island. A great nunlber of speeches were made. I am not going to weary the House by reading them. But there was one terse speech upon this question in the House at that time made by Mr. Duncan. He said:
As to the general legislature-
That is, the Dominion Parliament:
-I consider the representation in it allowed to this Island unfair and unjust. The five representatives allotted to us in the Lower House would not give this colony much influence there,
but as our population will not increase so
[Mr. A. A. McLean 1
rapidly as that of Canada, there is a prospect, through the operation of one clause in the report, that our five representatives would dwindle down to three.
That is what happened. These men were objecting to a representation of five and it was the principal objection in the Legislature of Prince Edward Island in 1865, immediately after the contention of the delegates of Prince Edward Island for a representation of six was rejected by the delegates from the other provinces in the Quebec conference. Mr. Duncan goes on and says:
Taking all these points into consideration, therefore, it is clear to me that we have nothing to gain and much to lose hy adopting the Quebec scheme.
It may be said we are a small province, and that we to-day are only on a level with any three other constituencies in any other part of the country. I do not look at the matter in that light at all. We were a separate province; we had certain valuable rights and privileges as a separate colony, we were asked to give those rights away; we made an agreement with the Dominion Government that certain of these rights should be granted away for all time. We wanted a representation of six members in the Parliament of Canada as one of the considerations and we would not go into the union unless we got a representation of six. The Imperial Parliament, through one of its principal officers, said:	Be
generous to Prince Edward Island. They were generous; they gave us one more representative than we were entitled to. That solemn compact should be ratified by this Parliament to-day, by inserting the amendment which I read, in the resolution which, is going to the Imperial Parliament for ratification. This will only be doing what is fair and just. We got six members then. Are we any less important to-day than we were in 1873?
So far as wealth is concerned, we have gone ahead with rapid strides; in proportion to our extent of territory, we have advanced perhaps more rapidly than any other part of Canada; yet our representation is now to be reduced to three. The rest of Canada has increased in population to a very considerable extent. Within the-last few years the territory of Ontario has been increased by 150,000 square miles. We see by the legislation which is before us that two new constituencies are opened up in Northern

Ontario; two have been opened up within the last two years. By reason of the addition of 180,000 square miles in 1897 and of the Ungava territory in 1912, the population of Quebec is rapidly increasing. In 1912, in the Act ceding Ungava to Quebec, they were given their new representation. Outside of the 65, which is the pivotal number upon which the representation of Canada is based, they are getting additional representatives for the territory which was granted to them in 1912. If you read the discussions which took place not only at Quebec, but in the different legislatures of the provinces at the time of Confederation, you will see that the whole theme of the discussion was that the representation was to be based upon the various conditions, existing in and the influences acting upon the provinces. If the provinces gave away certain rights, they were conceded certain rights. Some hon. gentlemen say that the basis of Confederation is representation by population, but the representatives from Prince Edward Island never conceded that. The province of Manitoba also got a large extent of territory, and their population is increasing very rapidly. But nothing is given to the other provinces in respect of this great increase of territory, although there is a provision in the British North America Act that in case of increase, diminution or alteration of territory in respect of any province, provisions respecting the effect and operation of such increase or diminution or alteration of territory in relation to any province affected thereby must be considered. Although the three provinces which I have named have been largely increased in area by the addition of territory, no consideration is given to that in so far as the Maritime provinces are concerned. This is a matter which the British North America Act clearly states should be considered by this Parliament.
We had a clause in our terms of Confederation that we should be provided with continuous steam communication, winter and summer, between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I take it that this is a matter which should receive consideration by this House in the discussion of the matter now before us. It was brought up toy the delegates to the Interprovincial Conference last year and it was brought up by the members of the Government of Prince Edward Island when they appeared before the committee of this House a few months ago. We were to get continuous steam communication, and although immediately after we
entered the union we asked the Dominion Government to fulfil the terms of Confederation in that respect, we were totally ignored, and from 1873 up to the time the present Government came into power, we received no consideration at the hands of any Government. I may say that the people of Prince Edward Island are to-day rejoicing in the fact that within a very short time we will have continuous steam communication and that the terms of union in that regard will be fulfilled.

Mr. MoLEAN: I think that it has a certain connection with this matter and that I have a right to make the statement, but in deference to you, Mr. Speaker, I shall not continue to discuss the matter along that line.
Reference is made in this resolution to the colony of Newfoundland. In my opinion if would be a good thing if we were to obtain the consent of Newfoundland to their entering into this Confederation; it would be a good thing not only for the people of Newfoundland, tout for the people of Canada as well. I think that the real reason why the colony of Newfoundland did not come into the union is because the terms of Confederation in respect of communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland had not been fulfilled, and because the representation which was agreed upon has not been conceded to us. We are living contiguous to the colony of Newfoundland; we have trade communications with them; we have close commercial relations with them; the principal trade of the island in produce is carried on with Newfoundland. Notwithstanding the fact that it was known by the people of Canada and by the representatives of the people in this House that the terms of Confederation had not been carried out with the island, the matter was allowed to stand from year to year. Is it any wonder that the people of Newfoundland did not make any approaches to the Government of Canada in respect to their entering this Confederation? In 1864, when the first conference met at Charlottetown, the delegates from Newfoundland were there, and we were in hopes at that time that Newfoundland would come into the Confederation. But they saw how Prince Edward Island was being treated; the conference would not grant what Prince Edward Island asked for, and Newfoundland

backed out also. They were in hopes at that time that they would get the concessions for which they asked, but their requests were refused by the delegates from the other provinces. Now we have the opportunity of bringing Newfoundland in and of clearing up all the abjections and grievances of the provinces which did enter into the union in 1867.
Give to Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia what the people at that time thought they were getting. Be generous, as the right hon. leader of the Opposition said here in 1906, even though you may concede a little more than you think the people are entitled to. If you are generous, if you give to Prince Edward Island what I consider she is entitled to, but, what some hon. gentlemen seem to consider she is not entitled to, you will be heralding to the world the fact that you are acting in a generous way and the people of Newfoundland will see that Canada is desirous of fulfilling the contract which she entered into with the people. On August 18, 19 and 20 next we propose to have a celebration in Prince Edward Island of the conference which took place on September 1, 1864 Let this Parliament shew the people of Prince Edward Island, every man of whom believes that we are entitled to a representation of site in this House; every man of whom believes that a contract was made that we should have that representation; let, this Parliament show to the people of Newfoundland, many of whom will be present at this celebration, that the Dominion is willing and anxious and ready to hi Ini the contracts which were entered into with Prince Edward Island at that time. Then you will find that the people of Newfoundland will probably take a different view of the desirability of their entering into Confederation with us.
1 know that this measure has been introduced by the leader of the Government and that the Government are bound by it. But there is no law which we cannot change. Notwithstanding the fact that this committee represented that there should be granted to any province representation in this House equal to what it has in the Senate, still there is no reason why this Government, in my opinion, should not add the clause which I read to the House a few moments ago. I think it would be only fair, just and right that this Government should do that, in fulfilment of the solemn contract that was made

with the people of Prince Edward Island in 1873.

I think this motion
lacks one thing: this change in my opinion ought to come into operation at the same time that the representation of the people in the House of Commons is increased. In this Parliament the people are represented in this Chamber, and the Crown is represented by those appointed to the Senate. As a result of the increase in population it is proposed to give the Crown greater powers of nomination to the body which is not responsible to the people, but which is appointed by the Crown irrespective altogether of the wishes of the people. Provision was made in

I merely wi3h to add to what I said this morning when dealing with the irresponsible character of the Senate that even the high office of King
has been brought within the zone of parliamentary responsibility. In Great Britain, the dominant party in the House and the Government of the day assumes responsibility for all the King's acts.

speechtext:
They provide that
anything he does shall be on the responsibility of his ministers and of the dominant party in the House of Commons. In England, they passed the Parliament Act for the purpose of overcoming the irresponsible character of the House of Lords. Inasmuch as there is more or. less responsibility in all the progressive constitutions of the day, and especially in the case of those modelled on the British constitution, my contention is that we ought to provide some way of getting around the irresponsible acts of our Upper Chamber. The great thing that governs wherever British institutions exist is public opinion, and the well thought out opinion of the people as expressed in the various legislatures. The last thing we ever thought of in this country in connection with appointments to the Senate was that the men appointed to that body should reflect public opinion. Take a case in point- that I mentioned to the House the other day. Public ownership is one of the great questions in this country to-day. Since that question has been to the front a great many senators have been appointed, but has a single one been appointed for his championship of that principle? Take the question of banking. I have noticed that a great number of the men who have been appointed to the Senate represent the interests of the banking institutions of this country, but I have failed to see a s.ngle one appointed who was seized of progressive ideas in regard to banking and currency. It is altogether different with the Senate of the United States, which reflects public opinion in regard to this question of banking; they have recently passed the most progressive banking measure known to the American continent, reflecting the well-known views of the people. We have nothing like that in this country. I do not know of a single man being appointed to the Senate because he represented some great progressive measure. No appointment has been made to that body where the first consideration was regard for public opinion, regard for progressive ideas or regard for legislation for

the general uplift of the community. My object is to get a better Senate that will share with this House in the responsibility for legislation to a greater extent than it does now-a Senate that will take a greater share in framing new Bills, a Senate that will be in touch with public opinion, and therefore better able to crystallize into legislation the views of the public on the great questions of the day. Inasmuch as both parties in this country are on record from the platform in favour of Senate reform, I say that now is the psychological moment for us to declare for Senr.t'' reform in order to keep ourselves in good standing with the people we represent. I have advocated Senate reform on the platform, and have heard the party leaders advocate it both on the platform and in this House. I have read the platforms of both parties in this country, setting out that they were in favour of Senate reform, and therefore I say that this is the psychological moment for us to make good the pledges and statements that have been made by both parties in favour of Senate reform.
While I do not wish in any way to alter a single word of the address that is to be passed by the House, or to alter in any way the Bill which we asked the Senate to join with us in requesting the Imperial x'arliament to pass, I want to move that the following words be added to the resolution :
And be it further resolved that this House, while It recognizes the existence in the said Act of the right of the Governor General to summon persons to the Senate is nevertheless of the opinion that the constitution should be further amended in the direction of having the said Senate made elective for fixed periods, and thus constituted more in harmony with the principles of responsible parliamentary government.
This does not militate in any way against the resolution as it is proposed, nor does it change the Act which we are asking the Imperial Parliament to pass. But we do acquaint the mother of parliaments, which has only recently stripped the irresponsible House of Lords of its veto power, with the fact that what is good for her is good for democratic Canada and good for America, and that we, too, desire the responsibility which Australia and South Africa have in connection with their Senates. I do not wish to have a change brought about that will in any way militate against the contract rights of the provinces, or the other rights set out in the original pact of Confederation with respect to the constitution of the Senate, but I want to
l"Mr. W. F. Maclean.]
have such changes in the constitution as will bring the Senate within the zone of responsible parliamentary government. I am pleading in this House from sixty to eighty years after the great principle of responsible government was vindicated in this country by the Liberal party, by Baldwin and Lafontaine, whose statues, as I saw them out on the grounds here the other day, present such a magnificent picture of these two great patriots. They united Upper and Lower Canada on the great principle of responsible government. That meant that the irresponsible government by Governor in Council in the old days, which was partial government, should be completely removed. The time has came when an end should be put to a Chamber in this country which is absolutely irresponsible to puiblic opinion or to the legislatures which are the constituents of this Confederation. There is no way whereby the provinces, through their legislatures, can express their views in regard to the constitution of the country. If we had the Senate elected, as it could be under my resolution, by the votes of the legislatures, as they have it in the United States, or by a wider election by the people, or by having the provinces divided into districts- and I am not going into details at the present time-this country would be a modern country and it would be living in the twentieth century. To-day this country is living in ancient times and under ancient conditions. It is not in accord with the principles of liberty, it is not constitutional, it is not of the twentieth century, that we should have to-day an absolutely irresponsible Chamber in this country, possessing powers co-equal with those possessed by this House, which is elected by the votes of the people and which is, therefore, amenable to public opinion as it may be voiced in the elections, in the press, on the public platform, and in other ways. I call on both parties in this House to make good their pledges in the past, and to have the principle of an irresponsible Chamber removed from our constitution. I am not going into details, I am not going to make any exact proposal, but I say that the amendment which I submit now does acquaint the Imperial Parliament with our view upon the matter, with our pledges on the platform, and with the views of the people of Canada, and therefore it is worthy of adoption by this House. It is also worth our while asking the co-operation of the Senate, because I do not cast one reflection

on the Senate other than that it is irre-;, sponsible. I think well enough of thet Senate as a body to say that I respect them, and that 1 respect their co-ordinate powers of legislation, but I desire to see them made amenable to the great principle of responsible parliamentary government. To that end, I submit this amendment.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would be pleased to second the amendment of my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean). I believe that the Senate should be elective. Both parties have been thinking for a long time of reforming the Senate, but nothing has been done so far. The work of reforming the Senate, has, up to the present time, been left to Providence. I believe that the Senate should be made elective, that the term of office should be eight or ten years, that the districts should be large, that there should be proportional representation, and that there should be an age limit. We impose an age limit on county court judges. The senators revise most of the laws passed by this House, and if the county court judges are too old at seventy-five to continue administering the laws, I think the Senators, when they reach that age, should also retire and not be in a position to revise the laws passed by this Chamber. In the new constitutions of the British possessions, Australia and South Africa, the Senates have been made elective. An elective Senate is more consonant with democratic institutions than an appointive Senate. Deadlocks would be better avoided by having an elective Senate than an appointive one. I do not want to detain the House because time is
precious at this stage of the sessi n, but I will be pleased to support the amendment of my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean).

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is a rather large question to bring forward at this stage of the session; but that is no reason why an opinion should not be expressed in regard to it. My view is that it will be yet a long time before the last word has been said in regard to the best method of representative government. I am for progress, I am for betterment, I am for bringing legislation as closely in touch with public requirements and public opinion as it may be brought. But my experience and my reading do not lead me to the belief that an elective second Chamber is the best means of attaining effective and prompt legislation. My opinion is that if you want to be closely in touch with public opinion, and give effect to that opinion by legislation, you require to have a one-chamber parliament where action is direct from the people to the Parliament, and from the Parliament back to the people, in accordance with the expressed wish of the people. Experience, as far as I have been able to gather it, shows that, when two legislative bodies, deriving their respective authority from the same source, are dealing with the same questions, the result is in the first place more or less clashing and delay, in the second place more or less compromise and ineffectiveness, and in the end one body absorbs the larger proportion of authority and dominates the situation. That body who is given the higher position, if it derives its authority directly from the people, in the nature of things and properly asserts its dominance, having the authority to do so, and the more truly representative chamber has the less influence in the Parliament of the country. Today in the United! States, which my hon. friend has quoted as an example, the House of Representatives, elected directly by the people, is a negligible body in the important legislation of that great country. The Senate is the controlling authority; it is the Senate that settles everything, the Senate, the Millionaires' Club-[DOT]

speechtext: No, not now.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext:
Absolutely, notoriously
so, holding place and power for the purpose of advancing the interests of all those forces in the United States which are injurious to the welfare of the people. If you

cannot trust yourselves to govern yourselves by electing a legislature directly by the people, then you are not bettering the condition by electing some other legislature by the same people to prevent the One first elected from doing what you ordered it to do by your election. I am aware, of course, as I said in the beginning, that the last word has not been said in regard to these matters; but I am saying what I am saying now in order to bring to my hon. friend's attention the fact that neither has he said the last word when he has declared that an elective second chamber is a more truly democratic system of Government than the one under which we carry on our business to-day. Everyone knows that the reason why we have a second chamber in this country is because, without what was supposed to be the protection of a second chamber, we never could have achieved Confederation. It is a condition which belongs to our situation that we have a second chamber. If our condition calls for a second chamber in this country of Canada, I certainly assert that an elective second chamber would not achieve either the purpose that was intended by the establishment of the Senate or the democratization of the legislation of this Parliament. We have our Senate as a protection to the smaller provinces, to the minorities, to the sectional interests, if you like, of this country of Canada. We did not create it; we are not responsible for it; hut we do ourselves little credit to think that the men who fathered Confederation had not in their minds sound and, at that time, certainly good reasons for what they did. Our Senate is constituted to achieve certain purposes. I will admit that those purposes are not essentially democratic.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext: Not always.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext:
I will admit that they are not always democratic. Some of the principles, for instance, the protection of the minorities, are not essentially democratic. But so long as we have to provide for that protection, I do not see any other 4 p.m. way of providing for it than by appointment. Certainly we could not provide for it by election. The very fact of election would prevent it from being provided for. What is there objectionable in the matter of appointment to this body created to meet a certain specific purpose? The members of that body are appointed, and are appointed for life. I have given the reason why they are ap-

pointed; I will give the reasons why they are appointed for life. It may not be a good reason; but it is that, when appointed, they shall be absolutely independent of any possible outside influence in giving their votes on the subjects that come up for consideration. There may be disadvantages surrounding that appointment; (but it is only fair to say, in the first place, there is a good reason for their membership by appointment and, in the second place, there is a good reason why they should be appointed for life. But my hon. friend says it is not democratic. Well, our judges are appointed, and they are appointed for life, with a certain restriction mentioned by my hon. friend from Prescott (Mr. Proulx), which I have no doubt is a very proper restriction. I am free to say- and I think my hon. friend will not contradict it, that, undeT that system of appointment of our judges for life, our administration of justice is more truly in the interests of the common people than the administration of justice across the line where the judges 'are elected presumably in the interest of the principles of democracy. If as a democratic country, in the protection of the interests of democracy, we find it necessary to appoint our judges for life, I am not so easy to convince that it is at all contrary to the principles of democracy that, having a certain condition in this country which calls for the provision of a. second chamber, we should not provide for that second chamber on the same principle as we provide for the administration of our rights and privileges as between man and man.
As to the actual facts of the case, it is true that a vast power rests in the Senate, and it is true that that power could be abused. There is no doubt, if that power is ever abused, there will be a necessity for the reorganization of the Senate or for its abolition. But the proper exercise of the power that is placed in the hands of the Senate is not an abuse of that power. I have been in this Parliament since 1896, and have followed the course of legislation very carefully; I have seen the Senate go counter to a Liberal Government, and I have seen it go counter to a Conservative Government. I am bound to say that, in my humble judgment, the Senate is of most use when, by reason of its majority not being in accord with the majority of the Commons, political alliances do not govern the judgment of senators as thoroughly as they do when the majority is the same in both Houses. It is when the Senate is liable to bring upon itself the

objurgations of the Government and its supporters that it justifies its existence and protects the interests of the people.
But, of course, the Senate could abuse its rights and its privileges; it could make itself an unbearable incubus on our political institutions. That is what the House of Lords in Great Britain did, and if the Senate should do that it will have to be dealt with as the House of Lords was dealt with in Britain. Had the House of Lords in Great Britain only exercised its authority as it was entitled to exercise it, if it had used it and not abused it, it would not have been shorn of a measure of its authority. Until it has been shown that the Senate has gone beyond the use of its authority and has abused it, there is no reason for in any way taking from the authority that it exercises or finding fault with its constitution or actions. I am for improvement; I am for betterment; I am for democratic institutions. But I am for good government; I am for the best expression of the will of the people in legislation and in administration. And I find that best expression through the means of a House elected directly by the people and to whom the people look directly for [DOT] legislation, and for the results of legislation, and an upper chamber having large powers and exercising those powers with good, sound judgment and patriotism, having regard to all the conditions and circumstances of our country and to the reasons for the creation, existence and maintenance of the Senate itself.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext:
I wish to say a few words in reference to this matter. Like my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), I am for improvement and for betterment; but 1 would rather move slowly and surely than hastily and recklessly, especially in matters affecting the fundamental principles of our constitution. My adherence to the principles of the constitution is well known. In my opinion the fathers of Confederation were very wise in providing two bodies in this Parliament, one elective and the other appointive or permanent. The Senate, as the hon. member for Edmonton said so eloquently and forcibly, is the protector of the smaller provinces of this Dominion, as well as of the minorities. It is not to he expected that two bodies, elected .by the same people at the same time, could counteract each other's actions. The Senate is a safeguard, more especially for the Maritime provinces, which are the smaller body in this Dominion; and it was
owing to the fact that the smaller provinces could depend upon the protection of the Senate that the principle of representation by population was introduced in thi3 Dominion. I will try to be as brief as possible, because I expressed my views formerly when I could speak longer than I can to-day. We all know that without the protection afforded by the Senate, Confederation would not have taken place. Sir Leonard Tilley, of New Brunswick, with all his desire to have idle Intercolonial link the Maritime provinces commercially and nationally with the western provinces, would have come back to St. John without Confederation if his people had not been certain of the guarantee of a high representation in the Senate.
It has often been said in this House that it is not constitutional, nor according to good sense, that the Maritime provinces should have a larger representation in the Senate than in the Commons. It was with that object m view, in order to be able to counteract the increasing preponderance of western Ganada, that the Fathers of Confederation gave that constitution to the Senate. If it were elective we may rest assured that in the larger provinces more particularly, minorities would be apt to lack the protection which may be needed at different times. 1 remember very well a very eloquent speech on this question made no less an authority than Sir Kiehard Cartwright a few years ago in the Senate, in which he contended that while with all good-will possible the majority of the province of Ontario had endeavoured to give the Catholic minority of that province as fair and equal a representation as possible according to their numbers in the House of Commons yet through some uncontrollable political reasons it had not been able to do so; but that owing to the fact that the Senate was appointive, and that the Government of the day had the onus of protecting the minority, the 'Catholic minority of Ontario found its protection by representation in the Senate. Likewise, in ihe province of Quebec the Protestant minority might not perhaps in a public election find its due representation in the Senate; but, owing to the fact that the Government of the day is charged with tlie duty of protecting thait minority, it finds its protection in that body. As conditions are to-day in my province, the Irish Catholic minority has no representative in this House, but owing to

the fact of the Prime Minister of the day having the responsibility of fair representation	they have had a	representation greater than they are justly entitled to in the Senate to compensate for what they lack in this House. You must Temember that if you make the Senate elective minorities cannot be well protected in a country like ours.

Suppose that we had
proportional representation?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext:
It would come to about the same thing. I have always had faith in the extreme wisdom of the Fathers of Confederation, and I believe they had in view more particularly that a permanent and non-elective Senate would be a greater check to the popular prejudices which may at times prevail.
We have heard a great deal lately detrimental to the Senate because it has shown its independence in dealing with measures passed by this House. But our constitution, according to the wisdom of the Fathers of Confederation, is still left open to democratic ideas, and if, perchance, the Senate should be persistent in blocking legislation which is approved by the House of Commons, the Government of the day has the power to consult and appeal to the people. That is what could have been done last year, when we heard so much about the action of the Senate. The Government of the day could have appealed to the people and the Senate would have agreed with their decision. I contend that the Senate is a more important body in the destinies of this country than some hon. gentlemen seem to think it is. It is a permanent and responsible body; it is permanent m order that men appointed as senators may be free from the prejudices of the people. While they may not be perfect at all times, who can say that we in this House are all perfect ? The physical condition of a man is not always an index to his intellectual ability. In the Senate to-day we have men who are well advanced in years; I mention particularly the name of Sir Mackenzie Bowell, who is over ninety years of age, but who has at all times during this and other sessions shown the same vitality which he evidenced twenty years ago. The same condition may exist in particular instances in this House, and I am therefore opposed to any cnange in the constitution of the Senate.
[Mr Turgeon.]
Mr.BORDEN: I understand that the hon. member for South York has put forward his amendment only as an assertion of principle, and that he does not submit it with any idea that it is a proper motion at this time. It would hardly be compatible with the control we have over our own affairs to forward a resolution of this character to the Parliament of the United Kingdom and ask them to work out a scheme under which the Senate of Canada could be made elective. Any proposal for an elective Senate would involve a great deal more attention than it is possible to bestow upon the matter at the present time. Fault has been found with the constitution of the Senate; many men in Parliament have criticised it, and it has been criticised outside of Parliament. It is true .also the method of election to this Parliament has been criticised, and various suggestions have been put forward; for example, as to proportional representation, upon the view that the method of election at the present time does not do justice to minorities of population. A system of electing the Senate prevails in the United1 States and in Australia. It has been subjected to the criticism which the hon. member for Edmonton puts forward, that in the final result that system very often makes the Senate a more powerful body than the lower House, and one cannot be sure that the system is working out with perfect satisfaction either in the United States or elsewhere. The question of the method by which the House of Lords in the mother country shall be reformed has been under consideration for a number of years, and it is probable that within a year or two years some proposals will be placed before the British Parliament in that regard. It is an open secret that proposals have been under consideration by the Cabinet for some time; at least I so gather from what has been said' in the Imperial House of Commons on the subject. For us at the present time, and at this stage of the session, to attempt to solve the problems to which the hon. member for South York has drawn attention is out of the question. He has said that while he .sees need of some remedy for the conditions which he criticises, he himself is not prepared to come forward with a satisfactory remedy. In the meantime, while the Senate is constituted as it is, it is important that the western provinces of Canada should have their proper representation in the Senate. I do not think it

would be just that this should be hied in abeyance while we are working out a scheme for the improvement of the Senate. Therefore, we cannot accept the amendment for these reasons:	In the
first place, because it is entirely inappropriate as an amendment to the resolution which is now under consideration by the House; and, in the second place, because the subject has not received thorough debate in Parliament this session and the consideration which it undoubtedly merits before any distinctive steps should be taken in the way of reform.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext:
Whatever
merit there may be in the suggestion which has been made, as has been stated by the right hon. Prime Minister, it is too late in the session to give it consideration; and besides, the suggestion itself is not at all germane to the question now before us. There is a great deal of force in what was said by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sam. Sharpe) this forenoon, that that part of the constitution relating to the Senate, as it was planned and carried out by the Fathers of Confederation in 1864 and 1865, has not met with the same degree of success that has characterized the other parts of their work. He has stated, and truly so, that both parties in this respect ai'e committed to a policy of reform. The party to which I belong has certainly committed itself to this policy, and it has been said that after fifteen years in office we did not implement that part of our platform. The reason is the same ae has prevented the hon. member* for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) from offering a concrete suggestion. Nobody has yet been able in this House or in this country to suggest a plan of reform which would be acceptable to the large body of the people. The very way in which the member for South York has drafted his resolution shows the difficulty of the task. He asks the Imperial Parliament to be wiser than ourselves and to frame some amendmeqt. I am satisfied that the Imperial Parliament would not , think of changing our constitution except in the very terms in which we would direct such change. It would be vain to argue that the Imperial Parliament should make the reform; they would say to us: What is the nature of the reform you want? I think that the hon. member for South York would be averse to the Imperial Parliament making the reform 'for us. We want to have the authority of the Imperial Parliament, but
we must direct them as to the nature of the reform which we desire. In 1864, the united Canada of Upper and Lower Canada had an elective legislative council which was elected by groups of counties. The system worked fairly well, but it failed to command itself to the Fathers of Confederation and they accepted the nominative system. The nominative system has not been as successful as it ought to have been, on account of the large preponderance of party appointments. That was not the intention, as was stated at the time of Confederation. I remember very well that in the debate on Confederation Sir John A. Macdonald stated that the change of parties would keep the balance of parties in the Senate properly adjusted. It has not worked out so, and no government so far has been able to resist making the appointments on party lines. If we could devise a system to prevent having appointments made altogether on party lines we would attain the object desired. I thought at one time that we might adopt the American system and have a Senate elected by the local legislatures. But even in the United States that has not worked satisfactorily, and to-day there is an amendment of the constitution, which will shortly come into effect, providing that the senators shall be elected by the State at large. If we had an elective system the best thing would be to group the population. I do not think, however, that this is the proper time, in the dying days of a session, to discuss such an important question. My hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) might keep the matter in mind and present his views on another occasion, perhaps next session, when the matter could receive more consideration than it has hitherto received; and _ perhaps, having thought it over during the recess, he may be albLe to give us in concrete form the ideas which he wants to have implemented.
I think we have now come to the end of the resolution. I would call attention to the wording of the preamble. It says 'that a humble address be presented to His Majesty.' I would suggest that it should be 'a joint address of the Senate and House of Commons.'

speechtext:
This is the
psychological moment to deal with this question, when we propose to amend the constitution in regard to the Senate. If it comes at the tail end of the session I am not responsible for that. If the two great parties of the country are pledged to Senate reform, I think that they should have presented this question, and it should not have been left to a single member and a private member to implement their views. 1 do open the question and I do present it to the Imperial House. Perhaps the answer of the Imperial Government on receipt of this prayer of the Canadian people, in which I hope the Senate will join, will be that they have received this prayer from the House of Commons of Canada and would like to have further light upon it. In that way we would get the question advanced and have it discussed, but we will never get it advanced if it is to come up only in the dying hours of a session and if we are to increase the number of members of the Senate and ignore the pledges of the two parties in this respect. If that is not good doctrine, then it follows that the parties in this House-and I am not going to make that statement, but there will be people who will contend that the parties are not in earnest in declaring for Senate reform. I am absolutely in favour of Senate reform because I think it will widen the parliamentary institutions of this country, we will have a division of labour between the two Chambers, and the people will have an opportunity of appealing not only to this House but to the members of the Senate, and therefore enlisting their sympathies. While it is said there is no great urgency, England today is on the verge of civil war because an irresponsible body in connection with the Parliament of Great Britain has been repeatedly blocking progressive legislation and especially blocking great measures in the way of money Bills in the direction of progressive legislation. The result is that to-day the Liberals and the Progressive party in England are hampered by this condition, and they have to pass a progressive measure in three successive sessions of Parliament, under the fire of the greatest obstruction, while the reactionaries have only to vote it down once in the House of Lords and they kill the proposition. That is not progressive, that is not

what it should be. We must have something better in this country, and the people want something better. The United States would not submit to a single House of Parliament, nor would the people of Great Britain. There must be two Houses, and the two Houses, if there is to be parliamentary Government, must be responsible to public opinion. I respect what my hon. friend from New Brunswick says as to the rights of minorities; but I am not interfering with the rights of minorities; I am improving them so that public opinion in the provinces can make itself more efficient in guarding those minorities. I am not in favour of a second Chamber being created simply as a reward for political services. It ought to be created for the advancement of public legislation. Then, who is there who would justify in Canada a branch of Parliament having no age limit in it? I am not going to pass a reflection on the aged men of the Senate; I have too much veneration for age to do anything of that kind. But it is not fair to either the judicial or legislative interests that there should not be an age limit in connection with a great branch of the legislative scheme.

speechtext: I say that the principle of an irresponsible Senate is not a good one and ought to be improved. I am willing to improve it. I make a proposition here to-day in the line of improvement, and call for the discussion and cooperation of the Imperial Parliament, and I leave it there; but I leave it there standing by my resolution, and it is for this committee to deal with that resolution as they see fit.

in Ontario to further representation. I urge especially on the Postmaster General, who is the particular guardian of the interests of his compatriots in the 'Government, to urge the Prime Minister to recommend the appointment of another French-Canadian senator from Ontario.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext: I am very glad the Postmaster General has made the statement he has, because the hon. member for Queens, Prince Edward Island seemed to be under the impression that the Government was entitled to the credit of making this arrangement whereby a province shall always be entitled to a number of members in the House of Commons not less than the number of senators representing such province; and of course that is a protection more especially to the smaller provinces of New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and Nova Scotia.
