maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext:
It is well to have it
understood that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) was the first man to suggest that solution of the difficulty.
I would like to ask- if the Government has given any consideration to the representations which have been made from time to time by the Maritime provinces, and more especially by the Government of the province of New Brunswick, to the effect that the unit of representation should be applied to the province of Quebec as it existed at the time of Confederation. My hon. friend the Postmaster General knows that at the time of Confederation the province of Quebec was bounded on the north by the height of land, and that all the territory north of that belonged to the Hudson Bay Company, and was not included in the province of Quebec. Through a portion of that territory, which was added to Quebec quite a number of years ago, the Transcontinental runs, and in the future that district will no doubt have a very considerable population. The same remark applies, though perhaps not to the same extent, to that district which was added to Quebec since this Government came into office. No doubt there will be considerable population there as well, especially if mining developments should take place, as many people expect. What we in New Brunswick believe, and I think it is the view of the members of the Maritime provinces generally, is that the repre-

sentation of Quebec should be based upon the population in the original territory of Quebec, -and that the added territory should be entitled to additional representation -based upon representation. In other words, suppose that in ten years from now there should be thirty or forty thousand people in that new territory, then the people of that new territory should be entitled to a representation which would give the province of Quebec 66 members, but only the population of the original province of Quebec would count in determining the unit of representation for the different provinces. I think this question will be of considerable importance in the future. We in New Brunswick would not like to get below the representation we now have. -On the contrary, we are hoping to get back to the original fifteen members which New Brunswick had at the time of Confederation.
I -think the same remark would apply to the other provinces. Now, when we are for the first time since this new territory has been added, dealing with this subject, I think, in -connection with this resolution, that the Imperial Parliament should be asked to make a provision along the lines I have spoken of. If legislation by the Imperial Parliament is not necessary, I would ask that the Government introduce legislation into this Parliament because certainly now is the time to do justice in this Tespect. We in the lower provinces feel that a great injustice has been done and done more especially by the interpretation which the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council has given to the British North America Act. There is no doubt that at the time of Confederation the four provinces, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and, later on Prince Edward Island, were considered and the Fathers of Confederation never intended that representation by population should be- rigidly adhered to. For the protection of the smaller provinces it was- provided by section 51 that notwithstanding that a province is, upon the -basis of population, to be entitled to a certain representation, that representation shall not be reduced unless its population declines beyond a certain proportion relatively to the population of the four original provinces of Canada. That looks like a good protection. The Fathers of Confederation thought that New Brunswick would never have less than 15, Nova Scotia, 18, and, later on, Prince Edward Island, 6, -and -that with reference to Ontario the representation would never

decrease beyond what it was at the time of Confederation. But the judicial committee, unfortunately, were of the opinion that in interpreting the words ' provinces of Canada,' they were bound to include the added territory, to consider the western provinces where the population has greatly increased. This has prevented the saving clause from being of the slightest benefit to the smaller provinces and has rendered inoperative a clause that the Fathers of Confederation thought was going to be effective in preventing a reduction in the representation of the smaller provinces.
I would like to say, with respect to this provision that the representation shall not be reduced -below the number of senators, that the Imperial Parliament should be asked to amend the British North America Act so as to provide that the representation of no one province should ever be less than what it was declared to be at the time the province entered into Confederation. You could justify that proposition just as well as you could a declaration that Prince Edward Island should never have less than four, that New Brunswick should never have less than- -ten, that Nova Scotia should never have less than ten, and that Ontario should never have less than twenty-four based upon representation in the Senate. Quebec has always been the unit. It was done in the case of British Columbia. When British Columbia entered into Confederation the people had the same doubt that the people of Prince Edward Island had and they would not join the confederacy unless they had .a settled representation in the House of Commons. In the Act of Union, the people of British Columbia being a little more foresighted than the people of Prince Edward Island were, it is especially provided that the representation of British Columbia shall never be less than the number -at which it was when- that province entered the union. If that w.as right in r-egard to British Columbia, why would it be so contrary to British fair^play to apply it to the original provinces forming the confederacy? You would be just as much justified in asking the Imperial Parliament to say that Prince Edward Island should never have less than six, and that New Brunswick should never have -less than fifteen, as you would be in saying that Prince Edward Island shall never have less than four and that New Brunswick shall never have less than ten. You are doing the very same
JUNE li, 1914
tiling, only you are doing it in a roundabout way, but you make the number less than it otherwise would be.
These are two matters to which I would like the Government to give their attention. I know that members of the present provincial government, having visited Ottawa, have gone back to New Brunswick and have expressed great gratification and satisfaction at the interviews which they have had with this Government upon the .subject. They have reported that they have been received most sympathetically upon this question of representation and they have rather led the people to believe that their wishes were going to be met. I would like to know whether or not it would be possible to induce the Government to ask that provision be made to enable the British North America Act to go just a little bit farther and to provide that the representation of the original provinces shall in no case be less than it was at the time of Confederation; also that Quebec, in considering the ques tion of the unit of representation, shall be deemed to be the area forming the province of Quebec at the time of Confederation, that it shall not include the territory which has since been added, but that this new territory shall be entitled to additional representation according to its population and that the rule shall apply to the added territory as it applies to the other provinces of Canada.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE SENATE.
speechtext:
Referring to the different points raised by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and to the remarks which were made by my hon. friend from Queens, Prince Edward Island (Mr. McLean), I may say that the case of Prince Edward Island had .been put 'before council previously to the argument which was presented to the committee on redistribution. As imy right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) said when he introduced the Redistribution Bill, the impression made upon the members of the Government by the argument put before them by the Hon. Mr. Mathison and his friends was such as to lead the Government to believe that something should be done, although the Bill as introduced here did not suggest any solution of the Prince Edward Island difficulty, that -being left to the committee. The matter was again argued before the committee, and the members of the Government who were there, knowing the impression which had been made 334
upon their minds, and desirous of doing something, were quite in accord with the suggestions which were made and which have resulted in the suggestion which we find in the Redistribution Bill, and of which this claus-e before the committee, to a certain extent, is a reproduction. My horn, friend from Queens, Prince Edward Island, is right in saying that the Government have considered the proposition with a view of meeting the wishes of the people of that province as far as possible. If it had been possible to meet the full demand made by the Government of Prince Edward Island, it would have been done with the greatest pleasure, because I, for one, believe in treating the smaller provinces in the fairest possible way. The case of Prince Edward Island was not on all fours with that of British Columbia, the case of British Columbia is clearly settled by the statute which declares that the number of members for British Columbia will never be less than six. In the case of Prince Edward Island, the same wording is not employed, and the matter is very far from being as clear. There are elements and circumstances which go to show that there were expectations, at the time that Prince Edward Island entered Confederation in 1873, that the number of representatives might be reduced. Taking a broad general view of the situation in order to try to give general satisfaction, the members of the committee on redistribution, I am happy to say, adopted one of the suggestions the Government had in its mind. In order to be perfectly fair, I desire to say that the motion to that effect was moved by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) and seconded by the hon. member for Pietou (Mr. Macdonald). That is my recollection of the matter. This report is before the House; it is unanimous. I do not know whether or not we may have to give further consideration to this question; but for the moment the Government will stand by the unanimous report of the committee.
My hon. friend the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) said that, instead of reducing the number of members for the Maritime provinces and fixing the same limit as the one now in existence for the number of senators, we might have come to the conclusion to ask the Imperial Parliament to pass an enactment restoring to the Maritime provinces the number of members they had at the time of Confederation. I do not in-

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS

speechtext: tend to speak here for any province or for any one in particular. At the present moment I speak for the Government. My own personal views on the matter I have no right to put before the committee now; but I believe that something had to be done in order to prevent the Maritime provinces from going beyond at least a certain limit. We have adopted that policy for the moment; it is to a certain extent a relief of the situation, and at all events guarantees that the number of members for the Maritime provinces shall not be reduced below a certain minimum which is now fixed. Whatever consideration may be given later on to these questions remains for the future; but at this date my hon. friend from St. John will understand that, having this unanimous report from the -committee in this matter and the committee having endeavoured to meet the situation as best it could, the Government can not at the present moment, without breaking faith as regards what has passed the committee, do anything like what is suggested 'by the hon. member for St. John. We take it that this report which is before the House is binding on us.

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS
speechtext:
This is very important
legislation to bring in at this late stage in the session.

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS
speechtext:
Of course my hon.
friend knows that, if it is late, it is not entirely the fault of -any one, and at this stage no one would like to accuse any one else of being the cause of the delay. We have worked at this matter for a number of months; and we have -succeeded in bringing down a measure which gives su-ch an extent of satisfaction all around, with only one or two exceptions, that we may be given the credit for having accomplished something, if we have not done all that my hon. friend from St. John would like to see done.
In regard to the other point 5 p.m. to which my -hon. friend referred, namely, as to whether or not the unit in the province of Quebec should be according to the area or territory which existed at the time of Confederation, there is a distinction to be drawn here. If I -am wrong in this, I trust my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition who is to follow me, will correct me. Speaking from memory, I think the territory of the province of Quebec has been increased twice. The first time -an increase was made, no provision was made on the lines suggested by my hon. friend from St. John, but the

last time the boundaries of the province were extended to Hudson strait, giving the whole of Ungava to the territory of the province of Quebec, a special provision was inserted meeting the views, if I mistake not, of the hon. member -for St. John. I think I am perfectly safe in stating that, and I think my rigfirt -hon. friend will agree with me that I -am right in -my statement.
SiT WILFRID LAURIER: Yes.

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS
speechtext:
When the first Bill
was passed, extending the limits, no one seems to have thought of such a provision, and I have no recollection that it was ever
discussed'.

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS
speechtext: May I correct my hon. friend here? The first time there was an alteration of the limits was in 1896. No mention was made of such a provision at that time; but, whilst it is contended by my hon. friend the member for St. John that there was an increase in territory given to the province of Quebec, my impression has always been that the intention of the Bill was not to give any -more territory to Quebec than it was entitled to, but simply to rectify the boundary and substitute the natural boundary for what was the conventional one.

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS
speechtext: I was coming to that. I was not quite sure about the matter, and I am glad my hon. friend has made that statement. I think the first Bill that was passed was simply acquiescing in the demand or the legal pretension which the province of Quebec made that the limits were not where they should be.

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS
speechtext: That is, that the limits were not at the height of land, but extended to Hudson strait. That was really the point.

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS
speechtext:
The Bill which we
passed two years ago, that is, during our first session, provides that any new country which may be created out of the development of Ungava will not count against the other provinces.

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS
speechtext: That is not in this Bill.

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS
speechtext:
It is not necessary
that it should be, because it is in the Bill annexing Ungava.

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS
speechtext:
You think it is not
needed in the Redistribution Bill?

maintopic: KE7ISED EDITION COMMONS
speechtext: No, because that matter is fully provided for already. I am' speaking for the Government on this. We
understand that the Bill annexing Ungava makes this point perfectly clear. Therefore I think it was a fair clause to put in as regards the other provinces.

Keferring to the
point raised by my hon. friend from St. John, I think it is just as well that it should go on record in the discussion upon this question that the committee, in considering what the electoral unit in the province of Quebec was at that time in order to arrive at the number of representatives in the other provinces of the Dominion, treated the unit as having been made up of the number of population that was in the old portion of Quebec, and did not take into consideration at all the unorganized portion. We arrived at the unit in the same way as was stated by my right hon. friend the Premier when he introduced the Bill, namely, by dividing 65 into the population of old Quebec as it was organized.
Before Ungava was annexed?

Yes; so that hereafter in any future redistribution it is well to have it definitely understood that this Parliament, in dealing with this question at this time, so treated that point and left the new territory to be dealt with entirely apart from Quebec as it is mentioned in the British North America Act.
I might say in reference to the question mentioned by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) that, so far as I was personally concerned, I treated it as having been closed on account of the statements made by the Prime Minister on February 10 last, referring to the proposition that the representation of all the smaller provinces of the Dominion should be fixed at the number at which they entered the Confederation. The Prime Minister dealt fully with that question, and announced the policy of the Government as follow:
Under these circumstances, as the provinces at the conference to which X have alluded had declined to take any action or pass any resolution on the subject-although I understand there were a good many expressions of sympathy-it did not seem to us to be our duty to come to this Parliament and propose any remedy for the unfortunate situation with which the Maritime provinces find themselves confronted.
So that the Government on the appointment of the Committee, with that intimation as to what their policy was in regard to that whole question, practically closed the doors to the deliberations of the Com-334i
mittee reaching any end which would mean the preservation of the original representation. In regard to Prince Edward Island I regret that my hon. friend from Kings (Mr. Hughes), and my hon. friend from Prince (Mr. Richards) whose illness I am sure every member of the House deplores, are not here today at this discussion. Unfortunately, the hon. member for Kings was called home on business and went down with me on Friday and has been unable to return. He desired me to mention if this matter came up-and at that time it was thought that it would go over for the (session altogether-that were he present ha would represent the views of his constituents by moving a resolution similar to that moved by my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Maclean) to-day; and my hon. friend from Prince (Mr. Richards), and himself voicing, as I am sure they would, the feeling in Prince Edward Island, would have asked us, as we are now being asked, to assent to the proposition that this BiP should Ibe amended by practically providing for maintaining the representation of Prince Edward Island at its original figure. The Government, however, have barred the door to any action of that kind by the announcement of policy upon the introduction of the Bill by the Prime Minister, who said in addition the Bill he was then introducing he would leave blank the number of representatives to be named for Prince Edward Island, to be filled in by the committee. Every hon. gentleman will recall the discussion on the second reading, when it was the unanimous opinion that it was not within the power of Parliament, having regard to the provisions of .section 51 of the British North America Act, to pass any legislation which provided for a representation in any one of the provinces greater than what was fixed by that section. I ventured at that time to point out to the right hon. gentleman that the only remedy for dealing with the case of Prince Edward Island would be by a motion for an Address to the Imperial Parliament to fix the increased representation. My right hon. friend suggested that it would be possible for this Parliament to pass a Bill which would not come into effect until it was ratified by the Imperial Parliament. The matter came before the committee. The case of Prince Edward Island was presented to it by the Premier of that province and one of hiis colleagues, urging the ground that a mistake had been made in the preparation of the original Orders in

Council, or rather in the petition from the Parliament of Canada and from the two legislative bodies in Prince Edward Island, which, when ratified by the Imperial Order in Council, was their charter. It was put forth that the statement in these petitions which said that representation was to be reduced from time to time under the British North America Act was an error and that the proper intention of the parties at that time was that the clause should have read that the representation should have been increased. The decision of the committee was to the effect that the proper method of dealing with the question was by proposing an address to the Imperial Parliament fixing a minimum representation for all the Maritime provinces, which is now proposed to be done by this committee. I have not personally had the opportunity of seeing the report which has been submitted by the Redistribution Committee; I presume on account of my being absent. I had the opportunity of seeing the resolution which was submitted to it in the terms which it was understood would be presented by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes). That resolution, I assume, is in terms the clause of this resolution which is now in committee.
The situation, therefore, is that one must regret that the aspirations and feelings of the people of the smallest province of the Dominion with regard to representation cannot be met under existing conditions. The situation with them is a very keen problem; they regard the preservation of their original rights as of the utmost importance; and my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Maclean) has not put the case too strongly in regard to it. Naturally, their insular position, and the special interests which always develop under such conditions, cause a more intense feeling probably than might exist under other conditions and in other provinces. The Government, however, has taken the full responsibility of solving this question by proposing this limitation. In the province of New Brunswick, where now we have eleven representatives, this would prevent a reduction of their representation, no matter what the circumstances may be, below the number of ten. That same limitation would exist in Nova Scotia. It is to be hoped by every hon. gentleman in this House that the development of eastern Canada, which, at the present time, seems to be arrested- as indeed is the condition all over Canada -will be such that it will not be necessary to resort to this limitation, but that that portion of Canada will in future exceed its present representation in this House.

The hon. member for
Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) intimated at the outset of . his remarks his views with respect to the position of the Government on the question of a minimum representation of the Maritime provinces; and intimated, although he did not say so, that if the Government had not barred the door perhaps he might, have attempted to effect an entrance, or taken some other ground. The hon. member is not a man vyho is apt to be deterred by barred doors, particularly if they are barred by the party opposed to him. I do not rise for the purpose of attempting to make any political capital for the Government because of their attitude in connection with this matter; but I do rise for the purpose of having the record absolutely correct. It is true that the Prime Minister, in referring to Prince Edward Island, intimated that a certain course might be pursued. At the same time I wish to refer tny hon. friend to the remarks of his leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), on February 17, dealing with the manner in which the Prime Minister had referred to this very question. The right hon. gentleman says:
I have to represent to my right hon. friend that that is a matter upon which the committee cannot have any jurisdiction; it is a matter on which this House has no jurisdiction.

Hear, hear.
Parliament in this matter is not a free agent; the whole question is simply a question of arithmetic.
Mr. McKENZIE [DOT]. Is that right ?

I concur in that. My
object in making reference to that statement is to point out that it cannot be said in later days that it was the fault of the present Administration that an attempt was not made to have the old original representation of the Maritime provinces rerestored. My sole purpose in rising to-day is not to make political capital, but to make the situation perfectly clear and to prevent any attempt at the making of political capital out of a question of this kind in the years to come. It is quite true, as the Postmaster General has said, that I proposed the motion that was accepted by the committee that no province shall hereafter have less members in the House of Commons than it has representatives in the Senate, and it was my wish that the

hon. member for Pictou should be the seconder of that motion. I observe that he nods his assent; I am quite content with that, because I was not quite clear as to whether or not he had been the actual seconder. I shall not delay the committee by expressing my regret that Prince Edward Island is to be prevented from having its original representation of six members;
I shall content myself with the few remarks which I have made in explanation of the attitude both of the Government and of the Opposition with respect to the minimum representation of the Maritime provinces.

I want to take issue with my hon. friend the Postmaster General and also, as I do not often have occasion to do, with my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, with regard to what took place some years ago when the boundaries of the province of Quebec were enlarged. This matter is of deep interest to the people of the province which I represent, and I offer that as my excuse for taking up a few moments of the time of the committee in order that my position may be placed on record. The question is going to come up again; I warn the Government that it will come up, not only because I shall bring it up, but because the provincial Government of New 'Brunswick will feel bound to bring the matter up in the interests of the people whom they represent. They and I do not agree politically, but I give them credit for an honest and sincere effort to secure the rights of- New Brunswick as one of the smaller provinces which cannot get any additional territory. Our contention is that when a large area was added to Quebec a few years- ago that was not a mere settlement, according to our contention-I say it with all respect, in view of the statements of the right hon. leader of the Opposition and the Minister of Militia-of a dispute as to what were the boundaries of Quebec; it was the giving of an enormous additional and valuable territory to the province of Quebec. In this conclusion I think we are fortified by geography and by authority of the very strongest kind. This matter is important to us in the lower provinces not only in the matter of representation but as to the compensation which should be paid to the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, to	which there is
no opportunity of	adding	additional
territory, by reason of the vast area which belonged to the whole Dominion of Canada,
which belonged to the people of New-Bruns-wick as well to as the people of Ontario and Quebec, and which has been given by this Parliament to the two great provinces of Ontario and Quebec. I understand that we cannot get much support, unless on moral grounds, from the people of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta because vast territories in the north have been added to those provinces and additions may be made in the future as well. But in the case of the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, there is no chance for the addition of territory, and what we in New Brunswick do contend is that all that territory which was known as Rupert's Land, taking in all the territory north of the height of land; all the territory which was drained by the rivers which flow into the Hudson bay, belonged to the people of the whole of Canada. There is no question about the language of the old treaties which determined the matter, and I do submit, with all deference, that any one who looks into the question and examines these treaties must be forced to the conclusion that the first addition to the territory of Quebec was not the mere settling of a dispute; it was the adding of a vast area to the territory of that province. We may be wrong in this, but I should not be doing my duty as <a representative of my province if I did no-t bring the matter to the attention of the House and say that I do not believe that the representatives of the lower provinces will acquiesce in that view. I believe that they will continue to raise the point again and again until they secure what they believe to be justice. They have been promised by this Government that the matter would be taken into consideration. This afternoon we find the Postmaster General glossing the matter over and not giving us very much satisfaction with regard to it. I greatly fear that if we do not press our claims, they will get but scanty consideration. I regret that there is not a single member for the province of New Brunswick upon the Government side of the House present when such an important matter is under consideration. The Conservatives of New Brunswick promised the people over and over again that they would fight the battle of the people upon the question of representation and upon the question of compensation for the added territory whenever the opportunity arose. The opportunity

is here now, and I am sorry that they have found it impossible to be present, because I should like to have them add to my feeble voice their contention that the Government should give some consideration to the claims of the people of New Brunswick and the other Maritime provinces for justice in regard to these matters.

We are proceeding
with resolutions which are assented to by both sides of the House, and surely my hon. friend will admit that it is hardly fair to say that the members for New Brunswick on the Conservative side should be here to take part in the discussion. This may be a good political move, but I think my hon. friend will agree with me that he is going a little too far.

My hon. friend will
agree with me that we in New Brunswick who feel so deeply on this question; who feel that an injustice has been done and who have been appealing to this Government from time to time to do justice, may be pardoned even if even at inopportune times we raise our voices to urge that justice should be done. I am not blaming gentlemen supporting the Government for being absent; I merely express my regret that they have found it impossible to be present when there is an opportunity of discussing this most important question, in respect of which they have pledged the people of New Brunswick that on every occasion and at every opportunity they would urge their claims for justice in this Parliament.

My hon. friend the Postmaster General refers to the unanimous report of the committee. The pronouncement of the Government on the introduction of this Bill was to the effect that they did not purpose introducing any legislation dealing with the difficulties that exist in the Maritime provinces. Those of us who were members of the committee deahng with this question of dividing the constituencies regarded the policy of the Government as the policy of the majority of the committee and acted accordingly.

The records speak for themselves.
Resolution reported and read the first time.
Mr. PELLETIER moved the second reading of the resolution.
Mr. A. A. McLEAN (Queens, Prince Edward Island) moved in amendment:

That the resolutions be not now read a second time but that the same be referred back to the committee with instructions that they have power to amend the same as follows :
(4b) Prince Edward Island shall be entitled to be represented in the House of Commons by six members, the representation to be increased under the provisions of ' the British North America Act, 1867.' Prince county shall constitute one district to he designated ' Prince county district ' and return two members. Queens county shall constitute one district, to be designated ' Queens county district ' and return two members; and Kings county shall constitute one district to be designated ' Kings county district ' and return two members.
Amendment negatived, motion agreed to, and Resolution read the second time and concurred in.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, the redistribution of the seats in the city of Quebec does not appear to me to have been carried out in a spirit of fairness, either as regards the territory itself or the population included within its limits. I trust, however, that the House will believe me when I say that my criticism is not suggested by the blotting out of the constituency of Quebec Centre in the new arrangements. No, the data supplied by the census of 1911 rendered necessary a change in the limits of the various constituencies comprised within the bounds of the old city. The best evidence of my good faith in making the statements I am about to make in

this House, is my abstaining from any appeal to the Government for the restoration of that electoral district of Quebec Centre, though I would be delighted if it were restored.
Of course, and it goes without saying, I was greatly attached to that constituency, which I have had the honour of representing here since 1905, one of the finest constituencies of the province, and possibly of the whole of Canada. Its population is one of the most amiable and courteous that it is possible to meet; it comprises, in large numbers, all classes of society: men of the professional, business, commercial, industrial, labouring, merchant and banking occupations; and it is with sincere regret that I will have to sever my political relations with them all, Liberal and Conservative, as well; for the latter, though they opposed me strenuously, have always acted ae gentlemen towards me; and in regard to all of them I retain only the best remembrance. Indeed, from the honourable place which I occupy in this House, I wish to thank this evening once more my electors for the generous and full confidence which they reposed in me for the last nine years.
Now, reverting to my remarks in connection with this matter, I stated that the redistribution was not justified on the basis of the population comprised in each one of the new constituencies. As a matter of fact, the constituency to be designated Quebec South will have a population of 17,000 souls, while Quebec East and Quebec West, will have 20,000 souls. Why that difference of nearly one-half between the population of one of these constituencies and the two others? That discrepancy might have been easily avoided.
To carve out Quebec South, the constituencies of Quebec West and Quebec Centre are jointed, after eliminating, however, from the latter constituency St. John's ward, which is annexed to the new Quebec East; besides the parish of Sillery is detached from the county of Quebec. There were, nevertheless, two means available towards avoiding that disproportion between the various groups; the first means was to take in the parishes of Ste. Foye and Cap Rouge, which would have given a total population of 18,000 or 20,000 souls.
The second means was even more simple of application; it consisted in joining together Quebec Centre and Quebec West, which are contiguous to one another over the greater part of their length. That was

certainly the most rational, the most logical division which it was possible to adopt.
Why has St. John's ward been eliminated? Because, I imagine, that ward had been for many years the Liberal hive in Quebec Centre, and might have rendered very doubtful the chances of the Conservative party in the new constituency in Quebec South. It remains, however, that the carving out of these two constituencies has been accomplished in a most arbitrary manner, and though it may be considered of paramount importance to insure the safety of the Conservative party, such a procedure is inexcusable.
St. John's ward, which is annexed to the future Quebec East, might have been replaced by either St. Sauveur or St. Valier wards, which are included in the proposed constituency of Quebec West. As regards Quebec West itself, why was it not made out of one of those two wards of St. Valier or St. Sauveur, together with the Stadacpna and St. Malo wards, Petite Riviere, and the parishes of Sillery, Ste. Foye and Gifp Rouge? And if that was not enough, was it not possible to further take in one or two parishes of the county of Quebec, which on all sides borders and surrounds the city of Quebec. It may be alleged that the division proposed as regards the new constituencies of Quebec South and Quebec East was desirable inasmuch as it secured an increase of population sufficient to allow the city of Quebec to retain its three seats in the House of Commons. But it will be found impossible to justify on the same ground, or any other ground, the taking in of the parishes of St. Augustin, Ecureuils and Neuville (Pointe aux Trembles) detached from the constituency of Portneuf to complete the proposed electoral district of Quebec West. The inclusion of these three parishes will have the effect of creating an urban constituency thirty-one miles long, a county which will reach out as far as the parish of Cap Sant6, the county town of the second next rural constituency to the west of Quebec.
There was one very simple thing to do: take over from the county of Quebec one or two parishes, since that county is contiguous to the city on every side, and since, in many respects, its interest are identical with those of the city, and its population in daily intercourse with ours, and constantly found within the city limits on business of various sorts.
It seems to me, therefore, that the bound-

aries which are proposed are out of harmony with the principles of the most elementary justice. It is generally known that the electors of these parishes of the county of Portneuf have been found as a rule on the Conservative side of politics, and the intention, no doubt, was to have that influence to bear on the new constituency of Quebec West. There does not seem to be any other plausible explanation. So, I would be justified in drawing the conclusion that the taking in of these three parishes of Quebec West is a sort of political manoeuvering under the cover of the law, and I deem it my duty to voice my protest against such a course.
In conclusion', I call on the Government to amend their Bill in that respect and to replace these three muncipalities of the electoral district of Portneuf by municipalities comprised in the county of Quebec, for the reason I have stated.
The hon. Postmaster General has already given himself a free hand with the constituency of Montmorency; let him take another slice to replace what is to be taken off his county, and he may rest assured that in so doing he will not incur the ill-will of the hon. member for Charlevoix, who has been favoured with another section of that same county of Montmorency and has accepted that gift rather coldly, if rumour is to be credited.
On resuming my seat, I once more express the hope that the Government will modify the boundaries of the future county of Quebec West in the way I said yesterday.

There are also joint interests which should not be lost sight of.
We had before us three divisions, one of which had a population of 9,000 souls, and the general wish of the committee was that the old city of Quebec should retain its three seats.
The constituency of Quebec West, as it now is constituted, having only 9,000 of a population, it was necessary that we should increase that number, and the only means at our disposal was to transfer part of the population of Quebec Centre to the new constituency of Quebec South. Foye and Cap Rouge in the county of Quebec, and the parishes of St. Augustin, Ecureuils and Neuville, it may seem odd to some people that we should have made that selection. In this, case, it may seem strange that some parishes of the county of Portneuf should be transferred to the constituency of Quebec West. However, it is by that means that we succeed in retaining three electoral seats within the city of Quebec. True, one of those divisions extends some distance into the country, but I trust that on the whole the people will be satisfied. Some parishes might have been taken from the county of Montmorency and transferred to that of Quebec, while some parishes of the last-mentioned country might have been transferred to Quebec West. The object of the delegation was to prevent the parcelling out of the county of L'Assomption and to obtain that this country, which is one of the most beautiful, if not the most beautiful in the province and in the whole Dominion, should be left in all its integrality with na addition nor subtraction. However, I must say, in all justice, that the delegates expressed the opinion that they preferred to see it united to its neighbour, the county of Montcalm, rather than to see it divided. I understand that by deciding in favour of the union, the committee made a slight concession to the delegation which I had the honour to introduce to the Postmaster General. But, after all, is it very fair to deprive those two counties of theiT respective and separate existence which gave them two representatives, and to unite them into one county with but one representative? Mr. Chairman, I deem that, by so doing, the Government will have committed a very ugly injustice, and I protest with all my might against such determination. It is claimed that the representation of Montreal must be increased because the population of that city has increased, and that, as a consequence of this, some of the rural counties must he struck off the list. This kind of reasoning might bring about, after a few years, a result which would be most nefarious and somewhat absurd. For my part, Mr. Chairman, I deem that the population of a city, being very numerous and very thick, wants less representation than does a population scattered out in the country, and that it is easier to represent fifty thousand electors in a city than to represent fifteen thousand in the country. The representative of a city is in daily contact with his constituents, and at two hours' notice he can bring them to-

gether to consult them and to submit the questions which may be of interest to them. It is not so with the representative of a country population. He has to travel painfully over long distances and on rough roads if he wishes to come in contact with his electors. Therefore, I blame the committee and the Government, the author of this Bill, for weakening in thie way the influence of the countries to the benefit of the cities. [Moreover, if some of the rural counties must disappear, why should they unite L'Assumption to Montcalm rather than Brome to ,Missis-quoi or to Stanstead? Mr. Chairman, I desire to address a few remarks to the committee on this section inasmuch as it refers to the constituency which I represent. The measure that is before the committee is based upon the report of a joint committee composed of hon. members from both sides of the House. Their report, I understand, was practically unanimous and I have no doubt that this legislation will eventually be pdopted by this Parliament. Indeed, it is very obvious from the manner in which the various clauses affecting the redistribution in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec have been adopted this evening that such will be the case. By this Bill the province of Ontario loses four seats, New Brunswick two, Prince Edward Island one, and Nova Scotia two. Quebec holds its present number of seats, though many Changes are made, and all western provinces gain seats. But in all there are nineteen seats throughout Canada wiped out by this Redistribution Bill. The Bill seriously affects the constituency of Digby. At the present time, in western Nova Scotia, there are three electoral divisions, Yarmouth, Digby and Annapolis, and it is proposed to divide Digby, attaching the municipality of Clare to the county of Yarmouth, uniting the municipalities of Digby and Annapolis, and forming the constituencies of Yarmouth-Clare and Digiby-Annapolis. When, some time ago, it was persistently rumoured that the constituency of Digby was liable to be effected toy this redistribution, I conferred with my 'hoe. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), who was the Nova Scotia representative on the Redistribution Committee and I then presented my views to him and 'he noted my objections. At a subsequent time I wrote my hon friend restating my objections in this matter.
I have no doubt that the Redistribution Committee has acted according to its best judgment. I am sure that its responsibilities were great; that its difficulties were many, and that amidst con-flicting interests it had its own troubles; but, Sir, of course any member of this House, whose constitu-

ency is materially and prejudicially affected, naturally dislikes the situation, however necessary it may be to make changes of that kind in order to effect a redistribution in this country. In common with a large number of other members in this House from the province of Ontario and Quebec and the Maritime provinces whose constituencies are affected in that way, I must therefore express my deep regret that the committee has found it necessary to make this arrangement. The fact that the Maritime provinces lose five seats in this redistribution is a matter which I regret as well, as in the last two preceding redistributions those provinces have suffered considerable loss. But I believe that the Maritime provinces are to-day on the eve of a very considerable development, and that further redistributions may, in some measure at least, redress the losses which are now being sustained. In the meantime, this Parliament is confronted with the provisions of the British North America Act, with the result of the last census and with the necessity of passing a Redistribution Bill. In this situation of facts, I can merely re-state the regret which I have expressed, that it has been found desirable or necessary to make a redistribution which will so materially effect the constituency which I have represented in this House during the past two Parliaments.

I share with my hon.
friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson) the regret that the representation in the Maritime provinces has to be reduced under the provisions of this law, but as the law embodies the constitution of the country, we must observe it, and therefore it has been necessary to take this course. In view of that necessity, we had	to consider
in Nova Scotia, as elsewhere, the counties which would have to be altered. The county of Digby, adjoining on the one side the county of Yarmouth and on the other the county of Annapolis, is divided into two municipalities, namely, the municipality of Digby and the municipality of Clare. Adding the municipality of Clare to the county of Yarmouth, one gets 32,097, or just a little more than the electoral unit. Adding the municipality of Digby to the county of Annapolis, one gets practically 30,000, or almost the exact electoral unit. The population of Digby is partly Acadian, and partly of British origin; and in the adjoining county of Yarmouth the Acadians of Clare will, of course, have
associations with a great many of their own race who live in the county of Yarmouth. I have no doubt that the committee took these matters into consideration. It is absolutely impossible to make a redistribution in any province in Canada that will be thoroughly satisfactory to every one. The only thing at which the committee can aim is to take practically the best course; and it seemed that it was necessary to make this redistribution of the western part of the province of Nova Scotia, as well as to join the counties of Antigonish and Guysborough in the eastern part of the province.
My hon. friend the member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) has a splendid position in this House; and I am sure we all appreciate the service that he has rendered not only to his constituents, but to the country during his service as such member. I am absolutely sure that his constituents are as convinced of that as are the members of this House, who have seen his work in this Parliament and who know it. I can only say that I very deeply regret that it has been found necessary to take the course with regard to his constituency which the committee have recommended; but I am sure that he will appreciate that they have done so only by reason of the fact that they thought, on the whole, it was the proper and the best course to take under the circumstances.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Before this section is
accepted by the committee I desire to offer a few observations with respect to the subject of redistribution as it affects the counties of Richmond and South Cape Breton. It is rather unfortunate that this important legislation has been delayed until this late hour of the session. In many respects it is more important than any other legislation that has been introduced into Parliament during the present session. The Bill was brought down by the Prime Minister on the 10th February and received its second reading on the 17th February; and here we are in the last hours of a five-months' session of Parliament endeavouring to give consideration to this important question at a time when one might almost hear the booming of the guns on Nepean Point as they salute His Royal Highness, who comes to prorogue Parliament to-morrow afternoon.
I desire to point out that, with respect

to the distribution in Nova Scotia, it is absolutely unfair and unjustifiable. For some time since Parliament met, and when it was known that the Redistribution Bill was to be introduced at the present session, newspapers supporting the Conservative party were assiduous in their efforts to create the impression that there would be, on this occasion at all events, a redistribution that would be so absolutely fair and just to all parties concerned that it would receive the unanimous consent and approval of the House. Further than that, some days ago we were informed that, unless the Redistribution Bill was accepted by the minority, and they signed away all right to critise or censure it, they would be punished by the withholding of this Bill during the present session, and one would be brought down next session which would be less defensible and more inequitable than the one we are discussing to-night. I have here a quotation from the Regina Daily Province, under date of June 4, 1914. This is what it says with regard to redistribution, and this is the threat that it holds out to the Liberals of the House of Commons if they refuse to fall down and worship the creation of the Minister of Public Works and the majority of the Conservatives upon the Redistribution Committee. It says:
Among the Conservatives, while there is a feeling of disappointment that the work of the committee has been in vain, there is also a feeling that the concessions made were too great, oeyond what could have reasonably been expected, and that next session such great concessions would be unnecessary. Many Conservatives say they are thankful the committee has disagreed, as they were receiving much the worse of the deal.
To the fairness of Hon. Robert Rogers, Liberals pay the highest tribute. They say that in every case of dispute he stood for absolute . fairness to the minority. Many of them say that next to the non-acceptance of the proposed measure their greatest regret is that his efforts to get a fair redistribution have not been rewarded by the success they merited. There is still a possibility of the measure becoming law as the fair Liberals wish it, and they are using every effort tonight to have their party accept. They will likely prevail, but it will then depend upon the Conservatives whether they be permitted another opportunity to accept a redistribution, which for the first time in Canada, gives the advantage to the minority.
There is not a veiled but an open threat that unless the Liberals in this House accept the redistribution which the Minister of Public Works and his colleagues on the committee feel like giving to Parliament, the Liberal party would suffer in the
redistribution next year. I have here a quotation from the Montreal Star, dated June 8, which says:
In view of the fact that apart from redistribution, all the big Government Bills have passed the House and are being facilitated in ' the Senate-save the Farmers Bank Bill-the predominant desire is that the week-end should see prorogation, but to the Star to-day, it was plainly stated by the highest authority that if there is no more progress than of late, and no more disposition to accept redistribution as it stands, an adjournment is quite probable.
* We have spent three months in an effort to please the Liberals over redistribution,' said a Cabinet Minister to-day. * When next we take up the Bill it will be with the intent of pleasing ourselves.'
As I stated a moment ago, the Redistribution Bill was introduced in this House on the 9th day of February and received its second reading on February 19. The bringing down of the report was postponed from day to day and from week to week, until only in the dying hours of the session is the Bill brought down, when there is no proper or adequate opportunity of discussing its features. Notwithstanding the threat which was held out by our Conservative friends in this House, and by the Conservative newspapers in the country that if the Liberals constituting the minority of the committee did not sign a unanimous report, redistribution would be postponed until next year and i much more iniquitous Bill would be brought down for the approval of Parliament; to the credit and to the honour of the minority of the committee be it said that it did not propose being dragooned or browbeaten into what in their judgment was not a fair or proper measure to be adopted by this Parliament. It is not unusual for the members of the Opposition to be called into consultation with the members supporting the Government in the matter of redistribution. It is a well-established practice in Great Britain. It is well known that in 1884 when Mr. Gladstone introduced his Redistribution Bill, he invited to the deliberations of the Redistribution Committee Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote. These two distinguished leaders of the Conservative party accepted the responsibility of taking part in the preparation of the Redistribution Bill, but it was only on the condition that they should not, by their taking part in the work of the committee, surrender their right to criticise the report when it came up for consideration in the House of Commons. But the genius who presided over the Redistribution Com-

mittee in this House thought that he could improve upon the methods of Mr. Gladstone, and while Mr. Gladstone very readily assented to the proposal that members of the majority taking part in the Redistribution Committee should be free to criticise the report when it was brought down, some of the members representing the majority in the committee thought that in this particular case the Opposition should be gagged; that there should be no criticism and no censure with regard to the unfavourable and improper features of the Bill, and that the penalty of criticism, would be the bringing down of a more unjust measure at the next session of Parliament. It is fortunate that the hon. Minister of Public Works was able to bring down a redistribution which evoked as little criticism as the Bill which was
11 p.m. brought down yesterday afternoon, but I have no doubt that members representing the minority in the committee, although they were not getting fair-play and the kind of redistribution to which they were entitled, felt that probably it was a good deal better than they had expeoted, in view of the experiences that are so well known as to the election methods that prevail in other parts of Canada.
There are certain interests and certain conditions existing in this country that every person at the head of a government desiring to govern this country in such manner that the rights of all may be pr&-served and that equal justice may be meted out to all, cannot overlook. While this country is divided between different classes, religions and interests; while newspapers discuss these differences and while almost every condition of life is regulated according to those conditions, I am not one of those who think that thi3 House of Parliament should be the only place in Canada where consideration of these divisions ought to be tabooed. We are brought face to face day by day with the fact that in this country there are different religious beliefs, there are majorities and minorities, and that being the case it is the duty of the representatives in Parliament to bear these in mind and not be deterred from standing by what they regard as the rights of minorities solely because they may be charged with discussing matters the bringing up of which might be said to be not in the interests of peace and harmony. Some few years ago in another branch of

this Parliament the Right Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright, discussing a proposal to amend the constitution of the Senate, made use of the following language:
Then there is another and somewhat more delicate matter. Our Senate, as constituted, allows for recognition in the body politic of certain classes who, from various causes have not been able to obtain proper recognition on the floor of the House of Commons. In my own province of Ontario, I am bound to say that In the whole course of my long political experience I have felt it as more or less a reproach to the province and to my fellow-countrymen there, that the Catholic element in Ontario never did receive full recognition or representation on the floor of the House of Commons.
In Ontario to-day there are about 400,000 Roman Catholics-good subjects of His Majesty: nevertheless, although they comprise from one-fifth to one-sixth part of the whole population, there are to-day on the floor of Parliament- and they are better represented in this Parliament than I have ever known them to be before to the best of my recollection-there are but seven men representing these 400,000, and two of these are gentlemen of French extraction who represent almost purely French constituencies. Now, that is not quite fair. It is only too true that there are a great many constituencies in the province of Ontario as to which party managers on both sides will tell you there is no use in running Roman Catholic candidates. That is not the fault of the leaders on either side. For very good and excellent reasons, the leaders on both sides would he exceedingly glad to see an adequate representation of this important element.
Let us compare the case of the province of Quebec. In Quebec there are just one-eighth Protestants to seven-eighths Catholics. These one-eighth Protestants return, I find, twelve members out of the sixty-five. In other words, in Quebec, one-eighth of the population are able to return nearly one-fifth of the representation ; in Ontario, from one-fifth to one-sixth return one-twelfth to one-thirteenth of the representation.
Sir Richard Cartwright was net afraid to discuss this question in another branch of the legislature, and having established that precedent I feel that I am justified in ad verting to that particular aspect as it affects the Redistribution Bill which is now under consideration.
This Redistribution Bill provides for the elimination of two representatives from the House of Commons. That is done by virtue of an obligation cast upon the Government by section 51 of the British North America Act, which is as follows:
On the completion of the census in the year one thousand eight hundred and seventy-one, and of each subsequent decennial census, the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such manner, and at such time as the Parliament of Canada from time to time provides, subject and according to the following rules :

1.	Quebec shall have the fixed number of sixty-five members.
2.	There shall be assigned to each of the other provinces such a number of members as will bear the same proportion to the number of its papulation (ascertained at such census) as the number sixty-five bears to the number of the poplation of Quebec (so ascertained).
3.	In the computation of the number of members for a province a fractional part not exceeding one-half of the whole number requisite for entitling the province to a member shall be disregarded; but a fractional part exceeding one-half of that number shall be equivalent to the whole number.
4.	On any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards.
5.	Such readjustment shall not take effect until the termination of the then existing Parliament.
There is the authority by which the Prime Minister brings down his Redistribution Bill to Parliament. Under the census of 1911 and by the application of the rules laid down in the section I have quoted, Nova Scotia stood to lose two representatives. The selection of the two constituencies that are to be eliminated from the political map of Nova Scotia was determined by the committee. In their wisdom they thought well to unite the counties of Antigonish and Guysborough, and they divide the county of Digby between Yarmouth and Annapolis. Having done that, I contend that the obligation of the committee and of the Government ceased; there was nothing more to be done, the w'ork of the committee was ended. But the majority of the committee, having eliminated the two members from Nova Scotia as required under the census and by virtue of the British North America Act, went to the island of Cape Breton, the only portion on the Maritime provinces where the population has increased in the last decade, and brought about a condition of affairs which virtually eliminates a third constituency. I submit that there is absolutely no justification or excuse for any such interference with the constituency of Richmond.
I said a moment ago that we are bound to observe certain differences and certain divisions which exist with respect to the population of this country. At the present moment there are in the province of Nova Scotia three constituencies which are overwhelmingly Roman Catholic, three constituencies where Roman Catholics might be
elected at any time should the electors prefer representatives of that denomination. These three constituencies are Antigonish, Richmond and the county of Inverness. By this Redistribution Bill Antigonish, one of the three Roman Catholic constituencies, is practically eliminated by its union with Guysborough. They go into the island of Cape Breton and blot out Richmond as a Catholic constituency by merging it with Cape Breton, so that there remains, after this Bill goes into force, practically only one Roman Catholic constituency in Nova Scotia. I do not mean to say only one constituency having a majority of Roman Catholics, but I do say that this Redistribution Bill has the effect of wiping out two of the constituencies of Nova Scotia heretofore known as characteristically Roman Catholic, and leaves only one, Inverness.
What has been the history of the county of Richmond? I said a moment ago it was one of the three characteristically Roman Catholic constituencies in Nova Scotia. I have not the census returns previous to 1867, so I cannot give the proportion of Roman Catholics to members of other religious denominations before that time; but in that year there was elected to this House from the county of Richmond a Roman Catholic, William Croke. In 1869, out of 14,268 inhabitants of the county of Richmond there were 10,243 Roman Catholics; that is to say there were more than two Roman Catholics for every one of any other denomination. In that year the county of Richmond returned to the House of Commons Mr. Levesconte, an Anglican. In 1874, with the same proportion in respect of population, Mr. E. P. Flynn, a Roman Catholic, was returned. In 1881, when according to the census of that year the population was 15,121 of whom 10,722 were Roman- Catholics, the Hon. IT. N. Paint, a Baptist, was returned. In 1891, when the population was 14,339 the Roman Catholics numbered 10,238 and they elected Mr. J. A. Gillies, a Roman Catholic. In 1900 the population was 13,515, of whom 9,505 were Roman Catholics. In that year Mr. Joseph Matheson, a Presbyterian, was elected to this Parliament. In 1904, Mt. D. Finlayson, now Judge Finlayson, was elected. In 1908, I myself was elected to represent the county of Richmond in Parliament. So, taking the whole history of the county since 1867, there were four Catholics and four Protestants elected to represent the county of Richmond, notwith-

standing that the proportion of Catholics in that county was more than two to one. I say this to show to the committee the tolerance that has prevailed in Richmond at all times as regards political matters. Two years ago we had a question up in thiis House with respect to the rights which the Maritime provinces should enjoy in relation to the natural resources of the territory of the Northwest which it was proposed to add to the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan. It was argued by some hon. members in this House that a certain portion of those lands should be set aside and a fund be derived from the sale of these lands which should go to the credit of the Maritime provinces by way of increased subsidy. It was contended by other hon. gentlemen that inasmuch as the Maritime provinces had no added territory from which they could derive any additional revenue, it would only be fair and right that something should be done to prevent a further decrease in the representation of tire Maritime provinces in this Parliament. It is within your knowledge as that of every gentleman of this committee that for the past ten years a very considerable agitation has existed in the Maritime provinces with respect to the continued decrease in the representation in this House. In 1903 a stated case was sent to the Supreme Court of Canada with a view of testing the contention made by the Premiers of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island as to whether or not the Maritime provinces should be subjected to any decrease of representation arising out of the census of 1901 and the case was decided adversely to the contention of the Maritime provinces in the Supreme Court. It was sent to the Privy Council. The Privy Council dealt with that matter with the result that the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada was confirmed and no remedy was therefore found from the imminent decrease in representation of the Maritime provinces, a further instalment of which we are suffering at this moment. I have here the memorandum prepared by the Premiers of the Maritime provinces in the month of October last which was submitted to the federal Government with a view to the amelioration of certain complaints that were alleged to exist in the Maritime provinces. The question of the legal right of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island to retain

their original representation was referred to the Supreme Court of Canada in 1903, and was decided against these provinces. On appeal to the Privy Council, the answer of the Supreme Court to the question submitted was held to be correct.
We must bow to this decision so far as the strict interpretation of the written contract is concerned, but this was not the expectation and belief of the delegates at the time of the negotiation of the terms of union, for the Hon. George Brown in moving the resolution fixing the number of representatives which each colony should have in the House, stated: * The practical result will be that while Lower Canada certainly will not be less and the lower provinces may increase in population, they cannot decrease in the number of representatives. It keeps the House within a reasonable limit.' And the Hon. A T. Galt, in a speech delivered in Sherbrooke on November 23, 1864, shortly after the termination of the Quebec conference, and reported in the Montreal Gazette of that time, declared: ' The House would never have less than one hundred and ninety-four members.'
Representation by population while accepted as a guiding principle in fixing the representation of each province in the Dominion Parliament, was intended to be made subservient to the right of each colony to adequate representation in view of its surrender -of a large measure of self-government. In consideration ol surrendering its independent colonial status, each colony was entitled to such a representation in the federal parliament as would be sufficient to guard that right.
A self-governing colony was something more than the number of its inhabitants.
The principle that population was not ths sole consideration in fixing representation was recognized in the cases of Manitoba, British Columbia and Prince Edward Island when these provinces respectively entered the Union.
Manitoba with a population less than one unit of representation was given four, with a provision that after the "census of 1881 its representation should be ' readjusted ' under the terms of the British North America Act.
When the Maritime provinces entered Confederation it was impossible for them to have foreseen the extent and effect of the development of western Canada. They never imagined that in the days to come the growth of the West would strip them of their influence in the councils of the nation. Though the times were not over prosperous they contributed their share to the cost of purchasing the lands from the Hudson Bay Company and equipping them for settlement; bore their part of the cost to Canada of the Canadian Pacific railway and all the other vast expenditures that went to link together the far-flung provinces of Canada, and to convert the wilderness into thriving communities out of which have developed the splendid prairie provinces of to-day.
But most of all, they gave their sons and daughters to the West. Prom Manitoba to the Pacific coast the Maritime provinces people form an important element of the population who have played no small part in the development of these new lands.
Theirs also is a potent influence in binding together the east and the west with bonds of sympathy ' light as air though strong as iron.'
All these contributions the Maritime provinces have cheerfully made in the interests of

Canadian unity and progress, but they feel it a cruel exaction of the strict letter of the bond which will impose a lasting penalty upon them for the sacrifices they have made in such a cause.
Another ground upon which the Maritime provinces claim consideration in respect of their representation is that they had as good a right to share in the public demesne of Canada as had those provinces upon which it was bestowed. It is true that the Maritime provinces have claimed a share of the value of these lands, but that does not touch the question now under consideration. The territories added out of the public demesne will increase to a limit not now possible of calculation the representation of these provinces in the federal Parliament.
The Maritime provinces, situate as they are, could not well obtain their share in actual territory, but it is surely just that they should not by reason of the aggrandizement of the provinces more favourably situate be compelled to accept a representation decreased not only relatively but absolutely in the Canadian Parliament.
I read this for the purpose of pointing out how strenuously the representatives of the Maritime provinces fought against the decrease of representation, but they never contemplated that the right hon. gentleman the First Minister would bring down a Bill to Parliament during the present session which would provide not only for the actual decrease necessary under the British North America Act, but which would virtually result in a decrease altogether outside of that required by the British North America Act. In the session of 1911, there was some discussion in the House with regard to the question of the natural resources of the Dominion and the share which the Maritime provinces were entitled to. On that occasion, the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) took part in the debate, and speaking with respect to the enlarging of the boundaries of the provinces of the West he said:
During the time my hon. friend was Attorney General of New Brunswick, he was asked to place before the Privy Council at London the question of the loss of representation suffered by the province of New Brunswick by reason of her population not being able to keep pace with the growth of the population of Quebec, and one of the strong points in the argument he made before that court was that, by reason of the fact of the boundaries of Quebec having been increased, we in the Maritime provinces should have a readjustment of the British North America Act, so that we would not lose our comparative representation, the added territory of Quebec allowing her to have an increased population. That was one of the arguments. That same argument would apply in the case of Ungava bo*ing added to Quebec, as was proposed under this agreement.
Referring tq the hon. member for St. John, he proceeds:
So there is a chance for my hon. friend to repent. I am glad to see he is repenting, and I welcome him again to the fold of those loyal and .patriotic men in the Maritime provinces who are always prepared to stand up for the interest of those provinces. Although I am a supporter of the Government, I shall oppose any resolutions that come down here giving territory to the western provinces-
