During that discussion the question turned upon whether or not the Maritime provinces were entitled to any consideration in respect of the amendment to the British North America Act so as to prevent any further decrease of representation, and from the turn the debate took, I think I am fairly inteirpreting the language of the hon. member	for	Kings and Albert
when I say that, when he spoke of the consideration to which the Maritime provinces were entitled before the Dominion lands were divided among the western provinces, he had in mind something with respect to fixing the representation of the Maritime provinces so that no further decrease should take place. In 1906, the hon. member for Kings, Prince Edward Island, moved a resolution in the following terms:
That an humble address be presented to His Majesty, King Edward VII, praying that he may be graciously pleased to cause a measure to be submitted to the Imperial Parliament, for the purpose of amending the British North America Act, so that no province of the Dominion shall at any time have fewer representatives in Parliament than it was given when it entered Confederation.
There was considerable discussion on that resolution, and, on a motion to adjourn the debate, the leader of the Opposition, now the right hon. Prime Minister, said:
The subject is one of great importance, and it is desirable that it should he discussed and

brought to a conclusion, and not buried. Therefore, I trust the adjournment of the debate does not mean that we shall have no more of it.
At that time the present Prime Minister had a very kindily interest in the subject of the representation of the Maritime provinces, and he was fearful that the adjournment of the debate might result in no action being taken upon the resolution moved by the hon. member for Kings, Prince Edward Island. We had hopes that the right hon. gentleman would find some means out of the dilemma on which the people of the Maritime provinces find themselves, but, inasmuch as he has not seen a way to restore to us the representation we formerly had, and in view of the sympathetic sentiments he expressed on more than one occasion for any proposal that might bring about that end, I extremely regret that the Redistribution Bill which he has presented to the House results not only in decreasing the representation of the province of Nova Scotia, as provided for by the British North America Act, but practically means the obliteration of three constituencies from the province of Nova Scotia.
In the county of Richmond, which I represent, we have a population which is made up almost entirely of farmers and fishermen. Our people live upon the soil and upon the sea. Our population is fixed. There is no moving about from one place to another, and we receive no accession to our population by reason of immigration. Our population has interests not in common with the population of the county of South Cape Breton. By this Redistribution Bill it is proposed that the county of Richmond shall be added to South Cape Breton, which, as is well known, has a very large industrial population at the present time. They have their coal mines, their steel works and other industrial concerns, and the population of South Cape Breton have sympathies and interests far different from those of the people of Richmond county, which I represent at the present moment. The county of Richmond is the only county in Nova Scotia that has a majority of French Acadians. We all know how much the people of Nova Scotia are indebted to the enterprise of the Acadians, who form such a large proportion of the population in that province. Their lives are pure, they live happily together; for the most part they remain at home and give their time and industry to the upbuilding of the
[Mr. Kyle. 1
community in which they live. The description which Longfellow gives of the Acadians of Grand Pre applies absolutely to the Acadians of Richmond :
Men whose lives glided on like rivers that water the woodlands
Darkened by shadows of earth but reflecting an image of heaven;
Alike were they free from
Pear that reigns with the tyrant and envy,, the vice of republics;
Neither locks had they to their doors nor bars to their windows ;
But their dwellings were open as day and the hearts of the owners;
Then the richest was poor, and the poorest lived in abundance.
This is the condition that exists in Richmond county, and has existed for many years. The people of that county have always had the privilege of sending a representative to Parliament to represent their modest wishes, ambitions and aspirations, but that right is about to be taken away from them, and Richmond is to be merged with the large population of South Cape Breton for the purpose of making a double constituency. The reason given for joining Richmond with South Cape Breton under this Redistribution Bill is that the population of Richmond is only 13,273 and it is not to send a representative to Parliament when the unit of representation at the present time is 30,000. I do not imagine that any great value can be put upon a difference in population as between two constituencies of one or two thousand. Peterborough East, in the province of Ontario, has a population of 15,499 and the constitution, as incorporated in the British North America Act, receives no wrench by reason of that riding sending a representative to Parliament in the future, but the very heavens will fall if Richmond, with 13,273, should continue to do the same. I quote these figures for the purpose of showing that there appears to be no principle upon which the county of Richmond has been added to South Cape Breton. Brome, in Quebec, with a population smaller than that of Richmond, is retained upon the electoral map and will continue to send a representative to Parliament, and East Peterborough, with a population very little larger than that of Richmond, will continue to send a representative to Parliament, whereas Richmond will practically cease to exist.
Let us see what the result of the union of these two counties is as respects territory. The electoral division of South Cape Breton has an area of 722 square miles and the electoral division of Richmond has an area of 500 square miles, making a total of 1,222 square miles in the combined counties of Richmond and South Cape Breton. The distance between Point Tupper, which is the extreme western limit of Richmond, and Scattarie, which is the extreme eastern limit of Cape Breton, is 140 miles. The width of the united constituencies is from twenty to fifty miles. Between Richmond and Cape Breton there is absolutely no communication. Should this union take place, the candidate, when he starts out from Sydney, will be obliged to drive sixty miles before he reaches a railway. There is no communication by rail between these two parts of the riding that is now formed.
1 stated a moment ago that there is no community of interest. At the time when the Ontario schedule was under discussion to-night the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) pointed out that one
of the principles which should guide in the delimitation of constituencies, and in the union of different parts of a constituency, is that of community of interest. I stated a moment ago that there is no community of interest between Richmond and South Cape Breton. Can you imagine the cost of running an election in this large constituency which is now formed, a constituency of 222 square miles and extending over a distance of 140 miles?
I shouia think that the principle that was laid down on a former occasion with respect to redistribution ought to prevail more particularly in this redistribution than it has at any other time. One of the principles laid down was that of community of interest. But there is another principle which has been acted upon in this and other redistributions, and that is the doing away of double constituencies as far as possible and particularly the doing away with double rural constituencies. There is not a double constituency from the Pacific ocean until we come to the city of St. John. It was proposed, I understand, to form a riding in Ontario with two representatives, but it was found to be contrary to that principle, which they felt to be a desirable one, and instead of creating one double riding they created two single ridings. The same thing happened in regard to Vancouver; in arranging the representation of Vancouver, the idea of a dual constituency was not entertained and two constituencies have been created in that city. The population of the county of Richmond, as I stated a moment ago, is 13,273. The population of the county of South Cape Breton is 43,350. The population of the county of Richmond is entirely rural, made up, as1 I said, of fishermen and farmers. The population of South Cape Breton, is largely industrial: 10,000 rural population and 33,350 urban. Therefore it is perfectly manifest that there cannot be very much community of interest between the county of Richmond and the riding of South Cape Breton.
Let us see what was done in the matter of counties falling below the unit of representation on other occasions When redistribution Bills were considered by the House of Commons. In 1891, the unit of representation was 22,000. The following counties in the province of Nova Scotia were at that time below the unit:	Annapolis, 19,-
350; Digby, 19,897; Antigonish, -16,114; Guys-borough, 17,195; Queens, 10,610; Richmond, 14,399; Shelburne, 14,956; Victoria, 12,432. At

that time it was necessary to reduce the representation of the province of Nova Scotia by one, so the committee united the counties of Shelburne and Queens, thereby reducing the representation as required by the census; but they did not interfere with other constituencies that were below the unit. At that time Victoria had a population of only 12,432, but it was not suggested that Victoria county should be united with another county because its population was less than the unit. Sir John A. Macdonald was the Premier of Canada at that time, and it is regrettable to say that he was fairer to the people of the province of Nova Scotia in the matter of redistribution than is the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government at the present time.
In 1901, the unit of population was 25,367. The following counties in the province of Nova Scotia were at that time 'below the unit: Annapolis, 18,842; Antigonish, 13,617; Colchester, 24,900; Digby, 20,322; Guys-borough, 18,320; Hants, 20,055; Inverness, 24,353; Kings, 21,937; Richmond, 13,515; Shelburne and Queens, 24,428; Victoria, 10,571; Yarmouth, 22,869. In that redistribution it was necessary to decrease the representation in the province of Nova Scotia by two. The committee took away one of the representatives from the county of Bictou, which up to that time had sent two representatives to Parliament; and for the other they added the county of Victoria to North Cape Breton. As I quoted from the figures given by the Government to the committee, the county of Antigonish and the county of Richmond were both far below the united of population which entitled them to representation in Parliament in 1901, but in that redistribution the leader of the Government of that day, the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Opposition, was fairer to Nova Scotia than is the right hon. gentleman, who (belongs to Nova Scotia and who is now leading the Government, because my right hon. friend the present leader of the Opposition was content to leave the representation of Antigonish and Richmond at it was, feeling that his duty was done when he reduced the representation according to the requirements of the census by virtue of the British North America Act.
In 1911, the unit of representation was 30,000. The following counties in the provinces of Nova Scotia are now below the unit: Annapolis, 18,581; Antigonish, 11,962; North Cape Breton and Victoria, 29,888; Colchester, 23,644; Digby, 20,167; Guysbor-ough, 17,048; Hants, 19,703; Inverness, 25,-

571; Kings, 21,780; Richmond, 13,273; Shelburne and Queens, 24,211; Yarmouth, 23,220. Therefore it will be seen that, even after Antigonish and Guysborough are united, and Digby is divided up between Yarmouth and Annapolis, and Richmond is added to South Cape Breton, there will- still be several constituencies in the province of Nova Scotia well below the unit of representation. It is absolutely impossible to arrange a redistribution in this country so that every constituency shall have a population up to or within the neighbourhood of the unit, and I contend that the British North America Act never contemplated that there should he an equalizing of population in all the constituencies of Canada. All the obligation cast upon the Government at the present time or cast upon any government is to reduce the representation of each province according to. the section of the British North America Act which I quoted.
In the beginning of my remarks I read a quotation from a speech delivered by the Right Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright in the Senate with reference to the representation of Roman Catholics and Protestants in Parliament. I have here some figures which i propose to place upon 'Hansard'.
The population of the province of Nova Scotia is 492,398. There are 144,991 Roman Catholics, or 30 per cent of the whole population. There are in Parliament to-day from the province of Nova Scotia fourteen Protestants and four Roman Catholics; that is, although the proportion of population of Roman Catholics in the province of Nova Scotia is 30 per cent, they have only 22 per cent of the representation.
The population of the province of Prince Edward Island is 93,728. There are 41,994 Roman Catholics, or 44.9 per cent of the whole population, but the Roman Catholics in the House of Commons from that province constitute only 25 per cent of the representation.
The population of the province of Quebec is 2,003,232. There are 1,724,683 Roman Catholics, or 86.6 per cent of the whole population, 13.4 per cent of the population being Protestants; and of the representatives, the Roman Catholics have 83.1 per cent, and the Protestants 16.9 per cent, or three and one-half over and above that to which they would be entitled by a strict application of the proportion with respect to the Roman Catholic denomination in the province.
The population of the Province of Ontario is 2,523,274. There are 484,997 Roman Catholics, or 19 per cent of the whole popu-

lation; but the Roman Catholics in the House of Commons from the province of Ontario only constitute 5.8 per cent of the total representation from that province.
The population of Manitoba is 455,614. There are 73,994 Roman Catholics, or 16.6 per cent. There are ten representatives from Manitoba in the House of Commons, only one of whom is a Roman Catholic; that is, while the Roman Catholics have 16.6 per cent of the total population of the province of Manitoba, they have only 10 per cent of the representation in the House of Commons.
The population of the province of Alberta is 374,663. There are 62,193 Roman Catholics, or 16.6 per cent. There are seven representatives from Alberta in the House of Commons, of whom one is a Roman Catholic; that is, while the Roman Catholics have 16.6 per cent of the population, they have only 14 per cent of representation in the House of Commons.
The population of the province of Saskatchewan is 492,432. There are 90,092 Roman Catholics, or 18 per cent of the population. Out of ten representative from Saskatchewan, there is not one Roman Catholic.
The population of the province of (British Columbia is 392,480. There are 58,397 Roman Catholics, or 15 per cent of the population. There are seven members of Parliament for British Cbluimbia, and there is not one Roman Catholic.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not give these figures for the purpose of showing that these provinces made a mistake when they sent these estimable gentlemen to Parliament who are not of the Roman Catholic faith; they made no mistake in sending here the representatives that they have. I merely point it out to show that, as a matter of fact, the Catholic representation in the House of Commons is very much less than it is entitled to be, having regard to the total percentage of Roman Catholics throughout the Dominion. I have no right or authority to speak for the minorities in other provinces. As I said a moment ago, I am well satisfied with the hon. gentlemen who come from these provinces of Canada to Parliament, and I am sure that the electors of those provinces, both Catholic and Protestant, are well satisfied with the services which these gentlemen render to their constituencies. But I put these figures on ' Hansard ' for the purpose of showing that at the present time we have not the full proportion of reptresentation to which we are entitled, under ouir population; that according to the census returns of 1911, while we in Nova Scotia are entitled to six (Roman Catholics in the House of Commons we only have four. I am not blaming that to any spirit of intolerance upon the part of any section or denomination in this country, and I should be very sorry indeed to convey any such impression. I showed a moment ago how widespread was the spirit of tolerance in the county I represent, when four Protestants and four Catholics have been elected since 1867; and the spirit that exists there exists in other parts of Nova Scotia. I say I have no right to assume that there has been any deliberate attempt on the part of any denomination to debar from public life men of the Roman Catholic faith; nevertheless I say it is not becoming on the part of the Prime Minister to	bring	down to	Parliament a
Redistribution Bill that will have the effect of further increasing unfairness and injustice with respect to the representation of the Roman Catholic body in this House from the province of Nova Scotia.
The question might be asked as to how the union of Richmond and South Cape Breton could possibly affect the religious representation of that county in the House of Commons. I wish to point out that dual representation ought to be avoided whenever it is possible to do so. I pointed out that double constituencies had been abolished throughout the whole of the Dominion except in the cases of the cities of St. John and Halifax, and having reduced the dual constituencies throughout Canada to these two cities, it seems to me rather extraordinary that under this Bill an additional double constituency should be created in the island of Cape Breton. When we have dual representation we have dual interests, and questions sometimes arise that are awkward and difficult to deal with; whereas, if those constituencies were separate and apart, and there was one representative for each, these complications would be arrested.
It might be stated that, inasmuch as the present hon. gentleman who represents South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll), and I, are Roman Catholics, there is no reason why the same representation by denomination, if not by individuals, should nolt be maintained. My answer to that is, that we have an instance in Nova Scotia where in a constituency where there



is dual representation, the matter of denominational representation has not altogether worked out to the satisfaction of the members in that community. I refer to the city of Halifax. In Halifax, for forty years there was an unwritten law whereby there should be elected one Protestant and one Roman Catholic to represent that city in the House of Commons. That law was observed well, and it worked well until 1896. But by some accident,	owing,	I will assume to
the superior character and the high in-lect of the two gentlemen who were candidates, who did not profess the Roman Catholic faith, these two gentlemen were elected to the House of Commons to represent Ha'ifax. In 1900, if my recollection serves me, of the two representatives elected neither was a Roman Catholic. In 1904, there was one Catholic and one Protestant elected; in 1908, one Catholic and one Protestant; in 1911, there were two Protestants elected to represent the city and county of Halifax in this House. I state these circumstances to show that there is always danger that results might not be, as we all hope and wish that they should be, as regards the fair representation in this House of all religious denominations. I desire, Mr. Chairman, not to be misunderstood with regard to this matter. As I have already said, I find no fault with the county of Halifax for electing the Prime Minister-we are all proud he was elected in the city of Halifax, and that he comes from our province-neither do we regret that Mr. A. K. Maclean was elected to represent that county in 1911. These gentlemen were probably the best men to select, and they were selected. Nevertheless, a certain feeling that both religious denominations ^should be- represented in the House of Commons has given rise to some disappointment on account of the failure to carry out the unwritten law, which was for so long observed in Halifax.
As I said in my opening remarks, it is contended by gentlemen supporting the Government, and contended in the newspaper press supporting the Government, that this was an eminently fair redistribution, and one which ought to receive the unanimous support of this House; but, as time went along, it appears there was something in this Redistribution Bill which appeared to justify the minority members of the committee from joining in the unanimous report so much desired by the 
majority of the committee and people began to inquire as to what the bone of contention really was. The Montreal Star on June 9, had the following article on redistribution.
If redistribution is as near a settlement as is rumoured, it would be far better for tbe parties to call in an impartial referee to decide the couple of points at issue than to leave tbe whole subject over to be wrangled about during tbe high tension of the last session before an election. Experienced politicians should remember that it is at least twice as easy to get a bi-party agreement this session as it will be next. They may, indeed, find next session that some of the points, on which they are now agreed, have become points of difference by reason of the inflaming effect of an approaching general election.
The committee has worked a practical miracle in getting so near a * settlement by consent ' as it is now. It would be a thousand pities if that achievement were to be spoiled because of two minor differences at the last moment. It is not as if we could calculate upon the lapse of time and the calm of the recess removing these differences. As we have pointed out, the area of dispute is far more likely to increase; and the whole Bill may be wrecked next session. If, then, they cannot hit upon any plan for now making the miracle complete and presenting to the country a full and final ' settlement by consent,' they should-as we suggested-call in a referee.
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, that the very excellent advice of the Montreal Star was not followed by the right hon. Prime Minister, because I would be willing to submit the matter to any referee of good common sense he would name, and abide by the result. If any referee, apart from the majority on the Redistribution Committee, had bad this matter submitted to it, I am bound to say that Richmond county would not, under the circumstances, have been united to the county of Cape Breton. What is the alternative proposal, it may be asked? It is not for me to suggest any alternative proposal; but I can suggest a solution which has been very effective in the matter of removing -difficulties with respect to the proposed union of other constituencies during the present session.
It would have been very easy, I think, for the committee to have taken the census returns and to have increased the population of the county of Richmond by taking in some of the rural districts in Cape Breton county, thus providing two separate constituencies without having the same disparity of population as that which exists at the present time between these two ridings. It would have been fair and reasonable, I think, to have treated the

county of Richmond as the counties of Brome and East Peterborough were treated, and leave it to send a representative to Parliament ae heretofore.
It has been contended that the redistribution is fair because it wipes out the Conservative county of Digby and the Liberal county of Antigonish. Upon the face of it, that appears to be reasonable, but no person knows better than the hon. member for Digby how precarious is the tenure by which he holds the representation of the count of Digby in this House. So that my genial friend from the county of Digby is, perhaps, entitled to not so much credit for self-effacement as would appear on the surface of it when he resigns himself with such fortitude to the wiping out of his constituency. Having eliminated a Liberal constituency and a Conservative constituency the result is practically to eliminate another Liberal in the island of Cape Breton under circumstances which, I believe, are entirely unjustified. Under the section of the British North America Act which I read, the only obligation cast upon the Government was to reduce the representation in the province of Nova Scotia by two, and, having done that, I submit that their work was done. It would have been fair, I am willing to say generous, on the part of the committee if they had been willing to leave the county of Richmond as it is, as the Government of Sir John A. Macdonald, in 1871, left several counties in the province of Nova Scotia which were below the unit of representation, and as the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Opposition in 1901 allowed several other constituencies in Nova Scotia which were far below the unit to remain as they were, without wiping them out for the professed purpose of equalizing the population in those constituencies as far as possible.
I stated in the earlier part of my observations .that the question of representation in the Maritime provinces was referred to the Supreme Court of Canada in 1903, and from there appealed to the Privy Council. A good deal of money was spent for the purpose of devising some means whereby the Maritime provinces should not suffer any undue decrease in their representation. Both parties were absolutely honest and sincere when they took what appeared to them to be the only reasonable and proper steps to avoid the calamity which was apparently overtaking the Maritime provinces. The 3361
late Government, having gone so far to preserve the representation of the Maritime provinces as they did in 1903, does it not seem extraordinary that the present Government should go out of their way further to reduce the representation, as is done . with respect to the county of Richmond under the Redistribution Bill which we are now considering? During the course of the evening, when this Bill was under discussion, the hon. Postmaster General said:
I believe In dealing with the smaller prov~ inces in the fairest possible way.
He had reference to the ^presentation of the Maritime provinces in Parliament. I should like to ask the right hon. Primet Minister to take those words to his heart-It is not yet too late for him to revise thd determination which he has come to and to adopt some means whereby the county of Richmond shall not be blotted off the electoral map, as will undoubtedly be the case if this Bill goes through in its present form. The Postmaster General, I am sure, was sincere when he expressed this desire to deal fairly by the smaller provinces, and I hope and trust that, as I have said, the right hon. Prime Minister will take his words to heart and find some means whereby he may allow the representation of the county of Richmond to remain as it is until another redistribution comes round.

In the first place, let me say that as a member of the Redistribution Committee it was with deep regret that I observed the necessity of dividing the constituency of Digby, represented by the hon. member (Mr. Jameson) who sits on this side of the House. He protested to me verbally and by letter as well against the dismemberment of his constituency, but I think from my experience with this committee that it may be laid down as an axiom that if members of the committee were to heed the representations made to them by either friend or foe, no redistribution could be effected, because we have yet to find any constituency which desires to be effaced or affected in any way whatever. Under the terms of the British North America Act, it was necessary that the representation of the province of . Nova Scotia should be reduced by two members. There was no option on the part of the Government or of Parliament as to the course to be taken; an imperative duty was imposed upon them, and that duty was delegated to the committee to work out in the best possible way. The committee do not pre-

I am not making any apology for so doing, because I consider I have a perfect right to do so, and if the House is detained by reason of my remarks, the responsibility is on the other side for bringing down legislation of this kind at this stage of the session.
In the first place I feel that I am in distinguished company this evening. Some are born to greatness; some achieve greatness; some have greatness thrust upon them. I come in the last class, inasmuch I am legislated out of my seat in this House by this Act of Parliament. That is quite a distinction; when I look around me and see the men who are martyrs to the glorious cause, it seems to me I have reason to be proud. This legislation, if it goes through, will mean the wiping out of Antigonish county. Therefore I suppose it would be in order for me to deliver a valedictory; but

it so happens that I am afraid I could not deliver a valedictory on this occasion that would be quite in accord with the idea of a valedictory. that the principle of dual representation was one that was to be tabooed as far as possible. If that be the ease, why in the name of common sense do you want to add Richmond county to the county of Cape Breton and then -give two -members?

Now, this is a case where it should have been avoided. The county of Richmond is largely French Acadian and Roman Catholic; they are distinctive in their character and characteristics. -So far as the county of Antigonish is concerned, I feel, Mr. Chairman somewhat keenly on the bill now under consideration. Therefore, I feel that it is my duty upon this occasion to say something of and for the county I represent. The objection that is made to the county of Antigonish holding its representation is that it is small in size and population. Well, Mr. Chairman, since first the county of Antigonish became known by that name in 1863, it was just as small in size as it is in this year of grace, 1914; yet it was big enough and important enough to toe represented by Hon. Wm. A. Henry, one of the fathers of Confederation, a delegate at the Charlottetown meeting in 1864, the object of which was to bring about the Confederation of the British North American provinces, and who was a delegate also at the Quebec conference, when the draft of our constitution was prepared, and later a member of the London conference, which fornjulated the plan of confederation, and one of the two members who on this last occasion actually prepared the original draft of the Confederation Act, the palladium of the rights and privileges enjoyed by all classes and creeds in this Canada of ours; a statesman, who, after having declined a seat on the Nova Scotia bench, offered tooth by Liberal and Conservative Administrations, afterwards was elevated to the Supreme Court of Canada in 1875, a position which he adorned until his death. Hugh McDonald from 1867 until the downfall of the Macdonald Administration in 1873, who sat for a time in the Cabinet, first as President of the Privy Council, and afterwards as Minister of Militia and Defence; a delegate with Messrs. Howe and Annand to England, who succeeded in securing better terms for Nova Scotia, when the Confederation scheme was under consideration in 1866-67; a Judge of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia from November 5, 1873 till his retirement in 1890.
It was big enough and important enough to toe represented in this Parliament by
Hon. Angus Mclsaac from December 1873 to September 1885, when he was appointed County Court Judge for Judicial District No. 6 in Nova Scotia, and then toy that brilliant and distinguished statesman, Sir John S. D. Thompson, from the autumn of 1885 until his tragic death at Windsor Castle in 1895, during which time he was Minister of Justice, and also Premier of Canada. All these great men have been gathered to their fathers; but, if they could speak to-day, they would lift their voices in unison against the political extermination of that county, which they loved so dearly, and they would boldly and confidently declare that, notwithstanding the fact that the population does not reach the unit of representation, it is contrary to the true spirit and intent of the Confederation Act, and a proper conception of the principles underlying the doctrine of representation by population, to wipe it off the political
map.	They would protest against destroying the political entity of that constituency, not because of the natural objection of its people to being degraded to the status of only a small part of a constituency, but because of the fact that that constituency occupies a position unique in its relation to the rest of the province, and is representative of a class in that province and the country at large which gives it a claim for special consideration in the adjustment now before the House. This I shall explain a little later on.
So far as the British North America Act goes, there is nothing in it that calls for equalization of the population to be represented in this Parliament. My hon. friend from Cumberland has admitted that. It provides for a certain representation. The number of members for Quebec is fixed and unalterable at 65; the number for each of the other provinces changes to bear the same proportion to their respective populations as the number of 65 bears to the population of Quebec. By dividing the population of Quebec at the last decennial census by 65, we get the unit of representation. That unit of representation in the redistribution that took place after the census of 1871, was 18,331; after the census of 1881, it was 20,908; after that of 1891 it was 22,900; after that of 1901 it was 25,367, and, under the present redistribution, it is 30,819. Whilst the Act provides for the reduction of the number of a province's representatives where the growth of its population does not keep pace relatively with the increase of the unit of representation, and the number of members

to which Nova Scotia will hereafter be entitled has therefore to be reduced from 18 to 18, as the hon. member for Cumberland stated, yet it does not require that a county, to be entitled to a representative, must have any certain minimum population. There is nothing in the law to prevent this Government passing a redistribution giving one or more members to a county with a population of 10,000 inhabitants, if it should see proper to do so. There have been scores of counties throughout Canada in the past that had each a member, although their population was much lower than the unit of representation ; whilst, on the other hand, there were very many constituencies with a population far in excess of double that unit that had only one representative. The city of Montreal, with a population now almost as large as the whole province of Nova Scotia, has had seven representatives in this Parliament since the last redistribution, whilst the province had 18 members. Now, I might also refer to the remark that I made when the hon. member for Cumberland was speaking. I find that, under the proposed Redistribution Bill, there axe in the province of Quebec the following counties whose populations are below the unit of representation: Brome, 13,216; L'Islet, 16,435; Maskinonge, 16,509; Argenteuil, 16,766; Montmagny, 17,358; Missisquoi, 17,466, which is practically half the unit of representation. In Ontario the population of East Peterborough is 15,499; North Ontario, 17,141; Prince Edward, 17,150; Grenville, 17,545; Dufferin, 17,740. In Manitoba I find that the new division of Nelson has a population of only 11,973. The point to which I direct attention is that the unit of representation is in no way a determining factor as to whether a county shall or shall not have a separate representative.
Now we come to the county of Antigon-ish. At no time since the first redistribution under Confederation has Antigonish county had the unit of representation; yet it always had a separate member in this House. The census of 1881 showed a population of 18,060, while the unit of representation in the redistribution that took place thereafter was 20,908. The census returns are not always an invariable guide as to population. For example, at the last^ census the enumerator was required to take into account every member of the household who happened to be found at home on the day of the visit of the enumerator. If one or two members of a family happened to be temporarily away; if they were in the States or employed in some city or town, they were not taken into account, on the assumption that they would be enumerated wherever they happened to be residing at the time. In this way the rural districts suffered very much in the census, whilst the cities and towns gained. In the census of 1891, I know as a fact that members of a family who were residing in the United States for years, and who had no intention whatever of returning to the province in the near future, were enumerated as if at home. It will be seen, therefore, that it makes a very great difference whether the system adopted in taking the census is what is called the de jure system or whether it is the de facto system. Whilst the de facto system was supposed to prevail in the last census and the census preceding the last, yet as a matter of 'fact the de facto system was only followed in the last census, and in the census of 1891 the de jure system was followed. At any rate, I am perfectly safe in saying that the actual population of the county of Antigonish in 1911 was within 500 or 1,000 of the actual resident population in 1891, although the census shows a very much larger falling off. But this is a digression. The point I was trying to make, and it cannot be controverted, is that the population of Antigonish county was always, after the first Redistribution Bill in 1872, considerably below 1 a.m. the unit of representation; yet it was permitted to enjoy full representation under Conservative and Liberal Governments alike, and the people of the county, Conservatives and Liberals alike, are naturally very much aggrieved and humiliated at the action of the present Government in depriving them of that right and privilege hitherto enjoyed by them. Why is it that all those years from the time of Confederation, although the county

of Antigonish was mu eh below the unit of representation, it was allowed to have its representation in Parliament? The reason is apparent. It is that in that constituency and some other constituencies which I shall mention later, a minority element, a Roman Catholic body, a French Acadian body, were justly and properly recognized. Besides Antigonish county, there are other counties which fall far short of the 31,000 in round numbers which is the unit of representation. The last census gives the population of some of these counties as follows: Richmond, 13,273; Annapolis, 18,511; Digby, 20,167; Kings, 21,780; Colchester, 23,644; Queens and Shelburne, 24,211; Inverness, 251571. You will observe that these counties range in their (populations from forty-three to eighty-three per cent of the unit of representation for Canada; yet only one of them is deprived of its representative. As I have already stated, whilst the population is a determining factor in limiting the number of representatives in every province except Quebec, it is neither by law nor by the practice that has obtained since Confederation, necessarily an element in settling the distribution of that representation in a province. The terms of the British North America Act call for a reduction of the number of members for Nova Scotia from eighteen to sixteen on account of proportionate loss of population by that province since the census immediately previous to the last; but there is no law to determine or suggest in what part of the province that reduction shall be effected. That is a matter for the Government of the day, having due regard to all the classes, conditions and elements of population, to settle. The underlying principle of true democracy, of popular government, of fair representation, is that all classes, industrial, commercial and agricultural, all creeds, and nationalities shall, as far as possible and practicable, be represented in the Government of the country. That proposition has been repeated and admitted over and over again in this discussion, and similar discussions on like occasions, and is universally accepted. When it becomes necessary to make reductions by uniting constituencies, or carving them up, community of interest is an important matter for consideration. When this test is applied to the union of Antigonish and Guysborough, we find that although for a considerable distance they lie side by side, yet there is no more community of interest
between them than there is between Inverness and Yarmouth. The trade between these two counties is practically nil. The farmers of Guysborough county practically do all their business in Guysborough and Sherbrooke in that county; and the farmers of Antigonish have virtually no truck or trade with Guysborough. Commercially, Antigonish is as far away from Guysborough, and vice versa, as it is from Sydney, Cape Breton, or even St. John, New Brunswick. In the union of these two counties you have created a constituency which no man can represent and give his constituents any proper attention. Just think of it, a constituency extending all the way across from Northumberland strait to the Atlantic ocean. Book at the map and observe the distance from Cape George in Antigonish to Canso in Guysborough, or from Cape Jack in eastern Antigonish to Point Ecuin Secum. The distance in the former case is over 100 miles and between the two latter points it is 170 miles.
It is true that we are below the unit of representation, but so are one-half the other constituencies in Canada. The same thing may be said of many constituencies in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and the same may be said of Quebec and Ontario. Referring again to this memorandum I have, I find that in Ontario, where there are 81 ridings, there are 45 that are under the unit of representation. In Quebec in the 65 ridings, there are 40 which are under the unit of representation. New Brunswick has 10 ridings and 2 are under the 30,000. In Nova Scotia, with 14 ridings, there are 8 under the unit of representation. In Manitoba, with 15 ridings, 7 are under the unit of representation, and in British Columbia, with 13 ridings, 9 are under the unit pf representation. That ought to dissipate the argument that the unit of representation has anything at all to do with the question whether any particular county shall or shall not have a representative. There is another aspect of the case, that is the average population per square mile. I find that the average population per square mile in Nova Scotia is 22.98. Antigonish county, which is entirely a rural constituency, has a population per square mile almost up to the average, and a larger population per square mile than any other agricultural community in the province, with the exception perhaps of Kings. If you take the census returns showing the production of agricultural products of various kinds, grain, vegetables, horses, cattle, sheep, etc., it will be seen that for her size Antigonish takes second place to no community in the province. The county is, as I have said, almost exclusively agricultural. True, there is considerable fishing done there, but every fisherman is a farmer on a larger or smaller scale. This fact that it is par excellence an agricultural country, and that farming is the backbone of the country, ought to be matter deserving of serious and most favourable consideration, particularly when the question of production is in this country at present of such vital importance, and should induce the Government to leave that county her representation. Antigonish is only about half, and in many cases, less than half the area of these other counties I have enumerated, but she is just as big or just as small, as you like, as she was at the time of Confederation, when she first received representation in this House; and she leads all the counties that have not large industrial centres in the population per square mile and in her production per square mile, with one exception.
My hon. friend from Richmond referred to the religious aspect of this matter and the hon. member for Cumberland deplored that reference. It is just as well to call a spade a spade. I cannot understand why men will not discuss religion when they will discuss politics or a man's qualifications of any kind. What is there in it that a man should be ashamed of? The trouble is that people are too fond of talking of matters of this kind outside of the House but will not discuss them in the House. The hon. member for Richmond was quite within his right in discussing this matter and calling a spade a spade and giving expression to his views. The hon. member for Cumberland should not take exception to what he said. We know the hon. member for Cumberland is too big, too broad and too generous to have any sectional or small view on any subject, and particularly is he above the prejudices

that unfortunately exist in this country. But there is no reason why the matter of religion should not be discussed, if an argument can 'be based upon it, as freely as any condition, agricultural or commercial or otherwise, that prevails in this country. I propose to deal plainly and frankly with this matter and to give my opinion. If I am wrong in the matter, then hon. gentlemen who hold a contrary opinion can put me right, or, at all events, they have the right to hold a contrary opinion. It is true that, generally speaking, in our provinces, the relations between the various denominations are most cordial. The people of that province, being generally intelligent and enlightened, the various denominations knowing their separated' brethren, and having an opportunity of seeing that all the good, all the loyalty, all the public and private virtue is not found in one claes or creed to the exclusion of all or any of the others, bigotry and intolerance, the natural offspring of ignorance and irreligion, are comparatively unknown to us in that province. But even there, we have the Pringles and the Burgesses and others of that mischievous stripe, who, in season and out of season, instead of preaching the Gospel of charity and brotherly love, and peace and good will, seek to create suspicion and distrust, bitterness and enmity, all in the name of religion, and for the extension of the Kingdom of Heaven. They seem particularly busy just now, their latest grievance being the imaginary encroachments of the Pope of Rome on our free school system, hitherto regarded as an imperishable monument to the genius, foresight and statesmanship of Sir Charles Tupper, and those who were associated with him in the movement when that system was introduced in 1864. When demagogues and mischief makers require a field for their activities, a school question is the theme best suited for their wicked purposes.
It has been said that in a big country like this, with diversified conditions as to religion and nationality, considerations of this kind should have no place, that the paramount, indeed the only consideration should be to remember that we are all Canadians. I do not unqualifiedly agree with that view. The millennium is yet far distant, and if you would have a happy, peaceable and contented people, you must give all classes and creeds their just and proper recognition. You must respect contrary opinions and honest prejudices. Those who say the lamb and lion should lie side by side, too frequently

mean that the lamb should be found lying inside the lion.
When this Government was formed, the Prime Minister recognized this principle. It is true he was disappointing in his selections. Instead of taking reasonable, moderate and patriotic Conservative Catholics from the province of Quebec as his associates in the Cabinet he chose men from the ranks of the Nationalists, who are regarded as extreme, fanatical, and in many Conservative quarters, disloyal Canadians. Instead of choosing men representative of the sane, loyal, fair-minded Christian Protestantism of Ontario, he preferred the aggressive, intolerant-and judging from recent events in connection with their attitude towards Carsomsm and Home Rule for Ireland, the disloyal element controlling or controlled by Orangeism in that province. But he recognized the principle that he must find a place in his Cabinet for the various elements of race and creed. Again in the appointment of even judges to the Bench, care is taken that a just balance be maintained among the various creeds and nationalities; and so on all through the various phases of administration, from the Premier selecting his Cabinet down to the people selecting their candidate, these considerations properly and necessarily are not ignored. Let me just give an extract from a speech from the present Prime Minister himself on September 18, 1901. ' Han-said ' reports him on the question of representation and redistribution, then under consideration as follows:
There is another consideration which has had much weight in other constituencies, but which does not seem to have had any weight ... in the division of Cape Breton. We know that in various constituencies in Canada, the county of Halifax, the city of Ottawa, I believe, and the county of Cape Breton as well, this has been a sort of custom or unwritten law, which has been very faithfully carried out, and which amounts to this. That as the population of these different constituencies is divided so far as matters of religious faith are concerned-
Here the right hon. gentleman was interrupted in his remarks by a noise in the Chamber, and he addressed himself to the Chair protesting against the disorder, so his sentence was not completed. After he had succeeded in subduing the recalcitrant members he went on:
As I said, this custom has been carried out in good faith and in a very friendly and harmonious manner in the constituencies to which I have referred . . . and while I do not attach too
great importance to a matter of this kind, we should be somewhat careful of the feelings of the people with regard to customs of that character, which have prevailed in some of the constituencies of Canada for something like a quarter of a century.
I find the late Finance Minister, Hon. W. S. Fielding, giving expression to similar sentiments on the same occasion. He said:
As to what I may call the religious side of the question which has been referred to by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, that is a matter which should never be entirely lost sight of.
The Finance Minister in his remarks on that occasion recognized, to quote his own language, that 'A rule prevails whereby it is supposed that both of the great denominations secure representation'. My hon. friend from Cumberland will see that it is not improper to introduce a matter of this kind into a discussion of this nature, particularly when such men as the present Prime Minister and the then Minister of Finance felt that this principle ought to he considered. Now, Sir, let us apply the principle. In the province of Nova Scotia, the Catholics are 34 per cent of the whole population. Of a population of 492,338, as shown by the last census returns, there were: Catholics, 145,000; Presbyterians, 110,000; Baptists, 84,000; Anglicans, 75,000; Methodists, 58,000. Following that proportion, one would expect the Catholics to have six representatives in this Parliament. When the reduction to sixteen seats is made, the Catholic population should be entitled to five seats. But the proposed redistribution takes away that representation in a most ruthless and inconsiderate manner. And notwithstanding the assurance of my hon. friend from Cumberland county, I venture to prophesy that you will not see three Catholics returned to this House from the whole province of Nova Scotia after this Bill comes into effect.
The Catholic counties of that province may be classified as follows, according to the last census figures: Antigonish with a population of 11,962 has 10,306 Roman Catholics or upwards of 86 per cent. Richmond with a population of 13,273 has 9,836 Roman Catholics or upwards of 74 per cent. Inverness with a population of 25,571 has 17,019 Roman Catholics or upwards of 67 per cent. Digby with a population of 20,167 has 10,454 Roman Catholics or upwards of 50 per cent. Leaving those counties as they are, the number of recognized Catholic seats would still be one short of their proportion. I agree with my hon. friend from Cumberland that these seats should not as a matter

I would implore the Government, in view of the situation, in view of the fact that the province of Nova Scotia is being denied its proper representation, that Antigonish is peculiarly and particularly Catholic by reason of its population being divided between Catholics and Protestants in the proportion of ten to one, that it is the seat of a Catholic university, that it is a diocesan see with the largest Scotch Catholic diocese in the world, that it is a small, compact county with a larger population per square mile than that of any other agricultural county in the whole province of Nova Scotia, that the census shows that its production is greater per square mile than that of any other county in Nova Scotia with one exception, to reconsider its determination and to leave the county of Antigonish intact.

Mr. Chairman, before
this Bill becomes law, I desire to enter a protest against it in so far as the county of Guysborough is concerned. The people I represent are almost invariably opposed to this measure without distinction of party. I would not be doing my duty as their representative if I did not voice tlheir sentiments here to-night. Speaking for the Liberal party of Guysborough county, I would say that they are proud of their political history. They have fought many a hard battle in the past with their opponents, and they were generally able to win. They are proud of their record in this respect, and they would like very much to perpetuate it and continue it in the years that are to come.
It is quite true that the county I represent has not a sufficient unit of population to entitle it to a representative under the law as it exists to-day, and I am sorry to say that of late it has been decreasing in population to a .small extent. But what has happened in other rural districts of Canada has happened in the county of Guysborough. The people are deserting the farms and the country, and deserting the fishing boats, and crowding into the cities and industrial centres. In my county a good many are leaving for the United States. The policy of the present Government has only aggravated that situation, 
as its effect has been to drive population away from the constituency rather than to keep it at home.
But I shall be told that we are up against the terms of the British North America Act, and who is to blame for that? I have no desire to open up old sores; but once in a while it becomes necessary to place the responsibility where it belongs. The terms of the British North America Act were settled at the conference at Quebec. That conference was self-constituted so far as the province of Nova Scotia was concerned. Sir Charles Tupper professed to represent the people of Nova Scotia at that conference; but he acted without the authority of the people, and he was backed up by only a very small handful of extreme partisans at that time. We are now reaping what the Tory party sowed on that occasion. My right hon. friend will ask me what has he to do with this? I will point out to him that he is the lineal descendant in the direct line of succession of Sir Charles Tup-p>er; that he stands in his shoes at the present time, and that in that sense he is responsible as the leader of the party.
When British Columbia was admitted into the union, the representatives of that province were astute enough to provide that, whatever happened in the rest of Canada, the representation of British Columbia would not be any less than it was at the time it came into the union. Why did not Sir Charles Tupper make the same provision as regards Nova Scotia?
Apart from that, my right hon. friend has to accept some responsibility on his own account. What has the Prime Minister done to prevent this condition of affairs as regards the province of Nova Scotia? I might be asked:	What did the Liberal
party do at the time of the last census? But in so far as Nova Scotia was concerned, the circumstances were very different on that occasion. At that time it is true that we lost two members; but we had dual representation in the counties of Pictou and Cape Breton, and we were able to adjust the matter without very much inconvenience to anybody; but under the terms of this Bill we are disturbing the representation of seven counties in the province of Nova Scotia, namely, Digby, Annapolis, Antigonish, Guysborough, Yarmouth, Richmond and Cape Breton. Therefore, you will see that it is going to make a very great disturbance in that province.
My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) has made a very strong case; and in

my opinion, his case has not been answered by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), or by any person on that side of the House. In my opinion, the proposal in regard to the county of Richmond is absolutely unfair. There is no good reason for it, and no good reason has been shown. It is quite true that the county of Richmond is small; but that is not a reason for wiping it out, and that reason does not prevail in other parts of the country, as has been pointed out by my hon. friend from Richmond and my hon. friend from Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm). If we are to carry out that principle, I would ask my hon. friend from Cumberland what he would say about uniting his own constituency with the adjoining constituency of Colchester. I find on looking at the census that the population of the county of Colchester is only 23,364 and the population of the county of Cumberland is 40,543. It would be just as reasonable that the counties of Cumberland and Colchester should be put together and that they should return two members, as that the counties of Richmond and Cape Breton should be put together and return two members. If it suited the interests of the Conservative party to do that, they would be just as willing to do it in the one case as in the other, because the populations when the counties are united are about the same. The disparity between Cumberland and Colchester is very striking. They are adjoining counties and could very easily be put together, but there is no proposal of that kind. The county of Hants might be joined with the county of Halifax for that matter and return three members, because the county of Hants has only 20,000 people whereas the county of Halifax has 80,000 people. It is not an argument to say that, because the county of Richmond has a slightly smaller population than have some of the other counties in Nova Scotia, it should be treated differently and joined on to the county of Cape Breton. There is no pretense that this is done in the public interest. It is done in the interest of the Conservative party and for the purpose of attempting to wipe out another Liberal county in the province of Nova Scotia.
The question arises as to whether or not this 'reduction in the representation of the province of Nova Scotia could have been prevented. It certainly could have been prevented, as I will show.
The Prime Minister was urged in the session of 1911-1912 to amend the statute so as to prevent the result that has overtaken 3371
us at the present time. In that session the Prime Minister led us to believe that he was going to do something. My hon. friend from Pictou on that occasion was referred in a discussion on the boundaries of Manitoba, to this question, and he pointed out to the Prime Minister the importance of taking such steps as would preserve the representation of Nova Scotia before the time came for dealing with the question of redistribution. Here is what the Prime Minister said. His words will be found on page 4713 of ' Hansard ' of 1911-1912:
I can assure my hon. friend from Pictou and the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), who take a great interest in this question, that all of us from the Maritime provinces are just as deeply interested in it as they are, and I can assure my hon. friend from Pictou that it will have the earnest and careful consideration of the Government.
That was the promise made by the right hon. gentleman on that occasion. He went on to say:
One suggestion is that a minimum representation should be established for the Maritime provinces. Another suggestion is that the British North America Act should be amended to the effect that in estimating the 1.20 diminution which is required under subsection 4 of section 51 only the four original provinces should be taken into consideration so far as any diminution of the representation of those provinces is concerned.
He appeared to agree with the view put forward at that time. Then on April 10, .1913, the matter was again up, and my hon. friend from Pictou urged the Prime Minister to deal with this question of redistribution. The Prime Minister said that no satisfactory progress could be made in dealing with the question of the Maritime provinces until a conference of the provinces should be called. He then said:
In the meantime I shall bear in mind the suggestion which my hon. friend from Pictou has offered, that action of some kind ought to be taken during the present session.
The conference of the provinces was held in October of last year; and I have not been able to find, in looking over the minutes of that conference, that the Prime Minister did anything in the way of implementing his promise to the House that, when this conference took place some proposal at all events, would be placed before the Premiers of those provinces and some attempt made to adjust the matter with the Maritime provinces. Did my right hon. friend do anything? Did he

attempt to find any remedy? What is the ' use of promising careful and earnest consideration if it is only empty words, and they are forgotten as soon as they are uttered? Every one who has studied this question knows that there is more than one way of escape. Section 51, subsection 4 the British North America Act was intended to meet this case. When the construction of this subsection was submitted to the courts, the decision was adverse to the contention of the Maritime provinces; but there are strong reasons at the same time to take the other view. This subsection reads as follows:
On any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards.
The whole question depends upon the construction of the word ' Canada.' Does it mean the four additional provinces of Confederation, namely, Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, or does it mean the nine provinces that compose Confederation at the present time? Is it not reasonable to suppose that the fathers of Confederation had in their minds Canada as it existed at the time that that subsection was written?
Now, if the word * Canada ' in that subsection was declared to contain the meaning that it referred only to the original four provinces, the reduction would not be made in the present redistribution; I mean that the Martitime provinces would not lose their representation. It was open to the Prime Minister to introduce legislation declaring that that was intended to be the meaning by the Fathers of Confederation, and that, notwithstanding the decision that has been given by the courts, that was the fair, reasonable and just meaning of that clause of the Confederation agreement, and in that case the reduction [DOT] of the representation of the Maritime provinces would not have taken place.
In protesting against the present measure, in so far as the county of Guysborough is concerned, I do not wish to be understood as objecting in any way to a union with Antigonish. If Guysborough is to share its representation with any other county in Nova Scotia there is none more suitable than that county. I am speaking for a

moment just to put before the House and the country the view of the people of Guysborough county, which I have the honour to represent. I have no right to speak for the people of Antigonish, but we have been assured by the hon. member who has a right to speak for them, that they are just as opposed to the union as are the people of Guysborough. All I can do is to enter my protest in virtue of the overwhelming majority on the other side of the House. That is all that it is possible to do on this side, to lay the blame where it properly belongs, at the door of the Conservative party.
