Just two or three words before this resolution carries. I am inclined to congratulate this committee very sincerely, because I know that in some respects their task has been a difficult and, one might almost say, a thankless one, in attempting to come to an agreement in respect to a matter which usually in this country has been the cause of severe political controversy. The fact that they have succeeded in agreeing in 233 constituencies out of 234 is distinctly a credit to the spirit with which they entered upon their duties, and to the manner in which they have carried them out.
Hon. gentlemen who have addressed the House this evening have alluded to the only case in which there has been a difference of opinion in the committee, and in the House itself. Do not let those hon. gentlemen imagine that there are not men on this side who have cause to complain, and who have made very strong appeals for a consideration which, under the circumstances, it was impossible to give. I have no doubt that the same thing has occurred on the other side of the House in respect of men whose voices have not been raised here to-night.
However, the hon. gentleman from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) has seen fit to make a very strong criticism of the Conservative members of the committee and of the report which they have brought in with regard to the county of Richmond and the electoral district of South Cape Breton. He has endeavoured to make it appear that the action of the Government majority on the committee was designed to, affect unjustly and unfairly a certain portion of the community in Nova Scotia. I need hardly pause to notice a suggestion of that kind, made for an obvious purpose, and I will not dwell upon it except to say that I think it was most effectively answered by the hon. member

maintopic: XI, 19X4

speechtext:
from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes). I do not think it redounds very much to the credit of the hon. gentleman who made that attack, and 'Who used the astonishing arguments with which he supported it, that he should have taken the course he has seen fit to pursue. He has spoken of the county of Richmond, and other hon. gentlemen has spoken of it; they have asked a number of questions with regard to it, and they have given a number of illustrations. Let me give them a few illustrations of the manner in which the committee unanimously dealt with many counties in Ontario .and Quebec, whose population was very much larger than that of either Richmond or lAmtigonish.
Let us take, for example, the county of Brockville, with a population of IK,531; it absolutely disappears by the unanimous consent of the committee as an electoral division, and is merged in the county of Leeds. Let us look at the three Greys: those constituencies have respectively a population of 19,650, 26,991 and 19,250; one of these constituencies disappears and the three former constituencies become two. Let us look at the three Hurons: As at present constituted they have respectivelv populations of 16,289, 19,508 and 17,186; one of them disappears and the three ridings are merged into two. Let us look at the ridings of North and South Lanark, the one with a population of 14,624 and the other with 19,751, merged into one riding by the provisions of this Bill. I say that every one of those would have just as much and more right to put forward criticism with regard to the unanimous action of the committee concerning them as any argument which has been put forward to-night by hon. gentlemen opposite.

maintopic: XI, 19X4
speechtext: Is there not a community of interest in those ridings?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: XI, 19X4
speechtext:
stituencies the majority of whose electorate were of an absolutely different religious belief. We have examples of that in the province of Ontario. A very distinguished Roman Catholic, Hon. J. J. Foy, represents in the provincial Legislature the con-' stituency of South Toronto, which, if I remember correctly, is a strong Protestant and Orange constituency; yet if the Hon. J. J. Foy in the course of the redistribution in the province of Ontario had happened to have the constituency of South Toronto interfered with, I suppose one would hardly say that that was intended as an injustice against the Roman Catholics of Ontario. This constituency, although strongly Protestant, very properly and worthily elected Mr. Foy, a prominent Roman Catholic, to represent it in the provincial Parliament. It elects IMr. A. C. Maedonnell, a prominent Roman Catholic, to this House.
With regard to diversity of interests and lack of communication, I desire to tell the hon. gentleman that my own constituency, the county of Halifax, is 140 miles in length. Its people make their livelihood by almost every means and occupation. We have an urban population in the city of Halifax of about 50,000, engaged in industrial and mercantile activities, in shipping and in all that pertains to shipping. We have mining districts, fishing districts, agricultural districts, and, more than that, we have absolutely no railway communication from east to west, although a railway is now in process of construction. When going to different ponds in the county, it is more convenient to take a steamer allong the shore; if one takes the road he must drive. Take the riding of North Cape Breton and Victoria, in which industries, mining, agriculture and fishing are extensively carried on; there is just as great a lack of communication and just as great a diversity of interests there as any that will arise by reason of the union of the present electoral divisions of South Cape Breton with the county of Richmond. Take the constituency of .South Cape Breton itself, as it is constituted at the present time. There we find a large industrial population, a large mining population, a large population engaged in agriculture and, I presume, a considerable population engaged in fishing. There is a considerable lack of communication in parts of that riding. Take the case of the riding of the hon. member for Pictou, where there is great variety of occupation. You cannot in making redis-
tribution secure complete uniformity of conditions; indeed, I am not absolutely sure that it is desirable that you should do so.
Let us look for a moment at the population and voting power of these constituencies. The population of Richmond is 13,273.
The population of South Cape 2 a.m. Breton is 53,352. In Richmond there are 3,489 and in South Cape Breton 15,404 names on the electoral lists. That is to say, South Cape Breton has on its electoral lists the names of 2,000 more persons than are included in the entire population of Richmond. In Richmond 2,251 persons voted at the last election, and in South Cape Breton 10,257. Under those circumstances the hon. member for Richmond contends that although these ridings adjoin and are contiguous to each other, we should leave them as they are and we should give to every elector in the riding of Richmond about five times the voting power allowed to each elector of the riding of South Cape Breton. It does not seem to me that that is a reasonable proposal. Why should we not join them? To supplement the illustrations which were given by my hon. friend the member for Cumberland, let me remind the committee that in addition to the city and county of Halifax, which, have always returned two members, the county of Pictou also returned two members to this Parliament. We had also the county of Cape Breton returning two members. They were cut down to one member eventually for the reason that the representation in the province of Nova Scotia in this Parliament had to be reduced. But as long as the representation of the province of \Nbva Scotia remained at twenty or twenty-one, we had not only the constituency of Halifax but the constituencies of Pictou and Cape Breton each returning two members at large. And then, in the adjoining province of New Brunswick, in the riding of the city and county of St. John joined to Albert, we have a dual constituency returning two members. The same thing is true of Ottawa. As the member forOumberland pointed out, it has been the universal practice both in federal and provincial redistribution in Nova Scotia, ever since Confederation, to have members at large and not to divide up counties; and that is *he course which we thought it best to pursue in this case. The electoral district of South Cape Breton and Richmond will have a population of a little over 66,000. They have a little over the unit which would entitle them to two members.

Then with regard to Guysborough and Antigonish, I would point out to the hdn. member for Guysborough and the hon. member for Antigonish that the recommendation of the committee with regard to the union of those counties was unanimous and I have not heard anything from these gentlemen as to what should otherwise have been done. They were the two counties with the smallest population, they were the two counties that lay contiguous to each other, and I do not know what the alternative suggestion would be.

My contention was
that there should be an attempt to adjust the law so as to give the Maritime provinces the representation they had at the time of the union, or the representation they have now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will come to that in a moment. We have to deal with conditions as they are; we cannot amend the British North America Act, although my hon. friend suggested, perhaps unwillingly, that we had the power to do so.
I contended that there were other constituencies in N'ova Scotia where there was a community of interest that could well be united and thus obviate the union of these two that have nothing in common.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The counties of Guysborough and Antigonish are both agricultural to a large extent, are they not? They are both fishing counties to a large extent, are they not? I do not know why there is not a community of interest. I do not think there is any hostility or any unfriendliness or ill will between the counties of Antigonish and Guysborough. I believe they will get on very well indeed and, further than that, hon. gentlemen seem to imagine that because the county of Richmond is to be added to the county of South Cape Breton, or because An-ti-gonish is to be added to Guysborough, these constituencies will lose all influence in the councils of the nation. I do not think any such thing as this is to be apprehended.	When	the county ofQueens was	added	to the countyof Shelburne	the	united county
was represented in this House for fifteen years by a man who occupied an exceedingly prominent place in the life of this country, the Minister of Finance in the late Government, Hon. W. S .Fielding. Is there any reason to suppose that the electors of Queens and Shelburne did not exercise a
legitimate and reasonable influence in the councils of the nation here in Parliament when they were represented by Mr. Fielding? What reasons are there to suppose that either Richmond or Antigonish or Guysborough will not have in the future legitimate and proper influence in the Parliament of Canada by the representation which it will now have. I do not know what else we could do with Richmond unless we left it as it is. Is it desired that we should unite Richmond and Victoria? We can do that and leave Cape Breton to return two members as it did years ago. Would any hon. gentleman find any objection to Cape Breton being represented in this Parliament by two members? Would it be necessary to divide Cape Breton? If it would not be necessary to divide Cape Breton, if it would be an eminently proper thing to leave Cape Breton to be represented in this Parliament by two members' as it was for a veTy long period, what is the strong objection to having the south riding of Cape Breton and the county of Richmond united into one riding and returning two members to this Parliament? I must confess that the attitude which my hon. friends have taken with regard to this matter is one that has surprised me very much, and one which I think will not be supported by public opinion.
What is the objection to having two separate ridings with two separate members instead of one riding with two members?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not make the report and I am not responsible for it. I suggested that very thing myself in the early stages when I knew that there was some difference of opinion. So far as I can gather from information obtained from members of the committee, there was a good deal of difficulty in doing that on account of the population being largely grouped around the cities of Sydney and Glace Bay. Further than that, the suggestion which I made did not receive any encouragement. In 1903, I think I suggested in this House that Richmond might be united with Victoria. It was not received with favour by hon. gentlemen opposite, and I did not press it unduly. I did not put it forward this time because hon. gentlemen, as I understood, had some marked objection to it. In. view of the enormous preponderance of population in the adjoining riding and in view of the fact that dual representation has been the custom of the people of

maintopic: COMMON8

speechtext:
Nova Scotia for many years, in the past, it was the proper thing to join the electoral district of South Cape Breton and the county of Richmond into one riding and have that riding return two members, just as would have been done if Cape Breton had been restored and were allotted the two members in this Parliament that it formerly had.
The hon. member for Guysborough has endeavoured to raise some question in the way of criticism upon the Government and especially upon myself because the British North America Act has not been so amended as to give to the province of Nova Scotia a representation of 18, 19 or 21 members. Perhaps he alludes to the number we had when we entered Confederation. He has heard his own leader in this House declare over and over again that when our province came into Confederation it came in upon a distinct and settled principle of representation by population and that that principle was embodied in express and distinct terms in the British North America Act, and it being so set forth and expressed in the British North America Act, Parliament should not depart from it.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: Why should we depart from it in the case of Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
We are not departing
from it seriously in the ease of Prince Edward Island. We are departing from it by adopting a principle which has been accepted unanimously by the hon. gentlemen's own political friends upon the committee, that no province in Canada shall be represented in the House of Commons by a smaller number than in the Senate.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: You are doing it for the express purpose of giving one more member for Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: Does my hon. friend object to that?

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: I am not objecting to it but if you are going to stand by the principle, stand by it. You are not standing by it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
We may be departing
from the principle to that very limited extent by reason of another principle which I think is entitled to certain consideration, namely, that it was not intended or foreseen by those who laid the foundations of the Confederation Act that any province fMr. Borden.]
should have a smaller representation in the House of Commons than in the Senate. That view impressed itself upon the committee and upon the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, although he stands firmly to-day upon the ground that the Confederation Act embodies a convention or treaty between the four provinces which entered into Confederation, and that one of the terms of that convention or treaty was that the representation of these provinces in the Parliament of Canada should be based upon population. I would like to ask my hon. friend whether or not in 1903 any steps were taken to remedy this unsatisfactory condition so far as the Maritime provinces are concerned? He knows perfectly well they were not, and he knows why those steps were not taken. The suggestion that we can undertake legislation on that behalf is of course absolutely futile. We could only pass an address, and if my hon. friend had seen fit to do so this afternoon when the resolution with regard to representation in the House of Commons was before us, he could have made such a motion, but I venture to say that he would not have got a great deal of support from his own side- of the House if he had done so. My hon. friend smiles his acquiescence in the statement I have just made. He knows perfectly well the reason he did not make it; he knows his own leader would not have supported him. The . arrangement made at Confederation was an arrangement based upon the understanding and agreement to which I have alluded. I am very sorry to have been obliged to inflict myself upon the committee at this hour, but as a good deal of criticism has been directed not only against the Government but against myself personally, I thought it due to myself and due to the House that I should make this explanation.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
As a member of the Redistribution Committee, and coming from the province where the question which has been discussed to-night at such length has arisen, I think it is only due to the men who have raised this question and to the House that I should say a word or two.
I am free to say that the desire of the members of the committee from the Government side of the House in dealing with this matter was apparently to deal with the question in a fair manner. I think that the Chairman in any disputes that arose between the- members acted very fairly, and it is a matter of regret that the' issue which raised the question we have

been discussing to-night should have arisen in regard to the province from which my right hon. friend comes. The case of Richmond county and its connection with South Cape Breton is an isolated and peculiar case, and constitutes one proposal in this Bill for which, to my mind, there is no justification whatever. My right hon. friend has referred to what has been done in Ontario. What occurred in Ontario was this: By reason of the fact that the census showed an increase in the population in northern Ontario and an increase in the population of the city of Toronto, it was necessary, having regard to the fact that Ontario's representation in addition was affected to the extent of four seats, to readjust the population within the province so as to make eight seats disappear and to provide eight new constituencies. The constituencies of Grey, Huron, Middlesex, Stormont, Lanark and the others to which my right hon. friend has referred were constituencies that had to be dealt with on account of their small population in order to provide for the disappearance of the eight seats and the creation of eight new constituencies. The same situation arose in Quebec. The increased population of the island and city of Montreal involved the disappearance of constituencies in the rural parts of the province in order to provide for representation where the bulk of the population was. In Nova Scotia we have this situation. Under the law we had to provide for the disappearance of two constituencies. The Government members on the committee proposed that Antigonish and Guysborough be united and that Digby be divided.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
I understood my hon.
friend to say that Ontario lost eight seats, and that eight new seats had to be provided in their place. Did the hon. gentleman intend to convey that?

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: What I meant to say was that Ontario lost four seats under redistribution, but by reason of the increased population in Northern Ontario and the city of Toronto it was necessary to provide for the disappearance of eight seats in order to create four others. In regard to Nova Scotia, I think the division of Queens and Shelburne would have been better than dividing up Digby. It would have been more satisfactory to the counties involved, as Shelburne and Yarmouth have closer business relations than Shelburne and Queens and the northern portion of Queens is in very close communication with the county of Annapolis. Having provided for the disappearance of two seats by combining Antigonish and Guysborough and dividing Digby an additional proposition was made for the disappearance of the county of Richmond and the creation of a double-member constituency coimposed of the constituencies of Richmond and South Cape Breton. To my mind there was no warrant or justification for that proposal whatever. There was no necessity for the committee to make any such report. We had gone over all this country from the Pacific to the Atlantic dealing with redistribution, and we had not found it necessary to create another double member constituency.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: What about St. John?

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: St. John is different. I am not going to discuss the question of dual representation at this hour of the day, as its merits and demerits would involve a very long discussion. I think the best judgment of those who have given this matter serious thought is that it is not desirable to have dual representation. The suggestion that we should have a dual member constituency because in Nova Scotia we have had counties represented by two and three men since Confederation is of no value, because under the Act of 1867 a certain number of seats were provided and the conditions naturally lent themselves to double representation at that time. The general sentiment of the country, however, is against dual representation and the fact that we had dealt with this question of redistribution in every province except Nova Scotia without creating another double member constituency was one that ought to have been regarded.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: We have one at St. John.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
St. John already
existed. The peculiar conditions in regard to the city of St. John and St. John city and county practically demanded dual representation.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
Not at all. There is a
separate member for St. John city and a separate member for St. John city and county:

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
My hon. friend
knows very well that a man who lived in the city of St. John had two votes. He elected, at the last election, Mr. Pugsley and Mr. Daniel, who is now in the Senate. But the man who lived in St. John county could only vote for one person. Practically

you had dual representation. In the case of Albert county, the committee were doing nothing more or less than dealing with a situation that already existed. This was the only case in which dual representation was found to be necessary on the part of the Government. My right hon. friend represents Halifax city and county which has been a county in Nova Scotia from time without memory, and which as far as bounds go, existed at Confederation, the capital county of the province, with diversified interests, with all the occupations of its people, and in that county you had a condition which was peculiar in. its way. But that is not an argument to be made in regard to establishing a new constituency in the island of Cape Breton. The suggestion that Richmond should go with Victoria is not a practicable one because you have the Bras d'Or lakes separating the two of them. The Acadian who lives at Isle Madame has nothing more to do with the Highlander who lives at Iona than he has to do with a man who lives in Yarmouth. What was proposed by the Government was to create a new constituency stretching from Sydney harbour down to Point Tupper. Why? Because Richmond had 13,000 of a population. I took [DOT]strong ground in the committee against it [DOT]and I still take strong ground against it. [DOT]I say that it is an anomaly, that it is [DOT]entirely unnecessary and there is no justification for it. I say that Richmond with its 13,000 people has as much right on account of the fact that it is a typical minority constituency in our province to be *represented in the House of Commons as the county of Brome in the province of Quebec. That is the position I took before the committee and that is the position I take here and now. The men who have grown up and have been associated with the county, and with its peculiarly interesting history for over half a century, have a right to be represented. They have always been represented since 1867. They have not varied very much in their population. There was no harm to be done by allowing them to go on as they were while there is a great deal of injury to be done by making this change. My right hon. friend pointed to the conditions that exist in my own county. There we have eight or nine coal mines in the centre of the county.
The farmers and fishermen of my county do business with these coal mines. They

sell their produce to them and their sons go and work in these industries. But the man who lives at Isle Madame does not go to Glace Bay or Sydney to do business; he has far more interest in the constituency of my right hon. friend in the city of Halifax where he sells his fish and produce than in Glace Bay or Sydney. What harm was there to be done?

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: Is my hon. friend aware that between St. John county and Albert county there is not even a highway road?

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: Quite so.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: The only way to get there is to pass through two or three other counties or to go by boat along the coast.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Royal, as we shall have to call him after this-
Mr. FOWLER i Not yet.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
-knows very well the problem that had to be solved; he knows that Albert county was peculiarly isolated and there was nowhere else to put it. Once it was decided that Kings and Queens were to be put together and that Sunbury was to go with York, Albert was left stranded like a child without a father and because it was stranded it was taken into the constituency of the city and county of St. John. But that is not the condition in regard to Richmond. Albert had no separate entity, it was only the fifth wheel to the coach of Kings county. But Richmond has always had a separate entity. It has as many people as Brome and it has within two or three thousand as many as Argen-teuil which is represented by an important member of the Government. It is typical in our province of the same conditions as those which exist in Brome and Argenteuil in Quebec. Being representative of a minority in our province, both in race and religion, there was no justification for the Government making the proposition that it should be destroyed. Its connection with South Cape Breton is entirely anomalous and were it not for other conditions that exist, were it not for the aspirations of certain individuals in South Cape Breton, I venture to say that it would never have been suggested that this union should be made. That is the only reason it ever was suggested.
I regret that the deliberations of this committee, which, on the whole, have been fairly satisfactory, should be marred by this blot upon its record with regard to the


province of Nova Scotia. I opposed the settlement of this question along these lines in the committee, I oppose it now;
I say it is unfair to the constituency, that it is unfair to the minority in our province, and that it creates an anomaly which ought to be removed at the earliest possible day. I am sorry that the right hon. gentleman did not accept the proposition which we have made, because otherwise we would have been saved this debate, and my right hon. friend would have had the satisfaction of putting through a redistribution without any question being raised as to its fairness.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
It Was well known months ago that certain gentlemen in South Cape Breton, who failed of election either in South Cape Breton or Richmond, weTe predicting that there was a new deal in prospect whereby it was hoped that either one of them, and perhaps both, might be able to squeeze his way into Parliament. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) is, no doubt, quite innocent of any such undertaking as that which was entered upon by the gentlemen I speak of.	My hon. friend from Pictou (Mt.
Macdonald) has put the matter in a way that 'I will not attempt to put it in view of the lecture which was read to me by the hon.	member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) and the right hon. Prime Minister. Brome, a minority constituency, representing a minority race, is preserved in Quebec; Richmond, in the island of Cape Breton, a minority constituency, representing a minority race and religion, is wiped out. Does any person believe foT an instant that the Government would have done that if it were not for the fact that there are political exigencies to be taken into account; that there are in the island of Cape Breton men who have political ambitions, but who, up to the present time, have not had a sufficient public opinion behind them to enable them to secure a seat in Parliament?
Amendment (Mr. Kyte) negatived on division.
Prince Edward Island:

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
Would my right hon. friend the Prime Minister permit me to say a word about Prince Edward Island? Supposing that the Imperial Parliament passes the Act which we asked them to pass to-day, and the result of the passage of that Act would 'be to provide for the additional representation of Prince Edward
Island, what would be the condition? Whether there is to be a general election or not is entirely a matter within the knowledge of my hon. friends opposite, but there does not seem to be any reason why we should not provide in this Bill for the additional representation of Prince Edward Island immediately upon the Imperial Act passing. I would, therefore, propose to amend the clause by adding at the end of the section relating to Prince Edward Island the following:
Provided, that if the British North America Act, 1867, should be amended by the Parliament of the United Kingdom, in accordance with the address of both Houses of Parliament of Canada in that behalf, passed at the present session, immediately upon the Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom amending the said British North America Act, 1867, in accordance with such address coming into force, there shall be in the province of Prince Edward Island three electoral districts defined as follows:
(1)	The county of Kings shall form and constitute the electoral district of Kings and shall return one member.
(2)	The county of Prince shall form and constitute the electoral district of Prince and shall return one member.
(3)	The county of Queens shall form and constitute the electoral district of Queens and shall return two members.
That would provide for the existing condition of things immediately upon the Imperial Act coming into force. I see no reason why it should not be done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: And save legislation next year. Perhaps my hon. friend will let it stand and have the Bill read the third time to-night, and I will consult with the Minister of Justice in regard to the matter. I do not see any objection to the proposal; it seems to me rather appropriate. I do not know whether my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island has considered it or not.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: I was not sure whether the resolution would pass in the Senate, where it now is; and if it did not, I supposed that the Bill would pass as it is, and that the amendment, if it were necessary to move it, would require to be moved to-morrow on the third reading. That is the reason I did not move it to-night. I had the matter in mind, but did not consider this the proper time to move my amendment.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: I consulted with the right hon. the leader of the Opposition before he went away, and he was desirous of facilitating the passage of the Bill after this controversial subject was discussed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: This will only take a moment if it is dealt with in the morning, and therefore it can stand.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
I would like to turn to the Ontario schedule, section 2, in regard to the county of Carleton. I heg to move:
That in section 2, line 3, after the words ' district of Ottawa ' the words ' Rideau ward of the said city and of the townships of Gloucester and Osgoode ' be inserted.
The reason I am asking that Rideau ward be put in there is on account of an amendment moved to-night to put Rideau ward into the county of Russell.
Amendment agreed to.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
I would like to draw attention to section 4 of the Bill, which reads:
Every town, village, township or place-
This does not include cities. Taking that section into consideration and referring to the districts in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta which have cities in their electoral districts not mentioned in the descriptions, for instance, the electoral district of Brandon which has the city of Brandon in the electoral district as described, I think it would be well to insert the word ' city ' after the word * every ' in the section.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext: I should think it would be necessary if there is any such case. I presume the reason it was not included before was that at that time there were no cities included within the electoral districts.

maintopic: COMMON8
speechtext:
Yes, there are very few cities in the East included in the electoral districts, but in the West there are small towns that we call cities included. That obtains in my constituency and in several constituencies in Saskatchewan. I would therefore move:
That the word 'city' be inserted after the word ' every ' in section 4.

Amendment agreed to.
Progress reported.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: The House proceeded to consider the amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 147, to amend the Post Office Act.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their Honours that this House doth agree to the amendment made by the Senate to the Bill No. 147, an Act to amend the Post Office Act, with an amendment as follows: Strike out the words * and shall not take effect 
until so revised or ratified,' at the end of said amendment, for the following reason:
Because these words would have the effect of preventing the Post Office Department from collecting postage.
And as a consequential amendment the words * one cent ' be inserted in the blank between the words ' exceed ' and ' for.'

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I would like to ask my hon. friend the Postmaster General if toe has consulted the press associations about this amendment which he suggests, because I am informed that the press is satisfied, only with the proviso that the Bill shall not take effect until so revised or ratified; that is, as to the rates. In other words, the press would like to be under the control of Parliament as regards the rates, whilst the contention of my hon. friend is that he should have that control, that is, the Treasury Board.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That is the way it is intended.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is too late to discuss this matter, but I simply state that, as the press is most affected regard should be had to their objection, and my hon. friend should not object to maintaining the old order of things. The rates have always been under the control of Parliament. Why should my hon. friend appropriate to himself the right to dictate the rates, without Parliament having its say? It seems to me an extraordinary power, and I make the objection on behalf of the Associated Press. My hon. friend may not perhaps succeed in convincing the Senate; at all events, he is taking a risk.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It would be too bad to see this Bill fall through. It provides for an increase in salaries for the railway mail clerks, and I take the view that the Senate has no right to amend what is a money Bill. They proposed an amendment to which I agreed, and after they had voted that amendment it came down, and the gentlemen of the press asked us for further concessions, which we consented to. When the Bill went back to the Senate, the Senate went back upon its first amendment. I understand that there is some desire that this should be made right, and I am moving that a message be sent to the Senate for that purpose.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I understand that the sections of the Bill affecting the railway mail clerks could very well stay, if this agreement is lost between my hon. friend and the Upper House. There is no connection between an increase of salaries and the rates of postage.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is a money Bill and the Senate has no right to amend a money Bill.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No objection has been taken there.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: But it was over-ruled. At all events, I wish to state that the only objection to the Bill is that my hon. friend assumes powers which until now have always belonged to Parliament-Otherwise there is no objection to the Bill.
Motion agreed to.

maintopic: MONTREAL HARBOUR COMMISSION.

speechtext: The House proceeded to consider the amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 221, to amend the Montreal Harbour Commissioners' Act, 1894.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MONTREAL HARBOUR COMMISSION.
speechtext: This is an amendment the effect of which is to provide that certain property of the Montreal Harbour Commissioners not within the limits of the harbour shall remain as it is at present, so that there may be jurisdiction exercised by the city of Montreal in respect to taxation, as I understand.

Amendment agreed to.
On motion of Mr. Borden, the House adjourned at 2.55 a.m. Friday.
Friday, June 12, 1914.
